sens: Make sharp, hone
Be sharpened, be sharp
Figuratively, be keen, be alert
H2300A.detail:
1. Make sharp, hone: this is the action of polishing and sharpening a blade to make it cutting. Ezekiel describes the divine sword prepared for battle: "It is sharpened, it is polished" (Ezekiel 21:14-16), a sword that is honed to be formidable in the hand of the one who strikes.
2. Be sharpened, be sharp: this is the state of a blade that has been worked on and is ready for combat. The text repeats that the sword is "sharpened, the sword, it is polished, to arm the hand of the one who slaughters": it is ready, keen, effective.
3. Be keen, be alert: the word also applies to living beings to express liveliness and agility. In Habakkuk 1:8, the horses of the enemies are described as "swift" like evening wolves, highlighting their speed and vigilance in battle.
H2300A.origine: The verb חָדַד comes from a root that evokes sharpness and acuity. The word is related to the idea of a sharp point and mental liveliness. In the Old Testament, it first applies to sharp objects (the sword, the arrow), then figuratively to promptness and agility of living beings.
H2300A.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in two prophetic passages. Ezekiel uses it three times (21:14, 21:15, 21:16) to describe the sword that God sharpens in judgment against Jerusalem; the prophet repeats the word as a mark of terror and certainty — the weapon is ready, relentless. Once in Habakkuk 1:8, the word shifts from the concrete to the vivid image: the horses of the Chaldeans are not "sharpened" but "swift," as if the same idea of sharpness becomes the speed of a prey creature. The meaning thus oscillates between material sharpening and liveliness.
H2300A.portee: This word reminds us that God's word of judgment is like a refined weapon, ready and formidable. For the believer, it also evokes the importance of having a keen and vigilant spirit in the face of spiritual threats, like the warrior who carefully prepares his weapon. The image underscores the effectiveness of what God prepares — nothing is left to chance.

sens: Make sharp, give an edge to a tool or weapon
Excite, stir up a feeling or reaction in someone
H2300B.detail:
1. Make sharp, give an edge to a tool or weapon: the verb describes the action of passing a stone or metal over a blade to make it capable of cutting. It is a practical, concrete task. In Proverbs 27:17, the image of iron sharpening iron illustrates how one person can develop another's skills through friction, confrontation, mutual exchange.
2. Excite, stir up a feeling or reaction: by extension, the same movement of stimulation or provocation applies to emotions. In the same verse, "exciting a man's anger" shows how one can rekindle or intensify an emotion in someone, just as one sharpens a blade. The contact between two people can sharpen either wisdom or anger.
H2300B.origine: The root חָדַה evokes the idea of becoming pointed, sharp, acute. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words related to sharpness and acuity. The verb is used literally for tools and figuratively for feelings, following the same principle: an action that creates or intensifies sharpness, liveliness.
H2300B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 27:17. In this context of wisdom, it plays on a double image: first that of iron sharpening iron (concrete, practical sense), then that of a man exciting another's anger (figurative, emotional sense). This proximity between the two meanings shows that the Bible often resorts to material images to illuminate the life of feelings and relationships.
H2300B.portee: This word reminds us that our words and actions carry weight: they sharpen or dull another's ability to react and grow. Just as iron sharpens iron through friction, our interactions with others transform them. It is a call to discern whether we are sharpening wisdom or stirring up anger — that is, whether we contribute to growth or destruction.

sens: son of Ishmael, Arab ancestor
H2301.detail: 1. Hadad is one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, listed among the descendants of Abraham's son. He appears in the genealogy of Ishmael in Genesis 25:15, where he is mentioned alongside his brothers Nebaioth, Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedmah. These sons of Ishmael are the ancestors of the Arab peoples who played an important role in the history of the ancient Near East (Genesis 25:15 and 1 Chronicles 1:30).
H2301.origine: The name Hadad means "mighty" in Hebrew. It shares a common root with other Hebrew words evoking strength and power. In the Bible, this name also appears as that of pagan deities of fertility worshipped in Syria and Phoenicia, but here it simply designates a man, son of Ishmael, without connection to these cults. It is an ancient Arab family name.
H2301.emploi: Hadad appears twice in the Bible, both in genealogies of the sons of Ishmael: in Genesis 25:15 and in 1 Chronicles 1:30. These two passages list the same twelve sons of Ishmael, ancestors of the Arab tribes. Hadad bears the nickname or title "Hadad" which appears without additional narrative context — he is simply named as one of the important sons of the one who became the father of the Arab peoples.

sens: Experience joy, gladness
Make someone happy, give joy to someone
H2302.detail:
1. Experience joy, gladness: this is to feel a deep and manifest satisfaction. In Exodus 18:9, Jethro "rejoiced" upon learning how God delivered Israel from the Egyptians — he expresses authentic joy at the good that God has done. It is the cry of a happy heart before God's action.
2. Make someone happy, give joy to someone: this is to produce this gladness in another person through an action or word. Psalm 21:7 expresses it this way: the Lord "fills" the king "with joy in your presence," meaning He fills his heart with happiness and satisfaction through His benevolent presence.
H2302.origine: The verb חָדָה comes from a root that expresses the fundamental idea of "becoming lively, flourishing." It is related to the image of something that springs forth, illuminates, or comes back to life. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms that depict the movements of the joyful soul. In Hebrew, this joy is often linked to the recognition of a divine intervention — to rejoice is also to celebrate what God has done.
H2302.emploi: The verb חָדָה appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 18:9, Jethro rejoices at a deliverance — it is the joy of one who recognizes God's work. Psalm 21:7 uses it to describe how God fills with joy the one He blesses, transforming a person's destiny. Job 3:6 offers a more difficult usage where the word seems to have taken on a particular nuance in this context of suffering. The three attestations show that biblical rejoicing is always linked to an external cause — divine action, deliverance, blessing — and never a mere state of euphoria.
H2302.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that true joy comes from recognizing God's work in one's life. It is not a superficial or fleeting joy, but a deep gladness that arises when one sees how God acts to save and bless. In rejoicing, like Jethro, the believer confesses that God is benevolent and faithful. And when God fills someone with joy, it is a sign of His favor and presence — a promise that whoever remains under His gaze will know happiness.

sens: Sharp and pointed part of an object
A sharp edge or protruding point
Image of something sharp, piercing, dangerous
H2303.detail:
1. A sharp point is a pointed and cutting part of an object, capable of piercing or injuring. In Job 41:21, the poet describes the sea monster Leviathan: under its belly are sharp points, like those of a harrow (an agricultural tool equipped with spikes) that it drags along the ground — in other words, protruding and sharp edges that can tear anything they touch.
2. More broadly, the word evokes what is sharp, cutting, or piercing: a sharp protrusion, a keen edge. This image makes the monster terribly formidable and insurmountable for man.
H2303.origine: The Hebrew word חַדּוּד (chadoud) comes from the root חדד (hadad), which means "to sharpen, to hone." This root expresses the action of making something pointed and cutting. The noun חַדּוּד thus designates what has been sharpened: a point, a sharp edge. The same root is the origin of חַרְבָּה (harba), which means "sword" — the quintessential instrument that must be sharp to cut.
H2303.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 41:21. It is a poetic description of Leviathan, the monstrous and untamable creature that God speaks of to Job to show the limits of human wisdom. The context is God's challenge to Job: can he dominate such a fearsome creature bristling with sharp points? The word reinforces the image of the monster's invulnerability and danger.
H2303.portee: This passage teaches the reader that certain creatures and forces in the world exceed our control and understanding. The sharp points of Leviathan symbolize everything that resists and injures us when we pretend to master what belongs only to God. It invites humility before the Creator and His creation.

sens: State of inner satisfaction and happiness
Exultation, delight in what pleases
Contentment and strength that come from God
H2304.detail:
1. Joy is primarily an inner state of satisfaction and contentment: it is the feeling of well-being experienced in the presence of what pleases or fulfills us. In 1 Chronicles 16:27, joy dwells in the house of God, like strength and majesty: it is an atmosphere of happiness that fills a place.
2. Joy is a manifest exultation, a celebration of the whole being. It is expressed through celebration, feasting, singing, and meals; it is a joy that is lived together and shared.
3. Joy is above all a gift from God, a strength that supports the heart and enables one to endure trials. In Nehemiah 8:10, it is precisely "the joy of the Lord" that becomes your strength: it is not a fleeting emotion, but a deep rooting in trust in God.
H2304.origine: The Hebrew word חֶדְוָה (ched.vah) expresses joy and exultation, particularly in religious and festive contexts. It is related to the idea of rejoicing and celebration. Aramaic uses the same root, showing that this notion was common among the peoples of the Levant. Joy in the Bible is never mere amusement: it is often linked to the action of God or obedience to Him.
H2304.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible (1 Chronicles and Nehemiah), both in contexts of praise and religious celebration. In these two passages, joy is associated with the presence of God or His action: it is the joy of His dwelling and the joy that the Lord gives to His people. It is not a superficial or selfish joy, but a deep, communal rejoicing rooted in the relationship with God. The two uses show that biblical joy accompanies the recognition of God and the gathering of the people to celebrate together.
H2304.portee: For the Christian, this entry reminds us that true joy does not come from circumstances or possessions, but from the presence of God and His faithfulness to us. In Nehemiah 8:10, the message is particularly strong: it is by entrusting ourselves to God, renouncing affliction, that we find the strength to live. The joy of the Lord is presented as a resource, a power capable of transforming and sustaining us daily.

sens: Exultation, contentment of the heart
External and communal manifestation of this contentment
Rejoicing linked to a happy event
H2305.detail:
1. Joy is primarily an inner state: a deep contentment, an exultation of the heart that fills the person. It is the opposite of sadness and discouragement.
2. Joy manifests outwardly, often visibly and collectively. When the children of Israel return from captivity and complete the temple, they "dedicated the house of God with joy" (Ezra 6:16): their joy is a public act, a celebration they perform together, with feasts and sacrifices.
3. This joy arises in response to God's acts and His blessings — liberation, reconstruction, restoration. It responds to grace received and transforms the present moment into celebration.
H2305.origine: The Hebrew word חֶדְוָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of satisfaction, pleasure, and gaiety. In Aramaic, the form חֲדוָה retains the same meaning and nuance. This biblical joy is not a superficial lightness: it is the fruit of God's action in history and in the heart of His people. It stands in contrast to the tears of exile and captivity.
H2305.emploi: The word appears only once in Aramaic in the Bible, in Ezra 6:16, at the moment when the Jews returning from Babylonian captivity complete the reconstruction of the temple. It is a moment of grace: after decades away from Jerusalem, they can finally celebrate worship in the restored house of God. The joy here is not only personal and religious but also communal and cultic — it is expressed through feasts, sacrifices, and solemn dedication. It is the joy of a people who see their prayers answered.
H2305.portee: This scene of return teaches the reader that after trial and discipline, God restores and reinstates joy. Biblical joy is not superficial or selfish: it springs forth when friendship with God is restored and worship can resume. It also calls the believer to visibly and communally celebrate God's acts in their own life.

sens: The front part of the human body, between the neck and the abdomen
By extension, the seat of feelings and inner life
H2306.detail:
1. The chest refers to the front part of the rib cage, between the neck and the abdomen — literally the area of the physical chest. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision in Daniel 2:32, the colossal statue has a chest and arms of silver, representing a distinct and symbolic part of the body in the succession of empires.

2. Among the Hebrews and Arameans, the chest was also considered the seat of emotions and inner consciousness, like the heart — a second figurative sense that is less direct here but carries the biblical symbolism of the body as an expression of the inner being.
H2306.origine: The Aramaic word חֲדִי (chadi) is related to the Hebrew word חָזֶה (chazeh, "chest"), a term that comes from a root evoking the idea of seeing or looking forward — the chest being the front part of the body exposed to view. This root conveys the image of the visible body, turned outward.
H2306.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:32, a text written in Aramaic. It describes the chest of gold, silver, and bronze of the giant statue that King Nebuchadnezzar sees in a dream. This passage is a prophetic vision where each part of the body represents an empire — the chest and arms of silver symbolizing the second empire (the Medo-Persian empire). The word is used in a literal and bodily sense, but in a highly symbolic context.
H2306.portee: This vision reminds the reader that the Bible speaks of the body in a concrete and embodied way, not abstractly. The detailed description of the statue — head, chest, belly, thighs, feet — emphasizes that biblical prophecy is rooted in visible reality. For the Christian, this reinforces the certainty that God ordains the history of empires and that His Word is fulfilled in the facts of the world.

sens: City of the tribe of Benjamin in ancient Israel
H2307.detail: Hadid is a fortified city in the territory of Benjamin, mentioned during the return from exile. It appears in the population lists after the Babylonian captivity: in Ezra 2:33 and Nehemiah 7:37, it is listed among the cities whose inhabitants returned, alongside Lod and Ono. In Nehemiah 11:34, it is mentioned again among the localities where the exiles settled upon their return. Its name means "sharp" or "pointed," possibly evoking its terrain or strategic position.
H2307.origine: The name Hadid means "sharp" or "pointed" in Hebrew, deriving from a root that expresses sharpness. The city bore this geographical name which likely reflected a characteristic of the terrain or its fortress.
H2307.emploi: Hadid is mentioned three times in the Bible, all in the records of the return from exile (Ezra and Nehemiah, 5th century B.C.). In Ezra 2:33, it appears in the list of families returning from captivity with a population of 725 inhabitants. Nehemiah 7:37 reports a very similar figure: 721 inhabitants. In Nehemiah 11:34, it is listed among the cities where the returning exiles resettled. The city was thus an important center of population in the tribe of Benjamin after the restoration of the kingdom of Judah.

sens: Stop an action, no longer continue what one was doing
Renounce doing something, abstain
Come to an end, disappear
Not accomplish, leave aside
H2308.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to stop an ongoing activity. When the men "ceased to build the city" of Babel (Genesis 11:8), they simply stopped their work. It is the interruption of an action that was taking place.

2. A related but more active meaning: to voluntarily renounce something, to choose not to continue. The prophet asks: "Should I renounce" going into battle (Judges 20:28), meaning to decide not to do it. It is less about suffering the stop than choosing it.

3. The sense of disappearance or natural end: an action or reality that comes to an end. "There will always be the poor" (Deuteronomy 15:11): poverty will never cease, it persists. A tree that is cut down "still produces shoots" (Job 14:7): it comes back to life, it does not cease to be alive.

4. A rarer usage: to not do, leave undone, omit. "Cease to do evil" (Isaiah 1:16) means abandon this practice, make it nonexistent.
H2308.origine: The Hebrew verb חָדַל (hadal) comes from a root that expresses the idea of stopping or discontinuity. The word originally evokes the image of something that interrupts or loses its momentum. In Hebrew, related words denote pause, rest, absence. It is a simple and concrete verb, very common in the Bible to describe both the stopping of an activity and the extinction of a state.
H2308.emploi: This verb appears 56 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Torah, historical books, and wisdom literature. It is used in three main contexts. First, the stopping of an action: ceasing to build (Genesis 11:8), to do evil (Isaiah 1:16), to fight or seek. Secondly, refusal or renunciation: "renouncing" an enterprise (1 Kings 22:6), "abstaining" from an action, refusing to continue. Finally, states that persist or cease: poverty that never ceases, youth that stops with age (Genesis 18:11). The context always determines whether the word expresses the stopping of a voluntary action, a suffered action, or simply the end of a state.
H2308.portee: For the biblical reader, this word invites examination of one's own actions: when should I cease, renounce, abstain? It is a verb of freedom and responsibility. It reminds us that obedience to God often involves not adding, but stopping, withdrawing from evil (as in Isaiah 1:16). It also invites recognition that some things have an end — youth, strength, and even our enterprises — and to accept these human limits wisely.

sens: The entirety of the living, the inhabitants of the earth
The sphere of human affairs and relationships
The stopping or end of something
H2309.detail:
1. The word denotes the entirety of the inhabitants and life on earth, the world of the living in contrast to death and the silence of the grave. In Isaiah 38:11, Hezekiah, facing death, exclaims that he will no longer see the Lord in the land of the living nor anyone among the inhabitants of the world, expressing the anguish of one who is about to disappear.
2. By extension, it is the sphere of activities, relationships, and daily life of humans with each other — what constitutes ordinary existence.
3. The word can also mean the stopping, cessation, or end of an activity, state, or existence — the underlying idea of cessation and rest.
H2309.origine: The Hebrew word is etymologically linked to the idea of ceasing, stopping, or coming to an end. Its root evokes the rest that occurs when something interrupts. Biblical usage directs it towards the concrete sense of the inhabited earth, the world of the living that death comes to cease or interrupt. It is through this link to the end and stopping that it has taken on the meaning of the entirety of the inhabitants and active life.
H2309.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 38:11, in the speech of King Hezekiah facing the deadly threat. The context clearly shows that it refers to the living inhabitants of the earth and active life on earth, in contrast to the silence and absence of the grave. Its unique usage in a moment of existential crisis underscores the importance of the world of the living for one who will be separated from it.
H2309.portee: This word reminds us that life on earth, with its human relationships and activities, is a precious and limited good. For the believer facing death, it invites recognition of the real loss of this world, but also to place hope in God who can, as for Hezekiah, prolong life and restore to the dying their years in this land of the living.

sens: That which is weak, without solidity, that can break or collapse
One who abstains or refrains from doing something
That which passes quickly, which does not last
H2310.detail:
1. The word first evokes what lacks strength or consistency. When the psalmist says in Psalm 39:5 that he is "fragile," he contemplates the brevity and fragility of his human life in the face of God's eternity — what was once a solid edifice proves to be dust.

2. The word can also refer to one who abstains or renounces action. In Isaiah 53:3, the suffering Servant is "despised" by men: he no longer counts for them, they turn away, they cease to look at him and honor him, as if he no longer existed.

3. Finally, the word expresses the idea of the fleeting and the transitory: what disappears, what ceases. In Ezekiel 3:27, "not listening" amounts to closing off, abandoning listening — an action that one lets drop, that one refuses to pursue.
H2310.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to cease, stop, abstain." It evokes a force that stops, a movement that interrupts. The verb appears in several forms: one who "ceases" to act, that which "stops" or "dies out." The basic image is thus the movement that interrupts, the solidity that dissipates.
H2310.emploi: The word appears three times in the Louis Segond translation. In Psalm 39:5, it qualifies the inherent fragility of human life. In Isaiah 53:3, it describes the Servant as rejected, abandoned by men who despise him. In Ezekiel 3:27, in a negative construction ("not listening"), it expresses the action of renouncing obedience or refusing to listen. Each usage underscores a form of cessation: the inevitable end, rejection or indifference, or the refusal to continue.
H2310.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize human fragility — not to discourage, but to turn towards the One who alone is stable and eternal. It also reminds of the reality of rejection and isolation of the suffering Servant, Christ, who bore the scorn of men. Finally, it poses a question of responsibility: will we refuse to listen to the word that God addresses to us, like this rebellious family?

sens: Man of Ephraim during the divided monarchy
father of Amasa
H2311.detail: Hadlaï is an Ephraimite from the 8th century BC, mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears as the father of Amasa, a leader of the sons of Ephraim who opposed the warriors returning from military campaign (2 Chronicles 28:12). His name literally means "rest of God" in Hebrew, reflecting trust in the divine power of the Lord.
H2311.origine: The name Hadlaï comes from Hebrew and means "rest of God" — a combination of the word for rest or cessation and the divine name. It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates a reference to God, which was common in ancient Israel to express the religious values of parents.
H2311.emploi: Hadlaï appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 28:12, where he is identified as the father of Amasa. The context places this mention during the reign of Ahaz in Judah, when Ephraim (the northern kingdom) had engaged in battle against Judah. Amasa, his son, is among the Ephraimite leaders who took a stand against the warriors returning from this campaign, demonstrating his involvement in the political and military affairs of the northern kingdom during this troubled time.

sens: Thorny plant with thorns or brambles
Obstacle or difficulty that opposes the path
Difficult or problematic situation
H2312.detail:
1. A wild plant covered with thorns or brambles — a hostile bush that stands in the way and makes it difficult to pass. In Proverbs 15:19, the way of the sluggard is described as "like a hedge of thorns," an image of the difficulties and obstacles that the sluggard creates for himself.
2. Figuratively, anything that poses an obstacle or makes progress laborious — it is the image of evil or sin that complicates life. The sluggard encounters "thorns" while the righteous man walks a "level" path.
3. More broadly, a thorny situation or person, difficult to manage, as in Micah 7:4 where "the best of them is like a thornbush" — even the best is complicated, irritating, impossible to grasp without getting hurt.
H2312.origine: The Hebrew word חֵדֶק (chedeq) literally refers to a thorny plant, a thornbush. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of prick or irritation. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms for harmful or hostile plants, such as קוֹץ (kotz, thorn) or שִׁיט (shit, acacia). The image is that of a natural barrier that wounds and slows down.
H2312.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the poetic and wisdom books. In Proverbs 15:19, the thorn symbolizes the difficulties that the sluggard brings upon himself through his laziness — the path of inertia is strewn with obstacles. In Micah 7:4, the prophet uses it to describe the moral corruption of his time: even the best men are thorny, impossible to approach without risk. These two occurrences show how the word shifts from the concrete (the plant) to the figurative (the moral or social obstacle).
H2312.portee: This word reminds us that sin, laziness, or injustice do not open a smooth path, but rather litter the surface with thorns — they wound those who come near. It invites us to choose righteousness and diligence, which smooth the path. It is a biblical invitation to flee from what is thorny, difficult to endure, and to seek what is clear and right.

sens: River flowing east of Assyria, identified with the modern Tigris
River along which Daniel received a heavenly vision
H2313.detail:
1. Hiddékel is one of the four rivers of the garden of Eden described in Genesis 2:14. It is the one that "flows east of Assyria," and its name literally means "swift," a vivid description of this rushing water. Ancient and modern geographers identify it with the Tigris, one of the two great rivers of Mesopotamia.
2. In Daniel 10:4, the prophet Daniel stood by this great river when he received a transcendent vision of the Lord; this context underscores the religious and historical significance of the place, a location both real and marked by divine intervention.
H2313.origine: The name Hiddékel comes from a Semitic root meaning "swift" or "quick," an image that captures well the tumultuous nature of the Tigris compared to the calmer Euphrates. The Hebrew word retains this sense of swift movement. In Greek, this river is called the Tigris, from which our French name "Tigre" comes.
H2313.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible: first in Genesis 2:14, where it is presented as one of the four rivers flowing out of the garden of Eden, and then in Daniel 10:4, where the prophet is by this river at the time of a divine vision. Both uses describe it as a concrete geographical reality, although in the second case it is associated with a major spiritual experience. This real river serves as a setting or boundary for the world of salvation: a source of life and fertility at the beginning, a place of prophetic revelation during the time of pagan empires.
H2313.portee: For the believer, Hiddékel reminds us that the God of salvation has not withdrawn from the real world, even after the fall; He reveals Himself in concrete and historical places. Daniel's presence by the Hiddékel shows that God speaks to His prophets in the very heart of the world of nations, where human powers reign.

sens: To encircle or enclose something on all sides
To pursue relentlessly, inevitably
H2314.detail:
1. To surround means to place around, to encircle on all sides — like an army encircling a city or a net enclosing game. In Ezekiel 21:19, the sword of slaughter "surrounds" the enemies: it encircles them, pursuing them from all sides, no one escapes.
2. By extension, the word evokes an inescapable pursuit, a fate that closes in on someone. The image remains that of encirclement, but in a figurative sense: one cannot escape what surrounds them.
H2314.origine: The root חדר comes from a primary image of enclosing or encircling on all sides. In Hebrew, it can also refer to an inner chamber, a closed space — the idea of being confined, limited by a fence. The verb expresses the action of establishing this enclosure around something.
H2314.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved biblical text, in Ezekiel 21:19. It designates the sword of divine judgment that "surrounds" or "encircles" the enemies. In this prophetic context, the sword is not just a simple instrument of war: it is the instrument of God's judgment, and its action of surrounding expresses the inevitability and universality of punishment — no one can escape it.
H2314.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's judgment is not a distant threat: it surrounds, envelops, pursues. For the attentive reader, this teaches that God does not strike randomly, but inevitably reaches His goal. It is also an exhortation to fear the Lord and seek His grace rather than live under the weight of this judgment.

sens: Living space or enclosed area in a house
Place of refuge or intimacy
Interior space of a building or structure
What is hidden, secret, or internal
H2315.detail:
1. A room is primarily a closed space in a house, an area where one withdraws. When Joseph "hurried into a room" (Genesis 43:30), he sought solitude to weep in peace. It is also the space where people sleep: Delilah calls Samson "into a room" (Judges 16:9) where she captures him.
2. The room is a place of refuge and intimacy, as when Queen Athaliah hides the young king Joash "in a room" of the temple (2 Chronicles 22:11) to save him from death. It is the place where one seeks safety.
3. In large buildings, a room refers to the various spaces and compartments: Solomon's temple includes "inner rooms," "upper rooms," and "treasury rooms" (1 Chronicles 28:11). It is the subdivision of a structure.
4. Figuratively, the word describes what is hidden, internal, secret. The frogs fill "even the rooms of the kings" of Egypt (Psalms 105:30), meaning even the most remote spaces. The thoughts of the heart are compared to rooms: "the spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all the innermost parts" (Proverbs 20:27). It is also the image of what is deep, intimate, and inaccessible.
H2315.origine: The Hebrew word חֶדֶר comes from a root meaning "to penetrate" or "to enter." The basic image is that of a closed space, the inside, what is within and remote. The root evokes the idea of withdrawing, sinking into a place. This word is also used for compartments of religious structures and the secret spaces of the human heart.
H2315.emploi: The word room appears 33 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in narratives and wisdom literature. In narratives (Genesis, Judges, Kings), it refers to ordinary spaces where one withdraws (Genesis 43:30, Judges 16:9) or hiding places for protection (2 Chronicles 22:11). In descriptions of the temple and palace, it enumerates the different rooms: upper rooms, treasury rooms, inner rooms (1 Chronicles 28:11). In Proverbs and Psalms, the word takes on a figurative tone: it symbolizes secrets (Proverbs 7:27, Ecclesiastes 10:20) and the innermost parts of the heart (Proverbs 20:27). Ben-Hadad escapes by going "from room to room" (1 Kings 20:30), an image of fleeing through the rooms of a city. The meaning remains constant: a closed, internal space, often related to secrecy or refuge.
H2315.portee: Meditating on the "room" invites us to recognize that there are intimate spaces — of the heart or life — that only God sees. Jesus teaches to pray "in your room, with the door shut" (Matthew 6:6), showing that intimacy with God is possible in secret. The word also reminds us that our most hidden thoughts and deepest intentions are never hidden from God: He searches the rooms of the heart.

sens: Ancient city of Syria, probably in Phoenicia or present-day Lebanon
H2317.detail: Hadrac is a city in Syria mentioned only once in the Bible, in the prophecy of Zechariah which announces divine judgment against various regions of the Levant. Its exact location remains uncertain, but it was likely situated in the territory of Phoenicia or present-day Lebanon at the time of the prophet.
H2317.origine: The name literally means "dwelling" or "habitation" (root thought to be related to the idea of residence). It was a known Syrian city from antiquity, although few details have survived in biblical texts.
H2317.emploi: Zechariah mentions Hadrac in Zechariah 9:1 as the starting point of the prophetic word of the Lord, alongside Damascus and other cities of the Levant. This unique biblical mention is part of an oracle that describes divine judgment extending over the enemy territories of Israel. The city serves as a geographical marker to situate God's action against the nations.

sens: Make new what was old or worn
Repair or restore a building, a structure
Rejuvenate or regenerate the soul, the spirit
Restart, relaunch an action or a covenant
Produce or create anew
H2318.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to make new: to take something old or damaged and make it as it was at the beginning. It is the image of the craftsman who rejuvenates a work damaged by time. For example: in Psalms 103:5, God "renews" the youth of the believer, restoring vigor and vitality to him.
2. To repair or restore a building means to put it back in order after it has suffered damage. In 2 Chronicles 24:4, King Joash decides to "repair" the house of the Lord, which had remained damaged. It is a concrete work of reconstruction.
3. To renew the spirit or heart means that God regenerates the inner person. In Psalms 51:12, the psalmist asks God to create in him a clean heart and to "renew" a right spirit within him — it is a profound moral and spiritual transformation.
4. To confirm or relaunch means to take something that already exists and affirm it again. In 1 Samuel 11:14, they come to "confirm" Saul's kingship, that is, to solemnly reaffirm it.
5. To produce or create anew: in Psalms 104:30, the Spirit of the Lord "renews" the face of the earth, constantly generating new life.
H2318.origine: The Hebrew word חָדַשׁ (chadash) comes from a root that literally means "to be new," "to be young." It describes the state of what has just been born or made. The adjective חָדָשׁ (hadash, "new") is also found in other biblical passages. The verb can be used in a form that means "to renew oneself," the inside transforming through divine grace.
H2318.emploi: This Hebrew verb appears about ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Chronicles, and the Prophets. It is used to describe both material renewal (repairing a temple, restoring an altar) and spiritual renewal (transforming the believer's heart). With a concrete object (temple, altar, house), it clearly means "to repair." Applied to man or spirit, it takes on an inner and regenerative dimension. The context often determines the nuance: in a political setting (1 Samuel 11:14), it is more likely to mean "to confirm"; in a divine context (Psalms 51:12), it means "to transform from within."
H2318.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer: it reveals that God never abandons us to the wear of time. The renewal He offers is not cosmetic — it is a deep restoration, capable of rejuvenating our strength, purifying our hearts, and making us able to serve Him again. It is a promise of hope for those who feel weary or failing.

sens: that has just been made, that is recent
that has not yet been used
that is new in relation to what existed before
H2319G.detail: 1. This word designates what has just been built, manufactured, or created recently: the new door of the temple in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 26:10 and 36:10) is a door that has just been constructed or restored, in contrast to the old doors. 2. It also applies to anything that has not yet been used or worn: a new garment, a new jug that has not yet been used. 3. More broadly, it qualifies what is new, distinct from what existed before, contrasting with the old or worn out.
H2319G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be new, to become new." It is related to words in the same family that express novelty or youth. In Hebrew, it regularly opposes the adjective "old" (עַתִּיק / yashān), marking a clear distinction between what is recent and what is worn by time.
H2319G.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the book of Jeremiah, to designate the new door of the temple. Jeremiah prophesies in front of this door, and it becomes a symbolic place where the people and leaders gather to hear the word of the Lord. Its use is concrete and localized: it refers to a geographical landmark at the temple, probably a door recently built or renovated that served as a passage or assembly point.
H2319G.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that renewal is possible: the temple itself is renewed by its new doors, just as the Lord renews His mercies every morning. It is a sign that God does not allow His sanctuary to fall into ruin, and that He can restore what is old.

sens: that has just been created, manufactured, or acquired, with no prior use
that did not exist before, never seen or known
that restarts, that renews periodically
that is young, fresh, recent in time
H2319H.detail:
1. This sense describes what has just been made or obtained: a new cart just out of the workshop, a house that has just been built (2 Samuel 6:3: "They placed the ark of God on a new cart"). It is the object in its first condition, intact and never used.
2. This sense evokes what has never existed, what arises for the first time in history: a new king replacing the old regime (Exodus 1:8: "A new king arose over Egypt"), or new gods that past generations did not know (Deuteronomy 32:17). The emphasis is on the break, the unexpected appearance.
3. This sense marks regular renovation: the new harvest that comes each year, the new covenant that God offers to His people (Jeremiah 31:31). It is the resumption of a cycle, the periodic renewal.
4. This sense emphasizes freshness, youth: as when the glory of the righteous "will flourish continually" (Job 29:20), regaining new vigor. The image is that of life returning, of what is revived.
H2319H.origine: This Hebrew root expresses the idea of change and renewal. It is linked to the notion of "new" in the broadest sense: what appears, what restarts. The root refers to the concrete experience of time passing and things transforming. In Aramaic, the parallel form is חֲדַת (hadat), used in the same contexts.
H2319H.emploi: This word appears 46 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives, psalms, and prophecies. In history, it designates what has just emerged: a new king (Exodus 1:8), a never hitched cart (2 Samuel 6:3), a freshly built house (Deuteronomy 20:5). In the psalms, it invites to sing "a new song" (Psalms 149:1; Psalms 33:3), expressing fresh praise and the renewal of the encounter with God. The prophets use it to announce unprecedented future realities: a new thing that God will do (Isaiah 43:19), new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17), a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31). Thus, it is a word filled with messianic hope: it signifies the divine intervention that renews all things.
H2319H.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is not a prisoner of the past: He intervenes with freshness and power to create the new. The psalms invite to always new praise, never routine, in light of the Lord's inexhaustible faithfulness. And for those who hear the prophecies, the "new" speaks of a hopeful future: God who renews the heart (Ezekiel 36:26), who establishes a deeper new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31). The word thus nourishes trust in a creator and renovator God.

sens: A period of time equal to the duration of a new moon (about 29 or 30 days).
The first day of the month, when the moon becomes visible.
A division of the calendar, generally numbering twelve in a year.
Any duration, without precise reference to the moon.
H2320G.detail:
1. The Hebrew word chodesh primarily designates the lunar month, that is, the complete lunar cycle: it comes from the root meaning "new" or "new," as the month begins with the new moon. It is a natural unit of time based on the movement of the moon in the sky (Genesis 7:11: "the second month").

2. The first day of the month — when the moon reappears — was an important moment, sometimes marked specially in the religious calendar of Israel. In Numbers 28:11, offerings are prescribed for each new month.

3. The month fits into a year of twelve lunar cycles, thus forming the structure of the biblical calendar. The months had names (like the month of Nisan, in spring) and numbers (first, second, etc.), as seen in Ezra 10:16 ("the tenth month").

4. By extension, the word can simply designate a period of about thirty days, without particular emphasis on the moon: in Judges 19:2, the woman stays "for four months" with her father, which is a common measure of duration.
H2320G.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root hodash (חדש) which means "new." Each month begins with a new moon, hence the name. It is an ancient word, present in Semitic languages, based on a simple observation of the sky: the regular and visible cycle of the moon. The biblical calendar, like that of the entire ancient Near East, was lunar, and this unit was fundamental for measuring time.
H2320G.emploi: The word month appears 199 times in the Old Testament, especially in the narratives of Genesis and Exodus, as well as in the legislative texts of the books of Moses. It is used concretely to date events: Genesis reports the flood in the "second month" of Noah's life (7:11), and the exodus from Egypt occurs in the spring, in the first month (Exodus 12:2). The laws of Moses use it to set religious festivals: Passover in the first month, Pentecost seven weeks later, the Feast of Tabernacles in the seventh month (Leviticus 23). It is also encountered to measure a duration: "four months" (Judges 19:2), "one month old" (Numbers 3:28). It is a neutral and practical word, without particular religious connotation, that traverses all literary genres of Scripture.
H2320G.portee: Understanding the word month means grasping how the ancient Israelites measured time and situated themselves within the rhythm of the created world — the movement of the moon was visible, regular, and reliable. It also reveals that the biblical calendar was lunar, based on the observation of the sky, and that the major religious festivals coincided with this astronomical reality. For the modern reader, it is a reminder that the Bible anchors God's promises in real and measurable time.

sens: The time of the month when the moon reappears in the sky after its disappearance
The period of about thirty days that constitutes a division of the calendar
A feast day when Israel offered sacrifices to God at the time of the new moon
H2320H.detail:
1. The "new moon" is the precise moment when the moon becomes visible in the sky after several days of invisibility. This marked the beginning of the month in the Hebrew calendar. This concept is seen in 1 Samuel 20:18, where Jonathan tells David that tomorrow will be the new moon and that his absence will be noticed.

2. The "month" is the period of about thirty days that extends from one new moon to the next, forming a unit of the calendar. Exodus 19:1 speaks of the "third month" after the exodus from Egypt, showing how the Israelites counted time in months.

3. The "new moons" are also days of religious celebration when Israel offered burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord. According to 1 Chronicles 23:31, burnt offerings were continually offered "at the new moons and at the feasts." Isaiah 1:14 shows that God rejected these celebrations when they were merely empty formalities without heart conversion.
H2320H.origine: The Hebrew word חֹדֶשׁ (hodesh) comes from a root meaning "new": it literally designates the "new moon," which regularly returned each month. This same root has given rise to words expressing what is recent or renewed. In the Greek Bible, this word is translated by the Greek μήν (mên, "month") or by νουμηνία (noumenia, "new moon"), depending on whether the context emphasizes the period or the day of the new moon.
H2320H.emploi: The word hodesh appears 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily to designate the months of the calendar. It is found mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Chronicles), in the laws of Leviticus (notably regarding sacrifices), and among the prophets. In cultic passages (1 Chronicles 23:31, Ezekiel 46:1-6), "new moon" names the feast day when special sacrifices were offered. David and Jonathan also use this term to set appointments (1 Samuel 20:5, 18, 24, 27). Isaiah and Hosea criticize the Israelites who celebrated the new moons without true repentance (Isaiah 1:14, Hosea 2:13). The word can also simply designate a calendar period (Exodus 19:1).
H2320H.portee: For the believer, the month reminds us that time is marked by regular renewal and God's provision. That God established the moon to measure time shows His wisdom and order. The feast of the new moon invited Israel to gather for worship, but God reproaches when this celebration becomes empty of heart (Isaiah 1:14): what matters is not the rite itself, but the sincerity of the worship rendered.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Benjamin, wife of Shaharaim
H2321.detail: Hodesh is a woman of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time of the divided monarchy. She was the wife of Shaharaim and the mother of seven children: Jobab, Zibia, Meshah, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah (1 Chronicles 8:9). Her name literally means "new moon" in Hebrew, but she plays no particular role in the biblical narrative.
H2321.origine: The name Hodesh comes from Hebrew and means "new moon" (the first day of the lunar month in the Hebrew calendar). This name likely evokes an event or circumstance of her birth or life, according to a common custom of the time. It is a typical name from the ancient Near East, where names often carried symbolic or religious significance related to creation and the cycles of nature.
H2321.emploi: Hodesh appears only once in the biblical text, in 1 Chronicles 8:9, in a genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. She is simply identified as the wife of Shaharaim and the mother of his seven children. This passage is part of the genealogical list tracing the descendants of Benjamin and shows how this tribe was reconstituted and developed. Her mention alongside her husband highlights her role in the genealogical continuity of Israel.

sens: City of Lower Judah
H2322.detail: Zena is a city in the low region (the Shephelah) of the territory of Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe of Judah during the land distribution after the conquest of Canaan.
H2322.origine: The Hebrew name Hadashah literally means "new"; the name may evoke a newly built or repopulated city.
H2322.emploi: Zena appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:37, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the land among the tribes. This city was located in the coastal and agricultural region of the Shephelah, west of Jerusalem.

sens: That which has just been born, made, or has not been used
That which is recent, not old
That which replaces something worn out or old
H2323.detail:
1. The word "new" describes that which has just been born or made, and which has never been used: it is the state of something just out of production. In Ezra 6:4, the temple being rebuilt must have "a row of new wood," freshly cut and prepared, never used before.
2. Broadly, "new" applies to what is recent, what is not old: it designates novelty in relation to the passage of time.
3. By extension, "new" can qualify that which replaces something old, worn out, or outdated: that which takes the place of what was before.
H2323.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew root "hadash" (חָדָשׁ), which means "to renew" or "to be new." In the Bible, the same family of words also describes the new moons (the new month) or anything that is renewed. The Hebrew verb "hadash" paints the image of what is remade, rejuvenated, restored to new.
H2323.emploi: This word appears in the Hebrew and Aramaic Bible only in this unique passage of Ezra 6:4. It is used to describe the new wood that must be used in the construction of the temple after the return from exile. The adjective "new" emphasizes the quality of the material: this wood, recently prepared and never used, represents the restoration of the sacred edifice in its purity.
H2323.portee: This word reminds us that the restoration of the temple after the exile was not merely a repair of ruins, but a glorious reconstruction. God allowed His people to build with new, fresh material, symbolizing renewal and grace. For the believer, this speaks of God's ability to restore and renew what has been broken.

sens: to make known the meaning of something obscure or hidden
to clarify, interpret
to communicate information, reveal
to make manifest, show
H2324.detail:
1. To make known the meaning of something obscure or hidden: the word refers to the action of clarifying what is enigmatic or secret. In Daniel 2:4, the Chaldeans ask the king: "tell your servants the dream, and we will give the explanation," meaning they promise to reveal the hidden meaning of the mysterious dream.
2. To clarify, interpret: this means to provide understanding of something confusing or enigmatic. In Daniel 5:7, the king promises a reward to the one "who reads this writing and gives me the explanation," because the mysterious writing on the wall must be interpreted for its message to be understood.
3. To communicate information, reveal: to transfer knowledge from one person to another. In Daniel 2:27, Daniel says that this secret "the wise men are not able to reveal to the king," showing that "to explain" means to bring to light before someone what they do not know.
4. To make manifest, show: the action of making visible or evident. This aligns with the fundamental meaning: to clarify, to make appear what was hidden.
H2324.origine: The Hebrew verb חוה (havah) belongs to a family of words related to the idea of showing and manifesting. In biblical Aramaic (the language of the book of Daniel), it particularly expresses the action of making visible and understandable. The root evokes the idea of bringing to light, making appear what was in shadow. This verb is mainly used when it is necessary to explicate a mystery or an enigmatic word.
H2324.emploi: This verb appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the book of Daniel (chapters 2, 4, and 5), where it describes the interpretation of dreams and mysterious signs. In chapter 2, the wise men of Babylon are summoned to explain the king's dream; in chapter 5, it is the enigmatic writing on the wall that must be explained. The context is always one of necessary revelation: something obscure or hidden must be made clear and understandable. Daniel himself, guided by God, becomes the one who can accomplish this task. The word is thus used in a context of wisdom, divine revelation, and communication of a hidden truth.
H2324.portee: This verb reminds the reader that true wisdom is not merely knowing secrets, but having the power to reveal and interpret them. For the believer, it illustrates how only God can clarify the mysteries hidden from the wise of the world. Daniel embodies this dependence on God: he does not possess wisdom by himself, but through divine revelation, he can provide the explanation that others cannot give. It is a lesson on the true source of wisdom and spiritual illumination.

sens: to put someone or oneself at risk, in danger
to compromise the safety or life of someone
H2325.detail:
1. To put someone or oneself at risk, in danger. This is the idea of placing in a situation where misfortune, punishment, or death becomes probable. In Daniel 1:10, the chief of the eunuchs says to Daniel: "You would expose my head to the king" — meaning that if the young Hebrews appeared weaker than the others after eating differently, it would endanger the life of the chief, who could be executed by the king for this outcome.
2. To compromise the safety or life of someone by making them responsible for a misfortune. The word emphasizes the idea of guilt and risk involved: one who exposes someone to danger makes them guilty in the eyes of the power that can punish them.
H2325.origine: The Hebrew root חוּב (chuv) carries the idea of being indebted or guilty, hence the meaning of being in danger or risking something. The verb in the Piel (causative) form means "to make guilty" or "to put in danger": one moves someone from a state of safety to that of peril.
H2325.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (in Daniel 1:10). It describes the fear of the chief of the eunuchs of Babylon: if the young Hebrew men, nourished differently according to their religious convictions, were found in worse health than the others, it would expose the chief to the judgment and punishment of the king. It is a term that concretely expresses the political and personal stakes of the captivity.
H2325.portee: This word reminds us that our refusal to compromise our religious convictions can affect those around us — and that faithfulness to God does not exclude seeking to avoid endangering those around us. It is a lesson in mutual responsibility: Daniel prays, but he also looks out for the safety of his superior.

sens: one who owes money or goods to someone
one who is obligated to a creditor
H2326.detail: 1. A debtor is someone who has incurred a debt: they have borrowed money or goods from another person and must repay them. In Ezekiel 18:7, the text mentions that the righteous man "returns the pledge to the debtor" — meaning he restores to the poor person who borrowed the item they had put up as collateral. 2. More broadly, the debtor is one who finds themselves in a position of moral or legal obligation to a creditor. It is the image of dependence and responsibility toward the one who has consented to give, often used in Scripture to speak of the debt of one who has received grace.
H2326.origine: The Hebrew word חוֹב (chov) literally means "what is due." It is related to the idea of obligation and debt. In biblical thought, the notion of debtor is situated within a social and moral framework: borrowing creates a relationship of dependence, and the law of Moses prescribed protections so that the debtor would not be crushed by their debt.
H2326.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible (in Ezekiel 18:7), in the context of describing a righteous man. The prophet lists the acts that characterize one who pleases God: he does not commit injustice, returns to the one who borrowed their pledge, gives to the poor, covers the naked. This verse is part of a moral reflection on social justice and equity in relationships between people, particularly toward the most vulnerable.
H2326.portee: This passage speaks to the dignity of the poor and the responsibility of the righteous. Returning the pledge of the debtor is to respect the human person and recognize their right to survival. For the Christian, it reminds us that true piety is not limited to our relationship with God, but is concretely expressed through mercy and equity toward our neighbor, especially those in financial distress.

sens: City north of Damascus
H2327.detail: Choba is a city located north of Damascus, toward present-day Lebanon. It is where Abraham pursued the kings who had plundered Sodom and taken his nephew Lot (Genesis 14:15).
H2327.origine: The name Choba means "hidden place" or "refuge." Its etymology evokes a secluded, out-of-the-way spot. Although the exact location remains debated among biblical geographers, the city was known in antiquity and marked a northern boundary of the region where Abraham was established.
H2327.emploi: Choba appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 14:15. It is mentioned as the limit point of Abraham's pursuit against the confederated kings who had kidnapped Lot. This brief mention shows that it was a geographical landmark known to the original biblical readers, marking the northern terminus of Abraham's campaign. It illustrates the extent of his authority and influence in the region.

sens: Draw or mark a curved line that returns to itself
Delimit an area by drawing a circular boundary
Surround or enclose something within a defined space
H2328.detail:
1. The word describes the physical action of drawing a closed curved line. It is the image of a tool or a hand drawing a complete circle. In Job 26:10, the author imagines God who "has traced a circle on the surface of the waters": it is as if the creator is drawing an invisible line to separate the calm waters from the area where light and darkness reign.

2. The word can also mean to set a limit or a boundary. When one traces a circle around something, one establishes a demarcation: what is inside and what is outside. This is why the circle appears as a line of separation — here between day and night, order and chaos.

3. More broadly, to trace a circle means to surround or enclose: the circle becomes a barrier, a protection, or a delimitation of space. The image evokes both precision (a perfect circle) and completeness (a closed shape).
H2328.origine: The Hebrew verb חוּג (chug) comes from the root חוג which expresses the idea of curving, bending, surrounding. The word designates the concrete action of tracing or marking a round shape. This same root is found in words related to circular movement and encirclement. The basic image is that of the gesture that creates a limit or a boundary by drawing a continuous curve.
H2328.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 26:10. It is a poetic passage where Job contemplates the wisdom and power of God in creation. God "traces a circle on the surface of the waters": it is an image of the delimitation of the universe, of the order established by the Creator. The context is cosmological — we see God mastering the elements and imposing clear boundaries between the known and the unknown, light and shadow.
H2328.portee: This word invites meditation on the creative power of God: by a simple and precise gesture, He establishes the order of the cosmos. For the reader, it is an image of divine sovereignty — God does not create randomly, He traces limits, distinguishes, organizes. This reassures us that the universe is not chaotic, but ordered by the One who holds everything in His hands.

sens: Round shape, line or surface without angles
Vault of heaven, firmament
Extent, domain or visible horizon
H2329.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a round geometric shape — a circle or circumference. In Proverbs 8:27, divine Wisdom says: "When He traced a circle on the surface of the deep," imagining the outline of the horizon or the surface of the primordial waters.
2. It also applies to the celestial vault, this arch of heaven that seems to overshadow the earth. In Job 22:14, the clouds "envelop" God who "only traverses the vault of heaven" — the word evokes the curved immensity of the firmament.
3. By extension, it designates the horizon or the land itself, what is visible and habitable. In Isaiah 40:22, the prophet proclaims that God "sits above the circle of the earth": the word paints the orb of the world inhabited by humans, tiny like grasshoppers.
H2329.origine: The Hebrew word chug comes from a root that evokes the idea of tracing, marking, delimiting. It is linked to the image of a line or curve that closes off a space. In the Hebrew Bible, it designates what has a roundable, circular shape, often in relation to great cosmic realities — the curved sky over the earth, the horizon that encircles our vision.
H2329.emploi: The word appears three times in Scripture. It is used in highly poetic and theological contexts, never for ordinary objects: twice to speak of the geometry of the sky and the created universe (Job 22:14 and Isaiah 40:22), and once to evoke the divine creative act of delimitation (Proverbs 8:27). Each occurrence emphasizes the greatness, order, and wisdom of the cosmos built by God.
H2329.portee: This word reminds the believer that the entire universe — its structure, its limit, its balance — is the work of divine Wisdom and God's omnipotence. It invites contemplation of creation, not as chaos, but as a harmonious, measured, and founded whole. For the reader, it is an invitation to humility and wonder in the face of the cosmic order that envelops us.

sens: State a riddle, a question difficult to decipher
Pose an intellectual challenge to someone by asking them to solve it
In a figurative sense: communicate a message or teaching in a veiled or symbolic form
H2330.detail:
1. The verb means to state a riddle, that is, to formulate an enigmatic question or statement awaiting deciphering. Samson does this literally in Judges 14:12: "I will propose a riddle to you." It is a play on words that requires cleverness to be understood.
2. Proposing a riddle is to launch a challenge: the one who states it bets that others will not find the answer. In Judges 14:13, the children of Israel accept Samson's wager: "Propose your riddle, and we will listen to it." The risk and stakes make the game captivating.
3. In a broader and spiritual sense, God asks the prophet Ezekiel to propose a riddle to Israel (Ezekiel 17:2), which means to communicate a message or teaching in a parabolic and veiled form, so that the people seeks to understand.
H2330.origine: The verb chud comes from a root that designates the act of proposing a wordplay or a cryptic question. Its basic image is that of the riddle as a mystery to be unraveled, something hidden that must be untangled. The word is close to the notion of riddle (khida in Hebrew, which is its corresponding noun), and reflects the ancient Semitic peoples' taste for riddles and enigmatic sayings as a form of teaching and entertainment.
H2330.emploi: The verb appears only 4 times in biblical Hebrew, always in situations where someone proposes a riddle to others. The most famous example is the story of Samson (Judges 14:12-16), where he proposes a riddle at the wedding feast, in a wordplay to test the intelligence of his companions. In a prophetic context, Ezekiel 17:2 uses the verb to ask the prophet to propose a riddle (or a parable) to the house of Israel, that is, to convey a divine message in a symbolic and mysterious form.
H2330.portee: This word shows us how the Bible uses the riddle and the parable, not only as entertainment but also as a means of divine revelation. Riddles force the listener to think, to seek, to exercise their intelligence: it is a way of respecting the reader by inviting them to participate in the discovery of meaning. For the believer, this reminds us that the Word of God can present itself in enigmatic or veiled forms, requiring active meditation and a sincere quest.

sens: To make known what one knows
To express one's thoughts or opinions
To transmit knowledge from one way to another
H2331.detail:
1. To make known what one knows: the verb denotes the action of revealing, bringing to light what was hidden or unknown. Eliphaz says to Job: "I will speak to you; listen to me! I will declare what I have seen" (Job 15:17), meaning he will declare a truth he has discovered.
2. To express one's thoughts or opinions: it also involves communicating one's convictions, personal views on a matter. Elihu hesitates at first because he is young, but he ultimately says: "I will also declare what I think" (Job 32:17), showing that he has something important to declare.
3. To transmit knowledge from one way to another: the psalmist speaks of a continuous transmission of knowledge: "Day to day pours forth speech, and night to night reveals knowledge" (Psalms 19:3), a poetic image of the silent declaration of divine glory that passes from generation to generation.
H2331.origine: The root חוה evokes the idea of showing, manifesting. It is related to Semitic roots that mean "to breathe" or "to speak"; the emphasis is on the act of making something evident, making it visible or audible. In Aramaic, the similar verb (חֲוָה) carries exactly this meaning: "to show, to make known." The biblical context confirms that it is a deliberate act of communication, not a mere enumeration.
H2331.emploi: The verb חָוָה (in the Piel form, which intensifies the action) appears six times in the Bible, all in the poetic or wisdom books: Job and Psalms. It is always used to express the act of speaking, recounting, or explaining something. In Job, the interlocutors use it to announce that they will share their thoughts or what they have understood (Job 15:17; 32:6, 10, 17; 36:2). In Psalm 19, it takes on a contemplative dimension: the heavens "declare" the glory of God in a silent yet eloquent manner (Psalms 19:3). The meaning remains stable: to communicate, to manifest, to put into words or signs what was unknown.
H2331.portee: This word teaches us that sharing what we have learned or discovered is a noble and necessary act. For the believer, it invites us not to keep the knowledge of God and His wisdom to ourselves, but to declare it to others, as the wise men of the Old Testament did. It is also an invitation to contemplate how God Himself "declares" His power and glory through His creation, in eloquent silence.

sens: The first woman, created by God and united to Adam
The mother of humankind
H2332.detail:
1. Eve is the first woman that God created, formed from a rib of Adam to be his helper and companion (Genesis 3:20). She is the woman with whom Adam shares life in the Garden of Eden before the fall.
2. She is the mother of all living, meaning all humanity descends from her and Adam. Her sons Cain, Abel, and Seth are the ancestors of all humans (Genesis 4:1). She is the first to conceive and give birth, realizing the divine gift of life.
H2332.origine: The name Eve means "life" or "living" in Hebrew. This name reflects her role as the mother of all living: she is the source of life for all humanity. Adam gives her this name precisely for this reason, as indicated in Genesis 3:20. It is a deeply symbolic name that summarizes her primordial vocation.
H2332.emploi: Eve appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 3:20 and 4:1. In the first passage, Adam names her Eve, recognizing that she will be the mother of all living. In the second, she conceives and bears Cain, concretely fulfilling this maternal role. Her story is inseparable from that of Adam and primordial humanity. The New Testament references her occasionally (notably 2 Corinthians 11:3 and 1 Timothy 2:13), but it is primarily through Genesis 3 and 4 that the reader knows her.
H2332.portee: Eve embodies the central place of women in God's design. She is created as Adam's equal, not as a servant, to stand by his side in managing the world. At the same time, Eve's story reminds every believer that they descend from her and share her humanity, marked by responsibility, motherhood or fatherhood, and the capacity to give life. Her name, "life," remains a promise: despite the fall, life continues to flow through human generations.

sens: Small human settlement, rural agglomeration
Group of dwellings dependent on a city or region
H2333.detail:
1. A borough is a small village or a cluster of houses, less significant than a fortified city but more structured than a simple encampment. The Hebrew word originally denotes grouped tents or semi-nomadic settlements. In the three biblical passages, the "boroughs of Jair" are villages conquered by Jair son of Manasseh in Transjordan (Numbers 32:41); these same boroughs are listed in the territorial divisions (Joshua 13:30; 1 Kings 4:13).
2. The borough can also refer to a group of dwellings administratively attached to a region or an urban center. In 1 Kings 4:13, the "boroughs of Jair" appear as villages under the control of a governor in a district of the Northern Kingdom.
H2333.origine: The Hebrew word chavvah (חַוָּה) literally means "enclosure" or "circular camp"; it comes from the root חוה which evokes the idea of enclosing or gathering. This word originally designates a community of grouped tents, and by extension, the villages that arose from them. The term contrasts with large fortified cities (יִר or עִיר) and isolated hamlets.
H2333.emploi: The word châvvah appears three times in the Bible, all in passages related to Transjordan. It always refers to the "boroughs of Jair," small agglomerations that this leader conquered and controlled (Numbers 32:41). These same settlements are then mentioned during the land distribution among the tribes of Israel (Joshua 13:30) and during the administrative organization of the Kingdom under Solomon (1 Kings 4:13), where they are listed among the tax districts. The word has a geographical and administrative significance rather than a narrative or theological value.
H2333.portee: This word reminds us that the people of Israel, once established in the promised land, had to organize space and establish structures for habitation and administration. The "boroughs of Jair" testify to a progressive and structured possession of the territory, far beyond mere nomadic occupation. This invites the reader to consider how God gives His people not only the land but also the ability to organize and govern it.

sens: Son of Manasseh, conqueror of villages in Transjordan
The boroughs he conquered and took his name from
H2334.detail:
1. Jair is a military leader, son of Manasseh, who conquered and governed villages east of the Jordan, in the region of Gilead and Bashan (Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14). He gave his name to these localities, which have remained famous under this designation.
2. The term "boroughs of Jair" refers to all the villages he conquered and organized under his authority. According to biblical sources, their number varies: 60 cities (1 Chronicles 2:23), 30 cities (Judges 10:4), or 23 cities according to some traditions. These boroughs formed a prosperous and fortified region in Transjordan.
H2334.origine: The name "Jair" literally means "he who enlightens" or "he who shines" (from the Hebrew root meaning "to shine"). The "boroughs of Jair" or "villages of Jair" are named after this leader who conquered and governed them. This type of naming, where a region bears the name of its conqueror, was common in antiquity.
H2334.emploi: The expression "Jair" or "boroughs of Jair" appears four times in the Bible, always in relation to this Transjordanian region. It first occurs during the initial conquest by Jair, son of Manasseh (Numbers 32:41), and is mentioned again in Deuteronomy 3:14 as an established possession. The book of Judges 10:4 recalls that thirty cities bore this name during the time of Judge Jair (a namesake descendant of the original conqueror). Finally, 1 Chronicles 2:23 documents the loss of these boroughs to the Geshurites and Syrians. The term symbolizes an important but fragile Israelite possession of Transjordan.

sens: Character who wrote a book about the life and repentance of King Manasseh
H2335.detail: Hozaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 33:19. He is the one who recorded the story of King Manasseh's prayer and how God answered him, including the account of his sins, his unfaithfulness, and his repentance. His name means "the one who sees" in Hebrew, suggesting that he was a seer or prophet. The biblical historian mentions that all these events in Manasseh's life are written in "the book of Hozaï," a work that has not been preserved in the canonical Bible but was an important source for the history of Israel.
H2335.origine: The name Hozaï comes from the Hebrew root חזה (chazah), which means "to see" or "to have a vision." This root designates one who has the ability to perceive spiritual realities. The seers of the Old Testament were often prophets who received visions from God. The term is related to the word חֹזֶה (choze), which also refers to a seer or prophet.
H2335.emploi: Hozaï appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 33:19. He is presented as the author of a historical book dealing with the life of King Manasseh of Judah. Manasseh was one of the most wicked kings of Israel, committing numerous sins and establishing idolatries, but he repented after being captured in Babylon. The book of Hozaï recounted his prayer, his repentance, and how God answered him. Although this writing is not included in the biblical canon, it bears witness to the significance of this remarkable conversion.
H2335.portee: The mention of Hozaï reminds the Christian reader that God preserves and values testimonies of repentance and spiritual transformation. The fact that the story of Manasseh—despite his deep sin—was deemed worthy of being written by a seer shows that God's grace is capable of restoring even the worst sinners. It is an encouragement for any believer struggling with their own past.

sens: Spiny plant with sharp points
Shrub or bush covered with thorns
Metal link or ring to restrain
Image of a despicable or insignificant person
H2336.detail:
1. The thorn is a plant equipped with sharp points or spines: it is a concrete botanical reality of the ancient Near East. Job wishes that thorns would grow instead of wheat in his field (Job 31:40), expressing a curse on his land.
2. The thorny bush refers to the entire bush, dense and impenetrable: the Israelites flee from Saul and hide in the bushes (1 Samuel 13:6), finding refuge in these thick thickets.
3. In metal, the word refers to an iron object that holds or pierces: the Assyrians bind Manasseh with chains (2 Chronicles 33:11), which includes chains and hooks; or the hook that would be thrust into the nostrils of Leviathan (Job 40:21), an image of domination.
4. In the fable of Joash, the king of Israel calls himself "the thorn of Lebanon" in comparison to the cedar, lofty and majestic: it is the insignificant thorn that pretends to equal the noble tree (2 Kings 14:9). The thorn then becomes a symbol of ridiculous pride or presumptuous weakness.
H2336.origine: The Hebrew word חוֹחַ comes from a root expressing the idea of sharpness, of that which wounds or pierces. It is related to חָוָח (thicket, tangle) and belongs to the family of words designating that which is thorny, pointed, or dangerous. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it often corresponds to ἄκανθα (akantha), which has the same dual meaning: thorny plant and restraining instrument.
H2336.emploi: The word appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the historical and wisdom books. As a plant, it describes wild and unusual places: bushes where fugitives hide, or thorns that grow on a cursed land. The thorn also becomes a weapon or instrument of constraint: Assyrian chains, hooks to dominate creatures. Finally, it serves as a derogatory image: Joash refers to Amaziah as a thorn in the face of the cedar of Lebanon, in other words, a small presumptuous king facing a great power (2 Kings 14:9; 2 Chronicles 25:18). The thorn thus synthesizes vulnerability, disorder, or ridiculous pride.
H2336.portee: The thorn reminds us that nature contains hostile or useless elements, a legacy of sin: the thorn grows where wheat should be (Job 31:40), it wounds, it obstructs, it symbolizes impurity or weakness. But it also teaches humility: to claim to be a thorn in the face of the cedar is to lose oneself in pride. For the believer, the thorn invites us to see that God masters even what seems weak, thorny, or despicable.

sens: To return to its former state, to repair what was deteriorated or damaged.
To restore to something its original function or integrity.
H2338.detail:
1. To restore means to put back in good condition what had been ruined or damaged. In the passage from Ezra 4:12, the Jews returning from captivity restore the foundations of Jerusalem: they rebuild what had been destroyed, they reestablish the city's foundations so that it regains its solidity and its role as a capital.
2. It also means to straighten, to raise up, to reconstitute the strength and authority of a thing. In this same context, restoring the foundations means not only repairing the stone but also giving the city back its power and political presence—hence the fear of the adversary who sees this restoration as a threat.
H2338.origine: The Hebrew word chut (חוּט) comes from a root that evokes the idea of binding, uniting, or joining together. The form used here is the aphel, an intensive verbal form in Hebrew that reinforces the action: one does not merely touch something, one actively and completely restores it. This verb is part of the lexical field of reconstruction and restoration, common in the accounts of the restoration of the temple and the walls of Jerusalem after the exile.
H2338.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 4:12. It is a letter addressed to the Persian king Artaxerxes by the adversaries of the Jews: they denounce their project to restore Jerusalem as an act of rebellion. The context is that of the reconstruction of the temple and the walls after the return from captivity in Babylon. The use of the word restore carries a political charge here: what in the eyes of the Jews is an act of national revival appears to the king as a threat.
H2338.portee: This word reminds us that after the fall and ruin, it is possible to rise again and rebuild. For the believer, it evokes the hope of restoration that God grants to His people even after judgment and exile. Restoring the foundations means not only building again but establishing on solid bases: an image of the divine work that renews and strengthens what had been damaged.

sens: Thin and long strand of textile material
Small cord or rope
Line that measures or delineates
Fragile or tenuous element
H2339.detail:
1. A thin and long strand, usually made of twisted fibers: this is the thread used for sewing or weaving. In Genesis 14:23, Abraham even refuses a simple thread from the spoils, demonstrating his desire to remain independent.
2. A finer cord, often of a particular color: in Joshua 2:18, the scarlet cord attached to the window serves as a sign to recognize and save Rahab's house.
3. A line, real or imaginary, that measures or encircles something: in 1 Kings 7:15, a thread of twelve cubits measures the circumference of the temple column, establishing its exact dimension.
