4. Something thin and fragile, easily broken: in Judges 16:12, Samson breaks the cords that bind him as one would break a simple thread, illustrating his superhuman strength.
H2339.origine: The Hebrew word חוּט (chut) primarily denotes thread or cord, symbolizing something very fine and tenuous. This root evokes the idea of stretching or drawing a line. Figuratively, it applies to anything fragile or ephemeral, hence its poetic use to describe lips (Song of Solomon 4:3): they are beautiful and precise like a scarlet thread.
H2339.emploi: The word chut appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the concrete sense of thread or cord. It denotes the measuring thread (1 Kings 7:15), the thread for tying (Joshua 2:18), the cord that can be broken (Judges 16:12). It gains symbolic value in Ecclesiastes 4:12, where the threefold cord illustrates the strength of union and mutual support: alone, one is weak; together, one is strong. In Song of Solomon 4:3, the image becomes poetic and romantic: the lips are compared to a scarlet thread, fine and colorful. The usage remains always concrete and visual, rooted in the realities of fabric and construction.
H2339.portee: This humble word reminds us that God sees and values small things. Abraham even refuses a thread: this shows his integrity, his refusal to owe anything to a man. The threefold cord in Ecclesiastes teaches that union, the weaving together of lives, creates a strength that no individual possesses alone — a lesson on marriage, community, and the Church. Finally, the image of the thread also speaks to the fragility of human life and our alliances, calling for wisdom and faithfulness.

sens: Canaanite people established in the Promised Land
Inhabitants of the mountainous regions of northern Canaan
Cultural group subjected to Israel's conquest
H2340.detail:
1. The Hivites form one of the ten Canaanite nations listed in Genesis 10:17, descended from Canaan, son of Ham. They are regularly mentioned as peoples that the Israelites encounter during the conquest of the Promised Land.
2. Their name suggests that they lived in villages or mountainous regions of northern Canaan, particularly near Mount Hermon (Joshua 11:3 speaks of Hivites under Hermon). They thus constitute a part of the ethnic mosaic that God promises to drive out before Israel (Exodus 3:17).
3. Unlike other Canaanite peoples, the Hivites of Gibeon find a modus vivendi with Israel through cunning and diplomacy (Joshua 11:19), showing that not all peoples encountered resist conquest in the same way.
H2340.origine: The Hebrew name הִוִּי (Hivi or Hivvi) appears in a genealogical list that divides the Canaanite nations according to their ancestor. The proposed etymology "villagers" refers to a lifestyle in the northern heights rather than in the large coastal cities. The word belongs to the nomenclature of ancient Near Eastern peoples, without a clear verbal root in Hebrew.
H2340.emploi: The term appears 25 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the enumerations of the peoples that God commands the Israelites to drive out. It is first encountered in Genesis 10:17 as a genealogical catalog, then repeatedly in the Lord's promises (Exodus 3:17, Deuteronomy 7:1) and in conquest narratives (Joshua 3:10, 11:19). The Hivites of Gibeon form a notable exception by negotiating a peace treaty with Joshua (Joshua 9:7, 11:19), demonstrating how one of the ten nations accommodates the presence of Israel through diplomacy rather than confrontation.

sens: fertile region traversed by the river Pishon, east of the garden of Eden
H2341G.detail: Havilah is the name of a region mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the geography of the garden of Eden is described. The Pishon, one of the four rivers that watered the garden, surrounds the whole land of Havilah. This region is famous for its riches: it has abundant gold, as well as precious stones and bdellium (Genesis 2:11-12). Havilah thus represents a place of prosperity and fertility, a symbol of divine abundance at the time of creation.
H2341G.origine: The name Havilah literally means "circle" or "circular region," likely evoking a territory bordered or encircled by a river. This same name is found elsewhere in Arabia, suggesting that the word designated a region known to the peoples of the East. The biblical context places it in the ancient lands of the Near East, probably in the Caucasus region or Mesopotamia, near the Caspian Sea.
H2341G.emploi: Havilah appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 2:11, within the account of the creation of the world and the description of the garden of Eden. It serves as a geographical marker that helps situate one of the four sources of the Pishon, one of the four great Edenic rivers. Although infrequent, this name anchors the creation narrative in a real or known geographical context, linking the divine garden to earthly regions endowed with exceptional natural wealth.
H2341G.portee: Havilah reminds us that God's creation did not take place in an isolated bubble, but was situated within a real geography, rich in concrete resources. This mention underscores the abundance and goodness of the Creator, who provided the earth from the very beginning with precious resources — gold, precious stones — for the men He created in His image.

sens: Son of Cush in the post-flood genealogy
H2341H.detail: 1. Havilah is a man who appears in the genealogy of Noah's descendants during the time of the Patriarchs. He is one of the sons of Cush, mentioned alongside his brothers Sheba, Sabta, Raamah, Sabtechah, and his famous brother Nimrod (Genesis 10:7). He is also listed in the parallel genealogy of 1 Chronicles 1:9 to show the continuity of this important lineage in biblical history.
H2341H.origine: The name Havilah means "circle" in Hebrew. It is a personal name in the post-flood genealogy, borne by a man from the time of the Patriarchs. The name is also used to designate geographical regions mentioned elsewhere in the Bible (as in Genesis 2:11 for a region of Eden, and in Genesis 25:18 for a region of Arabia), but both usages here exclusively refer to the person, son of Cush.
H2341H.emploi: Havilah appears twice in the Bible, in the two parallel passages that list the sons of Cush: in Genesis 10:7 and in 1 Chronicles 1:9. It simply records his inclusion in Noah's genealogy, establishing his place in the lineage of Ham through Cush. Like many names in this type of genealogy, Havilah marks the peopling of nations after the Flood and shows how the peoples of the earth were dispersed, although the Bible recounts nothing particular about his personal life.

sens: Son of Joktan, grandson of Shem
Region of Arabia, territory of the Ishmaelites
Region crossed by the river Pishon, near the garden of Eden
H2341I.detail:
1. Havilah is a man from the family of Shem, listed among the twelve sons of Joktan (Genesis 10:29). He belongs to the generation of the ancient patriarchs and appears in genealogical lists that show how peoples dispersed after the flood.

2. His name designated a region of Arabia, territory inhabited by the descendants of Ishmael. This area was known for its resources, particularly gold and precious perfumes (Genesis 2:11-12 mentions it as a fertile region).

3. Havilah was also the name of a biblical region near the garden of Eden, crossed by the river Pishon. It is one of the four rivers that watered the paradise, according to the creation account (Genesis 2:11).
H2341I.origine: The name Havilah means "circle" or "delimited territory" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that suggests the idea of a well-defined region. The same name designates both a person (the son of Joktan) and geographical locations, which is common in biblical genealogies: an ancestor gives his name to the territory inhabited by his descendants.
H2341I.emploi: Havilah appears twice in biblical genealogies: in Genesis 10:29 and in 1 Chronicles 1:23, where he is listed among the sons of Joktan. These two passages are parallel and list the peoples descended from Shem. Like many names in this genealogy, Havilah refers both to an ancestor and to a people or region. In the biblical context, it is primarily the region that captures the attention of readers, as it is associated with rich lands of the ancient East.
H2341I.portee: This name recalls the dispersion of peoples according to God's design and shows how, from the beginnings of humanity, nations established themselves in different regions. Biblical genealogies are not mere lists: they tell the story of God who directs peoples and establishes the boundaries of their habitual lands.

sens: region of Arabia
territory of the Ishmaelites
area in the southwest of the Arabian Peninsula
H2341J.detail: Havilah is a region of Arabia mentioned in the Bible as the territory inhabited by the Ishmaelites, descendants of Ishmael. It appears in two important contexts: first in Genesis 25:18, where it marks the northern boundary of the land of the sons of Ishmael, which extended "from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt." Then in 1 Samuel 15:7, where it delineates the battlefield of Saul against Amalek, again associated with the border region of Egypt. This location suggests a region in the southwest of the Arabian Peninsula, likely in Northwest Arabia, which served as a natural boundary between the Mediterranean world and the Arabian deserts.
H2341J.origine: The name Havilah literally means "circle" or "circular region," perhaps evoking a delimited territory or an enclosed area. The word comes from a Semitic root denoting the idea of limit or contour. It is an ancient geographical name used to designate a well-identified region of the Arab peoples in biblical times.
H2341J.emploi: Havilah appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always to delineate the boundaries of peoples or kingdoms. In Genesis 25:18, it marks the northern boundary of the territory of the Ishmaelites, thus establishing the borders of the land that this people occupied. In 1 Samuel 15:7, the same landmark is used to delineate the territory on which Saul pursued Amalek during his military campaign. These two usages show that Havilah was a well-known region recognized as an important boundary between Egypt and the Arabian lands.

sens: To have the body shaken by involuntary tremors due to fear or emotion
To fear, to be seized with dread or respect
To shake while dancing or contorting
To give birth in pain (for a pregnant woman)
To be in anguish or anxious anticipation
H2342A.detail:
1. The verb primarily describes the physical movement of trembling: the body oscillates, wavers, is shaken by involuntary spasms. It is the bodily expression of fear or intense emotion. Psalms 55:5 illustrates this well: "My heart trembles within me, and the terrors of death surprise me."
2. Trembling also becomes the attitude of one who fears or respects someone: to tremble before God means to fear Him, to revere Him. In 1 Chronicles 16:30, the inhabitants of the earth are invited to "tremble" before the Lord, which expresses a respectful and religious fear.
3. The word also evokes the movement of dance or contortion of the body. The root suggests continuous agitation, a whirling, visible in gestures and movements.
4. For a woman, "to tremble" means to give birth, to bear a child in the pain and convulsions of labor. The link lies in the convulsion, the agitation of the body under the influence of a dominating force.
5. Existential anxiety also enters in: to tremble with anxiety, with tormented anticipation, with inner concern — not just a sudden fear, but a prolonged emotion that shakes the soul.
H2342A.origine: The root חוּל (chul) fundamentally evokes the idea of turning, circling, agitating in a circle. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words that share this notion of agitation, circular movement, or convulsion. The image is of a body twisting, bending, losing its stability — whether shaken by fear, dancing, or in labor. This same root generates names for pain, anguish, and childbirth, where the body is subjected to violent forces that dominate it.
H2342A.emploi: The verb to tremble appears about ten times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms and Job. It is regularly used regarding creatures facing the power of God: Psalms 97:4, "The lightning lights up the world; the earth sees and trembles," or Jeremiah 5:22, where even the sea and nations tremble before the limits God has set for them. In personal misfortune narratives, such as Job 26:5 or Psalms 55:5, the trembling of the heart or soul expresses terror, anxiety in the face of death or danger. The cultic context is strong: to tremble before God is a means of expressing sincere worship and religious reverence, as commanded in 1 Chronicles 16:30 and Psalms 96:9. In Esther 4:4, the queen "is frightened" upon learning of the misfortune, showing how inner trembling can govern all behavior.
H2342A.portee: This word roots Christian faith in the reality of the body and emotions: God does not ask for theoretical worship, but for reverence that makes one tremble, that delights and disturbs the soul. It is a call to take seriously the greatness of God, not to treat Him with indifference. At the same time, the word suggests that the fear of creatures before God is natural and right, provided it is based on His power and holiness, not on illusion or falsehood.

sens: To be solid, stable, unwavering
To have strength, vigor
To succeed, prosper in one's endeavors
To persevere ardently in a desire or longing
H2342B.detail:
1. The word primarily describes physical or moral solidity: something that holds firm, that does not collapse. It is the image of what is unshakeable.
2. It also means to possess active strength, power, or vigor to act. In Psalms 10:5, the ways of the wicked "succeed": they advance, they hold firm, and prosper.
3. The word can describe a persistent, obsessive desire — something that grips you with force. In Job 20:21, it speaks of the "voracity" of the wicked: this need that gnaws at them, this burning desire that does not let go.
4. By extension, it is the energy with which one pursues an endeavor to the end, the tenacity that leads to success.
H2342B.origine: The verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of firmness, of strength that holds firm. It is related to Hebrew words meaning "army," "power," or "wealth" — any form of stable resource. The basic image is that of a rampart that does not yield, of concentrated strength.
H2342B.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 20:21, it describes the endless voracity of the wicked, that appetite that devours and drives them. In Psalms 10:5, it expresses the persistent success of the ways of the wicked, the fact that their endeavors hold firm and prosper despite everything. In both cases, the term paints a picture of strength or persistence, often linked to malice or iniquity — a firmness that does not serve the good.
H2342B.portee: This word reminds the reader that the persistence of evil in the world, its apparent success, is never the final word: the Bible acknowledges the strength of the wicked, but it also asserts that their enterprises, however "firm" they may seem, have no real stability before God. It is a call not to be discouraged by the fleeting prosperity of evil.

sens: To bring forth, give birth
To beget, to be the origin of
To create, to bring into existence
To twist, to convulse (pain or agitation)
To wait anxiously, to be in anxiety
H2342H.detail:
1. To give birth primarily means to bring forth a child, to deliver: it is the maternal or life-creating act. Wisdom in Proverbs 8:24 says "I was brought forth" to speak of her emergence, her appearance at the beginning of time.
2. The word extends to the idea of begetting, producing, being the origin: God "begets" man (Deuteronomy 32:18), creates and gives birth to all things. It is more general than the biological act.
3. To create, to bring into existence: Psalms 90:2 says that God "created the earth and the world" — here giving birth takes on the meaning of bringing existence from nothing.
4. The word also contains the idea of convulsion, twisting: when a goat "gives" birth (Job 39:4), it twists, suffers the pains of childbirth.
5. To give birth can express anxious waiting, anguish: to twist in impatience or fear, like a woman in labor awaiting her delivery.
H2342H.origine: The Hebrew word chul comes from a root that first evokes twisting, rotation, circular movement — hence dance, which twists the body. From there, it designates the convulsion of one who suffers (the woman in labor twists), and ultimately the act of giving birth itself. The root thus expresses the idea of painful agitation, of transformation of the body and being. This image of convulsive movement unites all the meanings of the word: to dance, to twist, to give birth, to create.
H2342H.emploi: The verb chul appears about 9 times in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is mostly found in the Psalms and in Job, where it designates the pains of childbirth or the sufferings that contort the body: "I was born in iniquity" (Psalms 51:7) means that from my conception I was in suffering and imperfection. In higher and more poetic passages, like Proverbs 8 and Psalms 90, the word takes on a cosmic significance: it is Wisdom and the creation of the world that are "brought forth" by God. Elsewhere, it simply describes the birthing of animals (Job 39:4) or the creative act (Deuteronomy 32:18, Isaiah 51:2). The word thus unites the biological and natural image with the spiritual reality of creation and suffering.
H2342H.portee: This word reminds the reader that everything that exists — including ourselves — comes from God who has "brought us forth." It unites the idea of creation with that of suffering: every birth costs, everything that comes into existence passes through pain and contortion. For the believer, this means that even our sin and weaknesses (Psalms 51:7) are born from this fragile human condition — but it is also the same creative power of God that can transform us and give birth to us anew in righteousness.

sens: To contort, to twist under the effect of pain or fear
To give birth, to deliver (image of the mother twisting in the pains of childbirth)
To be seized with fear, to tremble in anguish
To dance, to make swirling movements
To wait anxiously, to languish
H2342I.detail:
1. The verb first describes the movement of the body that twists and contracts: a convulsive twisting, like someone who suffers or is seized with panic. In Jeremiah 51:29, the earth itself "trembles" at the Lord's design against Babylon — it is the earth that convulses.
2. The image of childbirth is central to this verb: the mother "experiences pains," meaning literally twists in the contractions of childbirth. Isaiah 23:4 states it bluntly: Sidon, like a barren woman, says "I have not experienced pains, I have not given birth."
3. The word also designates the fear that seizes the heart and body: when Israel advances, the peoples "will tremble and be seized with anguish" (Deuteronomy 2:25) — it is fear that passes through them like a wave.
4. More rarely, the verb evokes dance, the swirling movement, which shares with suffering this idea of twisting and agitation.
5. A more internal nuance: to wait anxiously or to languish, this inner tension of the heart that contracts in waiting.
H2342I.origine: The root חוּל expresses primarily the idea of twisting, of movement that bends and contracts. It is linked to the image of physical pain that tightens the body, and naturally to that of childbirth — the most intense of human bodily twists. The verb has several forms in Hebrew that specify the action: the simple form describes the action without an agent, the intensive form adds force, the passive form means "to be turned" or "to be given birth to." This root belongs to the vocabulary of emotion and deep suffering throughout the Bible.
H2342I.emploi: This verb appears about 20 times in the Old Testament, particularly concentrated in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel). The most frequent usage concerns the pains of childbirth — the prophets use it to describe Jerusalem, Zion, or the world as a woman in labor. It also designates the physical fear that seizes men in the face of an enemy or before God. In Job 15:20, the wicked "passes in anguish all the days of his life" — it is a chronic anxiety that continually passes through him. The verb thus expresses a very concrete and embodied suffering, never abstract.
H2342I.portee: This word reminds us that suffering, whether physical, emotional, or spiritual, affects the whole being — it passes through, twists, convulses it. For the Christian reader, it speaks to the raw reality of pain in this world, including the pain of childbirth which is both a curse and the fulfillment of God's plan. It also invites meditation on the true birth, spiritual and terrifying, that God accomplishes amidst the suffering of the world.

sens: Jumping and moving to a rhythm (dance)
Twisting, contorting
To rush upon, to pounce violently
To give birth, to bring forth (in twisting pain)
To tremble, to shudder with fear or anxiety
H2342J.detail:
1. To dance: to move the body to a rhythm, to turn and sway. This is the primary and simplest meaning, that of the young women whom the Benjaminites abducted at Shiloh for the dancers (Judges 21:23).
2. To twist, to contort: the body moves in all directions, as if seized by convulsions, either from suffering or violent movement. The word depicts the very movement of the body that writhes.
3. To rush upon, to pounce: when speaking of a storm or an army that 'rushes' upon the wicked (Jeremiah 23:19), this image is used: something enormous that descends violently, swirling as it throws itself against its target.
4. To give birth: when the voice of the Lord makes the deer 'give birth' (Psalms 29:9), it is the cry of labor that causes birth. The woman writhes in pain to give life, and the verb captures both the movement of the body and the effort of childbirth.
5. To tremble, to shudder: from fear or anxiety, like the body that contracts under terror. It is the very idea of writhe or fear in the definition: the body does not remain still.
H2342J.origine: The Hebrew word חוּל (chul) expresses the idea of twisting and swirling of the body. Its root paints the rotational movement, the contortion. The word appears in several forms (simple, intensified, passive) that all retain this bodily image: to dance, to twist, to give birth with the pains of childbirth. This richness comes from observing life: dance swirls, suffering twists the body, childbirth mixes pain and twisting, the storm swirls. It is a very vivid, very physical word.
H2342J.emploi: The verb חוּל (chul) appears 8 times in the provided Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and the Prophets. Judges 21:23 shows it in the literal sense: dancers. But most uses employ it in a figurative sense. Psalm 29:9 couples it with the birth of animals under God's action. The prophetic passages (Jeremiah 23:19; 30:23; Hosea 11:6) take it up to describe the storm of divine wrath that rushes upon the wicked like a swirling force. The word then becomes a poetic expression of the terrible violence of divine judgment. Through these uses, we see the word slide from the concrete dancing to the figurative tormenting.
H2342J.portee: This verb paints the movement of body and soul: joyful dance, suffering that twists, anxious waiting, birth with its pains. For the believer, it reminds that the body is never inert before God — neither in joy nor in trial, it is shaken, transformed. When the Bible speaks of a storm of wrath that 'rushes' upon the wicked, it uses this same image of swirling: God does not act coldly, but with a power that overturns. It is an invitation to feel God's presence in all that stirs the body and soul.

sens: To stand still waiting for something with impatience or worry
To hope in someone, to place trust in him
To endure anxiety or pain while waiting for relief
H2342K.detail: 1. The word first evokes the image of someone waiting for news, a response, an action — but not passively: there is anxiety, tension. Noah 'waited' seven days before releasing the dove (Genesis 8:10), and the king's servants in Jericho 'waited' a long time for their master to open (Judges 3:25), both in a waiting that tightens the soul. 2. The word also means 'to hope', but not a simple wish: it is to place trust in God despite uncertainty. The psalmist says 'Be silent before the Lord, and hope in him' (Psalms 37:7), inviting a patient trust beyond worry. 3. Finally, the word carries the idea of suffering endured: the original meaning contains the image of the body twisting, tensing — which is why it can describe the pain of childbirth or the agony of waiting. Job says 'wait for him' (Job 35:14), calling for a valiant waiting before God.
H2342K.origine: The Hebrew verb חוּל comes from a root meaning 'to twist', 'to turn', 'to dance'. The starting image is that of a body in motion, contorting — hence the meanings 'to dance', 'to squirm', 'to tremble'. Gradually, the word has been applied to anxious waiting (the one who waits twists internally) and to trust in God (waiting while being shaken by emotion). In the Greek Old Testament, it is often translated by verbs meaning 'to wait' or 'to hope'.
H2342K.emploi: The verb חוּל appears 5 times in the provided uses, mainly in the sense of 'to wait' or 'to hope'. It is found in historical accounts (Genesis 8:10: Noah waits before releasing the dove; Judges 3:25: the servants wait for their master), in wisdom and prayer (Job 35:14; Psalms 37:7; Micah 1:12). In all these contexts, waiting is never neutral: it is mixed with anxiety, impatience, or a hope that calls for patience. The word suggests an action that traverses time with a certain inner tension.
H2342K.portee: This word teaches the believer that waiting on God is neither passive nor easy: it requires patience in the face of anxiety. But it is also an act of trust: 'to hope in God' is to accept the present uncertainty while counting on his faithfulness. Noah, the king's servants, Job himself — all wait. It is an invitation to live the Christian wait, not resigned, but active and confident.

sens: Son of Aram and grandson of Shem
H2343.detail: Hul is an ancestor mentioned in the genealogy of peoples established after the flood. He is the second son of Aram, who himself is the son of Shem, one of Noah's three sons. His brothers are Uz, Gether, and Mash (or Meshech according to variations).
H2343.origine: The name Hul means 'circle' in Hebrew. It designates a man from the Syrians living in the time of the Patriarchs, whose descendants formed a people or territory, according to the biblical way of recounting the history of nations through their eponymous ancestors.
H2343.emploi: Hul appears only twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:23, where he is listed among the sons of Aram in the 'Table of Nations' that enumerates the peoples descended from Noah's sons after the flood, and in 1 Chronicles 1:17, where the same genealogy is repeated. These two passages are the only ones that mention Hul, always in a strictly genealogical context, without any narrative of action or particular characteristic.

sens: Fine mineral particle that covers beaches and deserts
Innumerable multitude, incalculable quantity
Unbearable weight or burden
H2344.detail:
1. Sand is the fine, granular material that accumulates at the edges of seas and in deserts: Moses hides the Egyptian's body in the sand (Exodus 2:12), a material abundant and that erases traces.
2. Due to its natural abundance, sand becomes the biblical image of what cannot be counted: God promises Abraham a descendants "like the sand on the seashore" (Genesis 22:17), and the armies of enemies are "innumerable as the sand" (Judges 7:12). This comparison often recurs to describe a people or crowd too numerous to be counted.
3. By extension, sand also symbolizes what is heavy and oppressive: in Proverbs 27:3, "sand is heavy," but the folly of the heart weighs even more.
H2344.origine: The Hebrew word חוֹל (chol) primarily refers to the sand that every person sees at the edge of the sea. Egypt, the land of the Nile, was covered with sandy deserts, making sand familiar to the Israelites. Its visible and uncountable abundance early on made it a natural image of infinite multitude: one cannot count the grains of sand, just as one cannot count the stars in the sky.
H2344.emploi: The word חוֹל (chol) appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in the singular. It primarily recurs in two contexts: first, the promise to Abraham and his descendants — their offspring will be "like the sand" (Genesis 22:17, 32:12, 41:49) — a blessing repeated until the time of the kings (1 Kings 4:20). Secondly, it describes enemy armies: the Midianites, the chariots of the Canaanites are "like the sand" (Judges 7:12, 1 Samuel 13:5). Sand also appears in wisdom poems: Job associates his many days with sand (Job 29:18), and the wise compare the weight of sand to the weight of folly (Proverbs 27:3). This image runs throughout Scripture to express the immeasurable.
H2344.portee: Sand reminds us that God keeps His promises by giving a descendants more numerous than can be counted — a sign of His infinite blessing. But sand also speaks of what can become a threat: a large army "like the sand" is frightening to those who oppose God. This image helps us grasp the immensity of God and His plans, and to perceive that what seems uncountable and insurmountable to men does not escape His wisdom.

sens: Having the color black or very dark
Animal with black or very dark fur
Dark or brownish hue
H2345.detail:
1. Black is simply the dark color, either completely black or very dark: it is a hue without brightness. In Genesis, Jacob and Laban negotiate over the animals of the flock, and Jacob asks for all the "black" lambs as his wages — the sheep and goats of a very dark color that contrast with the spotted or striped animals (Genesis 30:32).
2. The word specifically refers to an animal whose coat is black or very dark. Laban agrees to give Jacob all the "black" among the lambs and to remove the "black" animals from the common flock to form the wages (Genesis 30:33, 30:35, 30:40) — it is a simple criterion for distinguishing between the beasts.
3. Black can also evoke a brown or very dark hue, a solid color without pattern, in contrast to marbled or spotted animals.
H2345.origine: The Hebrew word חוּם (chum) literally means "blackened" or "made dark." It comes from a root that expresses darkening or changing to a dark hue. The word is concrete: it describes the visual appearance of an animal, without moral or spiritual connotation.
H2345.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Bible, all in the account of Genesis 30, where Jacob and Laban dispute over the flock. Jacob chooses as his wages all the "black" animals — an easy criterion to verify and difficult to contest. The context is purely economic and pastoral: it is about distinguishing the beasts according to their color to clearly establish each one's right. The word carries no figurative charge.

sens: Defensive structure made of stone or brick that surrounds and protects a city.
Military fortification erected for defense against assaults or sieges.
Material element that creates a separation or physical protection.
Image of protection or strength of God's people.
H2346G.detail: 1. The wall is primarily the fortified structure in stone that cities built around themselves for defense: when besieged Jericho sees its walls collapse under the cry of the Israelites (Joshua 6:20), it is the collapse of all its protection. 2. It also refers to the reinforced walls of a besieged fortress, which must be breached to conquer the city: the text of 2 Samuel 11:20 mentions the battle against the enemy "near the wall." 3. It represents everything that encloses and separates, protecting but also isolating: the waters forming "like a wall" on the right and left of Israel (Exodus 14:22) illustrate this notion of salvific partition. 4. By spiritual extension, the wall becomes the image of divine protection over His people, especially when Nehemiah rebuilds the walls of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 6:15) — it is not just a matter of stones, it is the restoration of Israel's strength and honor.
H2346G.origine: The word חוֹמָה comes from a Hebrew root that means "to close" or "to enclose." The wall is literally what closes and delimits a space. It is a fundamental word in the Old Testament, particularly during periods when Israel had to defend itself (the time of the judges, royal, exilic).
H2346G.emploi: The word appears 121 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical accounts, psalms, and prophetic books. It carries several nuances: it is first the defensive wall that is assaulted (Joshua 6:20), that is reinforced (2 Chronicles 32:5), or that is destroyed (2 Kings 25:10). It then becomes central in the account of the reconstruction under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 6:15: "the wall was completed"), where it symbolizes the restoration of Jerusalem and its status. In the psalms and wisdom literature (Proverbs 25:28, Psalms 51:20), the wall becomes spiritualized: it represents God's protection or the moral firmness of the wise.
H2346G.portee: For the Christian reader, the wall reminds us that God protects His people and that order, security, and honor rest on solid foundations. The reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah tells how a humiliated and scattered people can rise again through trust in God and collective work. This image also invites us to meditate on what spiritually "protects" us: our convictions, the Word, the community of believers.

sens: massive wall built of stone or brick used to fortify and delimit a city
segment of the fortified enclosure of Jerusalem, particularly wide and strong
H2346H.detail:
1. The word refers to a wall, that is, a massive defensive structure made of stone or brick, thick and high enough to protect a city. It is the work that must be built or repaired to secure the inhabitants. In Nehemiah 3:8, the workers leave unfinished up to the wide wall, indicating that it is a particular section of the enclosure.
2. By extension, this word applies to the wide wall of Jerusalem itself, part of the fortified enclosure that the Israelites rebuild in Nehemiah. In Nehemiah 12:38, during the dedication of the walls, a choir walks on this wide wall, indicating that it was solid and wide enough for people to walk on.
H2346H.origine: The Hebrew word חוֹמָה (chomah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of surrounding or protecting. It is often combined with רָחָב (rachav), which means "wide" or "spacious," hence the expression "wide wall": not just a simple partition, but an imposing and spacious defensive structure. This term frequently appears in the Old Testament to designate the ramparts of cities.
H2346H.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided usages, both in Nehemiah during the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile. In Nehemiah 3:8, it refers to the section that the builders must leave until the wide wall, showing a precise physical marker in the reconstruction project. In Nehemiah 12:38, during the dedication ceremony, the processions ascend the wide wall, illustrating that this wall is not only built but also functional and solid. In both contexts, the wide wall of Jerusalem is both a physical reality, a symbol of divine protection, and a place of communal celebration.
H2346H.portee: The wide wall of Jerusalem evokes the restoration of God's people after the exile and the return to safety. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that God restores His people and strengthens their defense. The reconstruction of the walls appears as an act of collective obedience and trust in divine protection, showing that the rebuilt people can celebrate their restoration by walking on the ramparts they have built themselves.

sens: To feel compassion for someone, to desire their well-being
To refrain from punishing or harming, out of compassion
To look at someone with kindness and tenderness
H2347.detail:
1. To have mercy means to be moved by the misery of a person and wish to help them. Psalm 72:13 speaks of the king who "will have mercy on the needy and the poor, and will save the lives of the poor": it is a compassionate gaze that sees suffering and is moved.
2. It is also to hold back one's hand, to refuse to strike or condemn. In Deuteronomy 19:21, the Law commands to execute the sentence "without showing any mercy": in other words, without being stopped by compassion. It is the absence of mercy that allows for firm justice.
3. More broadly, it is to cast a benevolent gaze upon someone. In Ezekiel 5:11, God says "I will withdraw my eye" and "my eye will be without mercy": the eye that has mercy is one that protects and forgives; the one who withdraws their mercy abandons to justice.
H2347.origine: This Hebrew verb primarily expresses a visceral emotion: the compassion that arises in us when we see suffering. It is linked to the idea of tenderness and sparing. The root suggests a heart inclination towards the one who suffers. In Hebrew, mercy (חוּס) is often the expected attitude of the powerful towards the weak, of judges towards the supplicants.
H2347.emploi: This verb appears 24 times in the Old Testament, mainly among the prophets (especially Ezekiel) and in legislative texts. It describes God's attitude towards His people (Psalms 72:13, Joel 2:17), but also God's absence of mercy during His judgment (Ezekiel 5:11, 9:5, 24:14). The Law sometimes commands to act without mercy to maintain justice (Deuteronomy 19:21, 25:12). The word thus nuances judgment: mercy restrains vengeance, but the absence of mercy underscores the firmness of divine sentencing.
H2347.portee: This word teaches us that compassion is at the heart of God's attitude towards the poor and the unfortunate. It invites us to cultivate this tender gaze, this ability to see suffering and wish to help. But it also warns us: there is a moment when mercy must give way to justice, when looking at misfortune without acting becomes complicity. It is a call to discern when to pity and when to act.

sens: Edge of the sea, line where land meets the ocean
Coastal region, territory located along the sea
H2348.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the edge of the sea, the boundary between land and water: it is the shoreline itself. In Judges 5:17, Asher "sat by the seaside," which evokes both the geographical location and the idea of settling there, occupying it.
2. By extension, it designates the entire coastal region, the territory that borders the sea. In Genesis 49:13, Zebulun "will dwell by the coast of the seas," which means not only that he will live right by the water's edge, but that he will dominate the coastal region and maritime routes. Similarly, in Joshua 9:1, "the coast of the great sea" encompasses the entire western coastline of Canaan.
H2348.origine: The Hebrew word חוֹף (choph) comes from a root meaning "to turn" or "to surround": the coast is what surrounds, what borders. It designates both the physical limit of the shore and the coastal zone that surrounds it. The word is specific to biblical Hebrew and does not have well-attested cognates in other Semitic languages.
H2348.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, always to evoke the Mediterranean shoreline or the regions that dominate it. In Genesis 49:13, it refers to the promise to the tribe of Zebulun to possess coastal lands rich in maritime trade. In Deuteronomy 1:7, the coast of the sea is listed as one of the borders of the territory that the Israelites must conquer. Throughout the historical (Joshua, Judges) and prophetic (Jeremiah, Ezekiel) books, the word designates the coastal regions of Canaan, often in connection with the peoples who inhabited them (Canaanites, Philistines, Kerethites). The context is always geographical and political.
H2348.portee: The mention of the coast reminds us that God controls the borders of the promised land and distributes territories according to His plan. For the Israelites, the coast was both a boundary and a promise: it marked the edge of the known world, rich in commercial possibilities, but also a region where pagan peoples were to be converted or driven out. Understanding this biblical geography helps the reader grasp the reality of God's project for Israel.

sens: Son of Benjamin and head of a family in the people of Israel
H2349.detail: Hupham is a son of Benjamin, the founding ancestor of a family of Israel called the Huphamites. He is mentioned during the census of the tribes in the wilderness, where his descendants are officially recognized as one of the branches of the tribe of Benjamin (Numbers 26:39).
H2349.origine: The name means "man of the coast" or "inhabitant of the shore" in Hebrew. Hupham is also referred to as Huppim in some texts, and Huram in Chronicles, which shows the variations of the same name in textual traditions.
H2349.emploi: Hupham is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:39, during the census of the sons of Benjamin in the wilderness. His name appears in the genealogical list that enumerates the families descended from each son of Benjamin. This official mention establishes that his descendants formed a recognized social and administrative unit within the tribe.

sens: Members of the family descended from Hupham, son of Benjamin
H2350.detail: The Huphamites are the descendants of Hupham, who was one of the sons of Benjamin. Hupham is mentioned for the first time during the census of the families of Israel at the Exodus from Egypt (Numbers 26:39). Like the other sons of Benjamin, Hupham founded a family that has continued and bears his name in the genealogical records of Israel.
H2350.origine: The word "Huphamites" comes from the name Hupham, one of the twelve sons of Benjamin, who himself was a son of Jacob. The suffix "-ites" (common in Hebrew and French for forming names of peoples or families) indicates belonging to the descendants of this person. The name Hupham also appears in the forms Huppim and Huram in other biblical texts (1 Chronicles 8:5), which shows the variations in the transmission of names through generations.
H2350.emploi: The Huphamites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:39, during the great census of the Israelites in the plains of Moab, after forty years in the desert. This census lists the families of each tribe, including those of Benjamin. The Huphamites appear among the families of the clan of Hupham, alongside other Benjaminite families such as the Belaites and the Shuphamites. This text is a genealogical document that shows how the tribes of Israel were organized into distinct families, each tracing back to an eponymous ancestor.

sens: The outside space of a building, an enclosure, or a defined place, as opposed to the inside
The street, the public space of a city or village where people circulate
The exterior of a surface, the outer face of an object
The countryside or territory beyond a city or camp
The distance from a holy or protected place, the exclusion from a community
H2351.detail:
1. The space outside of an enclosed place. When Noah builds the ark, he covers it with pitch "inside and out" to make it watertight (Genesis 6:14): the inside and the outside are the two faces of the same surface. Elsewhere, the furnishings of the sanctuary are placed "outside" (Exodus 26:35), meaning outside the inner building, in the courtyard.
2. The street or public square of a city. At the well's gate, near the city, girls are met "going to the fountain, at the time when they come" — outside, in the public space (Genesis 24:11). In times of famine, "they cry in the streets" (Isaiah 24:11), this space where the collective life resonates.
3. The external aspect of a thing. The stones of the sanctuary have "outside" and inside (1 Kings 6:6), two faces distinguished by thickness. This is the visible aspect, the surface.
4. The countryside, the open territory beyond the protected enclosure. Around each Levitical city, the lands are measured "outside the city" for two thousand cubits (Numbers 35:5): this is the rural territory surrounding the settlement.
5. Exclusion, separation from the holy community. One afflicted with a leprous sore lives "outside the camp" (Leviticus 13:46), separated from communal life: this is no longer just a place, but a status of distance.
H2351.origine: The Hebrew word חוּץ (chuts) comes from a root meaning "to pierce" or "to dig," hence the idea of "what is outside the hollow, the closed." It is the opposite of inside. In Hebrew, the word regularly opposes "בַּיִת" (house) and "פְנִים" (interior). It is found in expressions marking the crossing of a boundary (to go out, to go outside). The Greek translates this word as "ἔξω" (exô) or variations of the same semantic field.
H2351.emploi: The word appears 158 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, where the topography of the sanctuary and the camp is central. In the Pentateuch, it designates the space outside the sanctuary, the tabernacle, or the camp — spaces where sacrifices, judgments, or ritual exclusions take place. In the historical books, it takes on the meaning of "street" and "urban public space." Isaiah and Lamentations use it to evoke urban life in distress (cries in the streets, famine). The meaning varies: sometimes it is a neutral geographical space, sometimes a zone of impurity or exclusion, sometimes the space of ordinary social life. Gradually, the word becomes charged with the tension between the sacred (inside, protected) and the profane or impure (outside).
H2351.portee: This word reveals how Israel understood the order of the world according to the presence of God. The sanctuary, the camp, the house form concentric circles of holiness; the "outside" is never neutral — it is the place of what escapes divine protection, or of what is excluded from it. For the Christian reader, this highlights the contrast between the people of God (inside, gathered) and those who are separated from it. But it is also a reminder that God first meets His people where He dwells, within them, before sending His messengers outside.

sens: Natural underground hollow, refuge for animals
Dungeon, underground prison
Figuratively: situation of captivity and confinement
H2352.detail:
1. A cave is a hollow, a natural grotto carved into the rock, where animals such as snakes live (Isaiah 11:8: "the den of the viper"). It is a dark and secluded place, a refuge from danger or fear.
2. In the human context, a cave also refers to an underground dungeon, a prison dug underground where captives are confined. Isaiah 42:22 describes a people "chained in caves, plunged into dungeons," an image of brutal oppression.
3. Figuratively, the cave evokes confinement, deprivation of freedom, and the miserable condition of the exiled people: being unable to go out, being held in darkness, losing all hope of deliverance.
H2352.origine: The Hebrew word חור (chur) comes from a root that expresses the idea of digging or piercing. It originally designates any hollow or natural orifice, but takes on a strong emotional charge when it speaks of confinement: a cave is primarily a refuge for animals but becomes a symbol of captivity when it contains chained men.
H2352.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. First in Isaiah 11:8, in a messianic prophecy where future innocence (the child) will not fear the most dangerous inhabitants of the caves — an image of the restoration of primitive harmony. Then in Isaiah 42:22, where "caves" designates the places of detention for the exiled people, emphasizing the total and brutal nature of their oppression. In both cases, the word evokes confinement: either that of wild beasts or that of prisoners.
H2352.portee: This image of a cave speaks to the heart of the believer in exile or distress. It narrates not only the harshness of physical captivity but also the trial of faith: being enclosed, separated from light and freedom. Recognizing that it is the people of the Eternal who lie in these caves is to cry out to the liberating God. This word also reminds us that the final redemption (Isaiah 11) will be such a complete restoration that even evil in the caves will lose its power.

sens: White color, that of snow or linen
H2353.detail: 1. The word designates the color white in its material manifestation: white fabric, a white cloth. In Esther 1:6, the white curtains are mentioned among the ornaments of the Persian royal palace, evoking the splendor and refinement of the decor; white is associated with green and blue in a luxurious composition. In Esther 8:15, the white garment worn by Mordecai signifies his newly acquired honor and his integration into the elite of the kingdom. Here, white evokes nobility, purity, and social distinction.
H2353.origine: The Hebrew word חוּר (chur) belongs to the Semitic family of terms denoting whiteness. It is related to the idea of what shines or radiates. In biblical Hebrew, this word can also refer to fine cloth or white linen, materials prized in antiquity. The context of the Book of Esther, set in the Persian court, explains the importance given to fine fabrics and their colors: luxury and prestige are expressed through the quality of the textiles.
H2353.emploi: The word חוּר (chur) appears twice in the Bible, exclusively in the Book of Esther. Both uses concern contexts of royal prestige and material wealth. In Esther 1:6, it describes the curtains of King Xerxes' royal banquet, highlighting the magnificence of the palace; in Esther 8:15, it qualifies the garment of Mordecai promoted to a high office. In both cases, white symbolizes honor and dignity. These uses reflect the role of the word in a formal and official register, linked to the visual codes of Persian royalty.
H2353.portee: The white in these two passages reminds the reader that honor and distinction are also expressed through visible material signs: clothing, decor, symbols of power. For the believer, these details from the Book of Esther illustrate how God lifts the humble and clothes them with glory, even in a Persian context far from Jerusalem. White becomes the visible symbol of Mordecai's elevation and the salvation of his people.

sens: Assistant to Moses and Aaron during the Exodus from Egypt
Ancestor of Bezalel, the chief artisan of the tabernacle
Military leader or dignitary during the time of Moses
Ancestor of several Judean lineages
H2354G.detail:
1. Hur is the companion of Moses and Aaron who assists them at the decisive moment of the battle against Amalek: he goes up with them to the top of the hill while Joshua fights below (Exodus 17:10). He is also the one before whom the Israelites can present their disputes when Moses is absent (Exodus 24:14), showing that he enjoys recognized authority among the people.
2. Hur is the grandfather of Bezalel, the son of Uri: it is through this genealogical link that he is known, as Bezalel becomes the chief of the artisans who make the tabernacle and all its furnishings (Exodus 35:30; Exodus 38:22). His grandson receives the Spirit of God directly to accomplish this sacred work.
3. In the genealogies of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:19-20; 1 Chronicles 4:4), Hur appears as the son of Caleb and Ephrath, founder or ancestor of Bethlehem and several Judean cities. He is the firstborn of Ephrath and the father of several sons, including Shobal, who will be the father of Kirjath-Jearim.
H2354G.origine: The name Hur literally means "hole" or "cave" in Hebrew. It designates a man from the tribe of Judah who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. Several Hurs are mentioned in Scripture, making it difficult to ascertain whether they are all the same person or descendants of the same original Hur. Biblical tradition places him among the important leaders of the time of the Exodus.
H2354G.emploi: Hur appears twelve times in the Bible, mainly in Exodus and Chronicles. In Exodus, he plays a political and military role: he helps Moses during the crisis of the battle against Amalek and replaces Moses when he goes up to receive the Law at Sinai. In Chronicles, he is presented as a major genealogical ancestor, father of several sons and grandfather of Bezalel. The genealogy places him as the firstborn of Ephrath and associates him with the founding of Bethlehem and other cities of Judah. The biblical uses do not allow us to assert with certainty whether all these Hurs are one person or homonyms.
H2354G.portee: Hur shows us a faithful and discreet servant who supports the leaders of God's people in crucial moments. His role as a judge and arbitrator among the people reminds us that spiritual authority is also manifested in fair judgment and listening to disputes. Finally, the fact that God fills his grandson Bezalel with wisdom and artistic talent for the construction of the tabernacle suggests that the faithfulness of ancestors can open doors to the blessing of future generations.

sens: One of the five kings of Midian killed after the battle of Peor
H2354H.detail: 1. Hur is one of the five kings of Midian who were defeated and killed by the Israelites after the battle of Peor (Numbers 31:8). He is mentioned alongside four other kings: Evi, Rekem, Zur, and Reba. These kings represented the political power of Midian at that time. His name means "hole" in Hebrew, but nothing more is known about this character as a person, except for his role in this conflict.
H2354H.origine: The name Hur literally means "hole" (from the Hebrew verb "chur"). He is a historical figure from the time of the Exodus and the desert crossing. The source definition mentions that other characters named Hur exist in the Bible (notably an assistant to Moses and Aaron, and a father of Rephaiah during the time of Nehemiah), but the provided biblical uses exclusively refer to the king of Midian.
H2354H.emploi: Hur is a king of Midian known for having been defeated and killed by the Israelites under the leadership of Moses. He is mentioned twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages: in Numbers 31:8, which directly recounts his death during the campaign against Midian after Peor, and in Joshua 13:21, which summarizes this same event by outlining the borders of the territory of Israel. He is always listed among the five princes of Midian, and the order of names varies slightly between the two passages (Hur appears in 4th position in Numbers, and in 4th as well in Joshua). His historical importance lies in his status as a Midianite chief and his defeat by Israel.

sens: Father of Rephaja, a district chief in Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
H2354I.detail: Hur is a man who lived during the time of the return from exile, known only as the father of Rephaja. In Nehemiah 3:9, his son Rephaja is mentioned among those who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile to Babylon, leading half of the district of Jerusalem. Although the text tells us little more about Hur himself, the mention of his name suggests that he came from a family of important local leaders.
H2354I.origine: The name Hur literally means "hole" in Hebrew, but its real meaning in biblical genealogies remains uncertain. This name may refer to several biblical characters from different times — an assistant to Moses and Aaron, the grandfather of Bezalel who built the tabernacle, or a king of Midian — but these ancient traditions are not directly related to the Hur of Nehemiah mentioned here.
H2354I.emploi: Hur appears only once in the Bible in the sense designated by these uses: in Nehemiah 3:9, where he is identified as the father of Rephaja. He is cited simply to establish the genealogy of this individual, without description of his own life or deeds. His appearance in the context of the repairs of the walls of Jerusalem indicates that he came from a family with influence in local governance at the time of the Jewish restoration after the exile.

sens: fine white fabric
white linen cloth
white garment or white linen
brilliant whiteness (figurative)
H2355.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a fine white fabric, particularly bleached linen, like that produced in Egypt. It is a luxury item, the result of meticulous weaving and bleaching work. In Isaiah 19:9, the workers who dye the linen and weave these white fabrics are artisans of a prestigious industry. 2. By extension, the word can refer to any white fabric, white linen, or white garment — a precious material used for prestigious clothing or funeral adornments. 3. Finally, the whiteness of these fabrics becomes in biblical language the very image of moral and spiritual purity, innocence, or restored holiness.
H2355.origine: The Hebrew word חוֹר (chor) comes from a root expressing the idea of brilliant whiteness, luminosity. The Egyptian context of Isaiah 19 — the linen industry on the Nile — reminds us that this white fabric was one of the commercial riches of ancient Egypt. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this sense of fine white cloth is found in other related terms.
H2355.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 19:9. Moses lists the plagues of Egypt and their consequences: the confusion of the most prestigious Egyptian industries. The linen workers — a reputed, well-organized profession, a source of wealth — will be dismayed. This prophetic text evokes the collapse of a once-powerful economic order struck by divine judgment. The unique usage is sufficient to show that the word paints a detail of Egyptian life with realism.
H2355.portee: This verse reminds us that no human industry, no wealth or craftsmanship can withstand divine judgment. The most skilled artisans, the most envied products, collapse when God has decided. For the Christian, it is an invitation not to place trust in earthly achievements, no matter how brilliant they may be, but to seek first the kingdom of God.

sens: Opening, cavity in a surface or wall
Natural hollow in the ground, cave or underground refuge
Space through which one sees, window or opening
Den of a wild animal
H2356.detail:
1. An opening made or perceived in something: the priest Jehoiada makes a hole in the lid of the chest (2 Kings 12:9) to deposit the money for offerings, or Ezekiel sees a hole in the wall of the temple (Ezekiel 8:7).
2. A natural cavity in the ground where one can take refuge or live: the Hebrews hide in holes (1 Samuel 14:11), and Job speaks of rocky caverns where lost men live (Job 30:6).
3. An opening through which light passes or through which one sees: the beloved of the Song puts his hand through the window (Song of Solomon 5:4), a poetic image of tender communication.
4. The den or underground lair of a wild beast: the lion fills his dens with prey (Nahum 2:13), evoking his hunting lairs.
H2356.origine: The Hebrew word חֹר comes from a root expressing the idea of digging or penetration. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words related to opening and excavation. The word concretely translates the image of an empty space, pierced or dug, whether by man or by nature.
H2356.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly to describe material realities: war hideouts (1 Samuel 14:11), religious installations (2 Kings 12:9 and Ezekiel 8:7), human or animal habitats (Job 30:6, Nahum 2:13). The Song of Solomon uses it in a poetic and tender manner (Song of Solomon 5:4). The contexts vary from military to liturgical, from natural to figurative, but the concrete meaning of "hollow or opening" remains constant.
H2356.portee: This word brings the reader back to the simple reality of things: the holes where men hide in danger, the chests pierced to receive gifts at the temple, the caves where the wretched live, the lairs of wild beasts. It anchors Scripture in the concrete of the sensible world and reminds us that God dwells in a temple built by human hands, receives the gifts of His people, and knows the secret places where His children take refuge.

sens: to become white or whitish
to lose one's natural color
to show shame or fear through a pale face
H2357.detail: 1. The word first describes the physical change of a surface that becomes white or loses its initial hue. 2. It applies to the human face: the skin loses its usual color, becoming pale. This is often a sign of strong emotion — fear, shame, affliction — that is visible on the body. 3. In Isaiah 29:22, God promises Jacob that he will no longer "turn pale," meaning that shame and fear will no longer visibly mark him: his face will regain assurance and dignity. This is the promise that redemption frees him from humiliation.
H2357.origine: The Hebrew verb חָוַר comes from a root that evokes whiteness and paleness. The same family includes words for "white" or "gray." The basic image is that of color fading or discoloring, particularly visible on the human face where it reflects inner agitation.
H2357.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 29:22. God addresses the house of Jacob after redeeming Abraham: He affirms that henceforth Jacob will no longer "be ashamed" and that his "face will no longer turn pale." The context is one of restoration and salvation. The paleness of the face, often linked to shame or fear, will disappear, giving way to confidence and restored honor.
H2357.portee: This promise speaks to the heart of the believer who knows shame and fear. God assures that through redemption, the face of His people will be lifted — no more pale humiliation or fear. It is a powerful image of the dignity and assurance that comes from a restored relationship with God.

sens: Of the color of snow or milk, without a mixture of dark hue
Pure, immaculate, free from stain or blemish
H2358.detail:
1. The word describes the color white in its clearest and brightest form: that of snow or pure wool. In Daniel 7:9, the garment of the Ancient of Days is white like snow, an image of brilliant purity and absolute holiness.
2. Figuratively, white evokes moral and spiritual purity, the absence of guilt or stain. This symbolic dimension is already present in the description of the eternal God: His whiteness signifies His perfection and holy character, without any blemish.
H2358.origine: The Hebrew word חִוָּר (chivvar) designates brilliant whiteness. It is related to the idea of luminosity and clarity: what is white reflects light and stands out sharply from dark things. That is why, in biblical thought, white naturally becomes a symbol of holiness, purification, and victory over the forces of evil or impurity.
H2358.emploi: This word appears only once in the biblical text, in Daniel 7:9, in the prophetic vision where the Ancient of Days takes His throne in heaven. The whiteness of the garment and pure wool underscores the transcendent majesty and absolute holiness of the eternal God. This apocalyptic context reinforces the symbolic meaning: white is not just a color, but a manifestation of the eternal and perfect divine nature.
H2358.portee: For the reader, this image of white evokes the inaccessible holiness of God and His absolute perfection. It also reminds us that whiteness can be restored: in other biblical passages, scarlet sins become white as snow through divine forgiveness. It is an invitation to aspire to purity in the relationship with God.

sens: man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H2359.detail: Huri is a man of the tribe of Gad, mentioned only once in the Bible, during the divided monarchy of Israel. He is cited in 1 Chronicles 5:14 as the father of Abichail and son of Jaroach, in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad.
H2359.origine: The name Huri literally means "linen weaver," suggesting that the name once evoked a profession, although the Bible does not mention anything about this man's occupation. His name has come down to us through the family genealogy of the tribe of Gad.
H2359.emploi: Huri appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:14. He is listed in the genealogy of the sons of Gad, where he is mentioned as the father of Abichail. This genealogy dates back to the time when the Northern and Southern kingdoms were separated, and it allows us to trace the lineage of the Gadite families who owned land and livestock in the Transjordan region.

sens: Warrior in the service of King David
H2360.detail: Huraï is one of the thirty elite warriors who formed the king David's personal guard. He is mentioned only once in the Enumeration of the Mighty (1 Chronicles 11:32), among the trusted men that David gathered during his years of struggle before becoming king.
H2360.origine: The name Huraï literally means "linen weaver" in Hebrew, suggesting that this man was originally a craftsman before becoming a soldier. Unlike many other warriors of David, whose fathers or hometowns are known, Huraï is simply identified by his place of attachment: Nachalé-Gaasch, probably a valley or mountainous region. This is an example of a name that reveals a humble profession before its bearer was elevated to the rank of warrior in the service of the king.
H2360.emploi: Huraï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:32, in the list of the "thirty" — David's military elite. He is associated with Abiel of Araba, who accompanies him in this enumeration. Although few details are given about his life or specific military exploits, his inclusion in this honor list shows that he had earned the respect and trust of the king through his military skills and loyalty.

sens: king of Tyre, ally of David and Solomon
chief artisan of Solomon's temple
H2361G.detail:
1. Huram is best known as the king of Tyre who maintained close commercial and diplomatic relations with the kings of Israel. He sends cedar wood, stone cutters, and carpenters to David to build the royal palace (1 Chronicles 14:1), and then he helps Solomon even more significantly by providing materials and workers for the construction of the temple of the Lord (2 Chronicles 2:3-12). He even acknowledges that it is the Lord, the God of Israel, who has given Solomon wisdom and understanding (2 Chronicles 2:11-12).
2. Huram also collaborates with Solomon on trade expeditions: he provides ships and seafaring servants, and together they sail to Ophir to bring back large quantities of gold (2 Chronicles 8:18).
H2361G.origine: The name Huram means "of noble birth" or "born noble," which suits a king well. It is a variant of the name Hiram (חִירָם), more commonly used in the Chronicles. This king of Tyre, a great Phoenician trading city, represents the craftsmanship and wealth of the ancient world beyond Israel.
H2361G.emploi: Huram appears eight times in the Bible, all in the Chronicles. He is presented as the king of Tyre contemporary with David and especially Solomon. His relations with Israel are cordial and mutually beneficial: he provides construction materials (cedar wood, hewn stone), skilled workers, and even ships for trade expeditions. Huram acknowledges the greatness of the God of Israel and expresses respect and blessing toward the kings of Israel, which contrasts with the pride of other nations.
H2361G.portee: Huram shows how divine Providence extends beyond the borders of Israel: a foreign king becomes an auxiliary to God's purposes by helping to build the temple. His example invites the reader to see that God can raise up the assistance of those who serve His plans, even the unbeliever, and that true wisdom is to recognize the God of Israel above all earthly kingdoms.

sens: son of Benjamin and brother of Bela
name borne by several characters in the Old Testament
H2361H.detail:
1. Huram is first a son of Benjamin, the patriarch who founded the tribe of Benjaminites. He is mentioned in Genesis 46:21 among the sons of Benjamin who go down to Egypt with Jacob, and he also appears in 1 Chronicles 8:5 as the son of Bela, himself a son of Benjamin, making him a grandson of Benjamin.
2. The name Huram also refers to other important figures in Israel's history: a king of Tyre who allied with David and Solomon for the construction of the temple, and a chief architect of Solomon's temple. These latter figures are sometimes called Hiram, a spelling variant of the same name.
H2361H.origine: The name Huram means "of noble birth" or "well born." It comes from a Hebrew root evoking dignity and nobility. This name has borne several prominent figures in biblical history, from the simple son of Benjamin to the great artisans and foreign leaders who served the kings of Israel.
H2361H.emploi: Huram first appears as one of the twelve sons of Benjamin listed during the descent into Egypt. In 1 Chronicles 8:5, he is expressly named as the son of Bela. The text places him among the generations that established the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. This same name Huram has been borne by prominent figures: the king of Tyre and the master builder of Solomon's temple, for whom the spelling Hiram is also encountered.

sens: Chief artisan of Solomon's temple
King of Tyre allied with David and Solomon
Descendant of Benjamin
H2361I.detail:
1. Huram is primarily known as the master artisan sent by the king of Tyre to Solomon to oversee the construction of the temple in Jerusalem. He is a man of great skill, capable of casting bronze and creating intricate works of art for the house of God.
2. Huram also refers to the king of Tyre who maintains an alliance with David and then Solomon, providing cedar wood and other precious materials for the temple. This royal friendship reflects the importance and wealth of Solomon's kingdom.
3. In an earlier genealogy, Huram is mentioned as the son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, showing that this name appears at different periods in Israel's history.
H2361I.origine: The name Huram means "well born" or "of noble birth," reflecting the high status of those who bore it. It is a variant or nickname of the name Hiram (חִירָם), more frequent in the texts. The name underscores the distinction and honor attached to these important figures.
H2361I.emploi: Huram appears in the Bible as a major figure during the united monarchy in Israel. He is first mentioned in 1 Kings 7:13 as an artisan, then in 2 Chronicles 2:13 and 4:16 where he is designated as Huram-Abi, meaning "Huram my father," an honorific title given to him by Solomon. His role is central in the description of the temple's works: he designs and fabricates the bronze elements, including the great basin (the sea of bronze) and the ten basins. He is a man of great wisdom and talent recognized by the kings of Israel and by the king of Tyre.
H2361I.portee: Huram embodies excellence and mastery in the service of God. His story shows that the temple of Solomon could only be built thanks to the contribution of exceptional talents, and that God delights in using the skills of those who work for His glory. It also reminds us that wisdom and skill transcend borders: a Phoenician from Tyre becomes a valued worker of God's people.

sens: Bronze craftsman responsible for the decoration of Solomon's temple
Master builder of the casting and engraving works of the sanctuary
H2361J.detail: 1. Huram is the name of the chief craftsman hired by King Solomon to create the bronze objects for the temple in Jerusalem. He made the ashtrays, shovels, forks, and other utensils necessary for worship (2 Chronicles 4:11). His name is also given in the form "Huram-Abi," which emphasizes his reputation and status as a recognized master craftsman (2 Chronicles 4:16).
H2361J.origine: The name Huram means "of noble birth" or "one who is born free." It is a variant of the name Hiram (חִירָם), referring to the same individual. This name primarily designates the renowned architect and craftsman sent by the king of Tyre to collaborate on the construction of the sacred temple, reflecting the alliance between David-Solomon and neighboring kingdoms.
H2361J.emploi: Huram appears twice in the Bible, both times in 2 Chronicles, in the account of the construction of Solomon's temple (circa 960-950 B.C.). He is presented as the master craftsman responsible for all the bronze objects of the sanctuary: ashtrays, service utensils, decorative elements. The Bible highlights the excellence of his work by specifying that these objects were "polished bronze" (2 Chronicles 4:16), meaning they were crafted with refinement. His commitment to the temple illustrates the exceptional quality and considerable resources dedicated to the building of the place of divine worship.
H2361J.portee: Huram embodies the master craftsman whose talent and expertise are dedicated to the house of God. His story reminds us that God delights in seeing human talents, even those from neighboring nations, used with excellence for His glory and the good of His people.

sens: Mountainous region east of the Sea of Galilee
Desert territory at the borders of the Promised Land
H2362.detail:
1. Havran is a mountainous and rocky region located east of the Sea of Galilee in the Holy Land. Its name literally means "caverns," evoking the rugged and cavernous landscape of this area. It is a hard-to-access region characterized by rocky formations and natural caves.

2. Havran constitutes a border region of the territory of Israel, situated at the edge of the desert. It lies between Damascus to the north and Gilead to the south, forming the eastern boundary of the land that the prophet Ezekiel describes in his vision of the new land distribution (Ezekiel 47:18).
H2362.origine: The Hebrew name חַוְרָן (chav.ran) literally means "caverns," deriving from a root that evokes hollows, caves, and hollow rock formations. This etymology reflects the actual geography of the region: Havran is indeed a volcanic area dotted with caves and basalt formations. The word thus describes the physical character of the territory rather than a mere administrative designation.
H2362.emploi: Havran appears only twice in the Bible, both in Ezekiel 47, where the prophet outlines the ideal borders of a restored Promised Land. In Ezekiel 47:16, Havran is mentioned as an eastern reference point in the delineation of the northern border of the land. In Ezekiel 47:18, it again marks the eastern limit of the territory, situated between Damascus and Gilead. These occurrences show that Havran, although outside the territory of Israel proper, was a region known to the Israelites and served as a geographical landmark for delineating the theoretical borders of their land.
H2362.portee: For the biblical reader, Havran reminds us that the borders of the Promised Land extend beyond what Israel has actually occupied. This name evokes boundary areas, difficult and remote regions, symbolizing how God places His people at the heart of a vast territory at the edges of the known. It is a call to look beyond current borders and recognize the scope of God's plan for His people.

sens: to hurry, act quickly
to rush, run with urgency
to flee hastily
H2363A.detail:
1. To hurry means to act quickly, not to delay. For example, in Psalms 119:60, the psalmist says, "I hasten, I do not delay to observe your commandments": he means that he is eager to obey the Law without postponement.
2. To rush towards someone or something with urgency, often to help or intervene quickly. In Psalms 38:23, the supplicant cries, "Come quickly to my aid": he asks God to hasten to help him without delay.
3. To flee, to run away hastily in the face of danger. In Isaiah 28:16, the firmly laid stone symbolizes someone "who will not hasten to flee": the one who leans on it will not be seized by panic and will not escape running.
H2363A.origine: The Hebrew verb חוּשׁ (chush) fundamentally expresses the idea of rapid movement and speed. The root seems related to energy and promptness. The word appears mainly in biblical poetry (Psalms) and among the prophets, where it serves to express the urgency of an action, particularly the request for God to come without delay.
H2363A.emploi: This verb appears 19 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Psalms (about 10 occurrences) and in the prophets. It is found in the literal sense of acting quickly (Numbers 32:17: to prepare in haste), but also to ask God to intervene quickly in danger (Psalms 38:23; 70:2). It can also evoke fleeing (Isaiah 28:16) or natural speed (Habakkuk 1:8: the leopards' horses). In prayer, "to hurry" is a request addressed to God for Him to come to help quickly, expressing the urgency of the need.
H2363A.portee: This word shows how the believers of the Old Testament experienced the expectation of God. When they ask God to "hurry," they do not doubt that He can act quickly; they express their distress and their confidence that help can come instantly. For us today, this term reminds us that the presence and intervention of God do not adhere to our human timelines.

sens: To feel pleasure, to taste joy in something
To take possession of something with satisfaction
H2363B.detail:
1. The word designates the act of feeling pleasure or enjoyment: it is to experience joy in tasting or possessing something. In Ecclesiastes 2:25, the Preacher wonders who else but he can eat and enjoy — that is, feel the satisfaction and pleasure of eating.
2. By extension, to enjoy means to fully benefit from something, to derive personal satisfaction from it. It is an active, conscious pleasure that one savors.
H2363B.origine: This Hebrew verb evokes the idea of feeling, experiencing a pleasant sensation. It is rare in the Bible and appears mainly in texts reflecting on happiness and the meaning of life. The root carries the image of tasting or sensing.
H2363B.emploi: The verb chush appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ecclesiastes 2:25. The context is one of meditation on the pleasures of life and on who can truly enjoy them. The Preacher asserts that enjoying goods — eating, rejoicing — depends on a wisdom given by God. It is a word linked to existential reflection on human happiness.
H2363B.portee: This word reminds us that the ability to enjoy the goods we receive — food, life, joy — is not a right, but a gift from God linked to wisdom. To enjoy is not synonymous with sin or unrestrained indulgence; it is to recognize that God gives us the ability to take pleasure in what He creates, and that this pleasure rests on a right relationship with Him.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H2364.detail: Huscha is a man from the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Ezer and is part of the genealogy of the descendants of Hur, the founding father of Bethlehem. His name, which means "haste," may evoke a prompt character or a quick action, but the Bible provides no details about his life or deeds.
H2364.origine: The name Huscha comes from a Hebrew root meaning "haste" or "speed." It is part of the genealogy of Judah, conveying both a tribal heritage and a figurative sense attached to its etymology.
H2364.emploi: Huscha appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:4. He is listed in a genealogical record of the descendants of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah and father of Bethlehem. This brief mention is part of the historical register of the tribes of Judah, where the ancestors of the people of Israel are enumerated.

sens: Faithful friend of King David
Strategic advisor to Absalom
H2365.detail:
1. Hushai is a trusted man of David, designated as "the Archite" (from Ark).
