When David flees Jerusalem due to the revolt of his son Absalom, Hushai meets him at the summit of the mountain, his face covered in ashes as a sign of mourning (2 Samuel 15:32). He is a loyal companion who shares the king's trials.
2. Hushai becomes an advisor to the rebel Absalom, actually to serve David in secret. When Absalom asks for his opinion on the plans of the advisor Ahithophel, Hushai contradicts him by highlighting the formidable military experience of David and his warriors (2 Samuel 17:8), thus buying time for David to escape. His counsel turns the situation in favor of David, showing how wisdom and loyalty triumph over betrayal.
H2365.origine: The name Hushai means "the one who hastens" or "swift." It comes from a Hebrew root evoking movement and urgency. This name suits a man of action and quick reaction, capable of seizing opportunities to serve his king.
H2365.emploi: Hushai appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the account of Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15-17). He is also mentioned as the father of Baana, a prefect under Solomon (1 Kings 4:16), and is listed among the advisors of King David (1 Chronicles 27:33). His role changes according to the context: a faithful friend at first, then a spy-advisor at the heart of the conspiracy, and finally an administrative figure under Solomon. In each role, he embodies loyalty to the power established by God.
H2365.portee: The story of Hushai teaches that true friendship persists in adversity and can accomplish great things in the service of justice. His dedication to David, even at the risk of his life, shows how a faithful heart finds a way to serve God through his king. His wise counsel reminds us that God protects His own through ordinary human means, often through trustworthy individuals.

sens: woman of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
wife of Shacharaim
mother of Abitub and Elpaal
H2366A.detail: 1. Hushim is a woman of the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the divided monarchy in Israel (1 Chronicles 8:8). 2. She is the wife of Shacharaim, a Benjaminite chief, and she was sent away by him after he left the land of Moab (1 Chronicles 8:8). 3. She is the mother of at least two sons: Abitub and Elpaal, who themselves establish families and become ancestors of Benjaminite families (1 Chronicles 8:11).
H2366A.origine: The name Hushim literally means "she who hastens" or "she who rushes," deriving from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of speed and urgency. It is a feminine name, borne by a woman of the lineage of Benjamin during the royal period of Israel.
H2366A.emploi: Hushim appears twice in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, only in chapter 8 which lists the descendants of Benjamin. She is mentioned as one of the two wives of Shacharaim (the other being Baara), and as the mother of his sons Abitub and Elpaal. These references fit into the Chronicler's project of tracing the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin, showing how the Benjaminite families were reconstituted after the exile.

sens: son of Dan, ancestor of the Danites
H2366B.detail: Hushim is the son of Dan mentioned during the census of the children of Israel who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:23). He is also called Shuham in the book of Numbers during another census conducted in the wilderness (Numbers 26:42). His name means "the one who hastens" in Hebrew, evoking swiftness or urgency.
H2366B.origine: The name Hushim comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to hasten" or "to rush." It is a name that describes a character disposition: eagerness or promptness. In the Old Testament, proper names often carried a meaning that reflected either an expected quality or a circumstance of birth.
H2366B.emploi: Hushim is mentioned only once in the Segond 1910, in Genesis 46:23, among the seventy souls of Jacob's household who went down to Egypt. He is simply presented as the son of Dan. Later, in Numbers 26:42, the same individual is called Shuham during the census in the wilderness, which shows that two names are given to him in the biblical texts. His descendants form one of the families of the Dan clan.

sens: Son of Acher, of the tribe of Benjamin
H2366G.detail: Hushim is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is presented as the son of Acher in 1 Chronicles 7:12, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. His name literally means "the one who hastens" or "who makes haste," evoking the idea of speed or urgency.
H2366G.origine: The name Hushim comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to hasten, to press." It is a theophoric or descriptive name, common in the genealogies of Israel. The form "Hushim" (with variants like "Hushom") appears in tribal lists, notably among the Benjaminites and Danites, family groups linked by their common ancestors.
H2366G.emploi: Hushim appears only once in the provided biblical texts, in 1 Chronicles 7:12. He is listed in the genealogy of Benjamin, alongside his brothers Shuppim and Huppim, all sons of Ir or Acher according to textual variants. This isolated mention suggests that Hushim was a clan ancestor within the tribe, whose descendants marked the Benjaminite history.

sens: King of Edom during the Patriarchs
Successor of Jobab and predecessor of Hadad in the royal lineage of Edom
H2367.detail: Husham is one of the kings of Edom listed in the genealogy of the descendants of Esau. He reigned after Jobab and before Hadad, the son of Bedad (Genesis 36:34-35). The Bible does not report any specific details about his actions or reign, except that he came from the land of the Temanites, an important region of Edom. His name appears twice in Genesis and twice in Chronicles, in identical royal lists that present the order of succession of the early kings of Edom.
H2367.origine: The name Husham literally means "haste" or "speed" in Hebrew. It designates an Edomite king, although the Bible does not specify anything about the origins of this name or its exact historical context. The people of Edom were descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob, and these royal genealogies show how this people organized politically before the establishment of a centralized monarchy in Israel.
H2367.emploi: Husham is mentioned four times in the Bible, always in royal genealogical lists: twice in Genesis 36:34-35, which enumerates the kings of Edom in the order of their succession, and twice in 1 Chronicles 1:45-46, in an identical textual parallel. These lists constitute a testimony of the political and dynastic structures that existed in Edom during the time of the Patriarchs. The context shows that Husham reigned after Jobab and before Hadad, without the Bible reporting any significant events of his reign.

sens: Small engraved object that is pressed onto a soft material to leave its imprint
Ring or signet bearing an engraved stone, used as a signature or mark of authority
The imprint itself left by the seal
Distinctive mark, sign of authenticity or ownership
That which seals, confirms, or authenticates something
Image of what is precious, inviolable, intimately linked to someone
H2368.detail:
1. The seal is a small engraved object, usually mounted on a ring, that is pressed onto wax, clay, or a document to leave a mark. In Genesis 38:18, Judah gives his seal (with its cord and staff) as a pledge to Tamar, showing that it is a valuable and identifiable personal item.

2. This object serves as a signature and symbol of authority: the one who bears the seal can sign documents or give orders in its name. The engraved stones of the priestly ephods (Exodus 39:6) function as seals that engrave the names of the tribes.

3. The imprint produced by the seal on the material is also called a seal: in Job 38:14, the earth receives an "imprint" like clay receiving the image of the seal.

4. Figuratively, the seal becomes a distinctive mark of authenticity or possession: a document sealed with a seal cannot be altered without being noticed.

5. The seal can signify that which confirms or authenticates: to seal with a seal is to make something official and inviolable.

6. Finally, the word takes on a poetic and intimate value: in Song of Solomon 8:6, the lover asks to be like a seal on the heart and arm of his beloved, expressing an indissoluble union and mutual possession.
H2368.origine: The Hebrew word חֹתָם (chotam) comes from a root meaning "to close" or "to seal." It is an object that "seals" or "closes" what is written or pressed into a material. The word is related to other Hebrew forms expressing the idea of closure or signature. In biblical texts, it designates both the sealing instrument (the seal itself) and the action or imprint that results from it.
H2368.emploi: The word seal appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the legislative and poetic books. It is common in Exodus, where it describes the engraved stones of the priestly ephod (Exodus 28:21, 39:6), precious and sacred objects. In Genesis 38:18, Judah gives his personal seal, emphasizing that it is an object of great value and personal identification. In administrative contexts (1 Kings 21:8, Jeremiah 22:24), the seal serves to authenticate royal orders. In Job 38:14 and Job 41:6, the image becomes natural (the earth transforms as if under the imprint of the seal). The Song of Solomon 8:6 uses it metaphorically to express deep romantic attachment. The word thus takes on nuances from the concrete (the object) to the figurative (the mark of authenticity and intimate bond).
H2368.portee: The biblical seal teaches the believer the importance of authentication and personal marking. It is a reminder that what is sealed by God is inviolable: in Haggai 2:23, Zerubbabel becomes the seal of the Lord, meaning he bears divine authenticity and protection. The image of the seal on the heart (Song of Solomon 8:6) invites the Christian to feel God's love as an indelible mark, sealed in the very heart. It is also an image of the Holy Spirit, who seals the believer for eternity.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher, ancestor of the people of Israel
H2369G.detail: Hotham is a character from the Old Testament mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher. He is the son of Heber and the father of several children, including Zophah and Imna. He is also known by the name Helem, two names likely designating the same person in the genealogical records of Israel.
H2369G.origine: The name Hotham means "seal" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking the idea of a mark or signature. This name, like many in the genealogies of Israel, was borne by ancestors of the twelve tribes and sometimes expressed a quality or circumstance related to birth or destiny.
H2369G.emploi: Hotham is mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 7:32, in the genealogical list of the tribe of Asher. This passage enumerates the descendants of Heber and his children, including Hotham who himself had children. He appears in the context of the genealogical records of David, which document the lineages of the tribes of Israel to establish the order and heritage of God's people.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher, father of two of King David's mighty warriors
H2369H.detail: Hotham is a man of the tribe of Asher mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Shama and Jehiel, two warriors who are listed among the "mighty men of David," that is, the elite soldiers of the king (1 Chronicles 11:44). These two sons fought alongside David and distinguished themselves by their valor in service to the king of Israel.
H2369H.origine: The name Hotham comes from the Hebrew חוֹתָם (hotam), which means "seal" — the object that engraves a mark of authentication and power. This symbolic meaning reflects the importance of the name: a seal confers authority and identity, just as a father confers his name and heritage to his children.
H2369H.emploi: Hotham appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:44, within the list of David's warriors. This list enumerates the most valiant men who followed David during his reign and enabled him to conquer and defend his kingdom. Hotham is mentioned as the father of two of these valiant soldiers, indicating that his family was honored at the royal court. No other biographical details are provided about him.

sens: perceive with the eyes, look
observe, examine carefully
contemplate a vision or a dream
attend, be a witness to
appear, seem (passive sense)
H2370.detail:
1. Perceive with the eyes, look: this is the simplest and most common meaning. Someone sees something in front of them, like King Nebuchadnezzar who "sees" four men walking in the midst of the fire without being burned (Daniel 3:25).
2. Observe, examine carefully: to look intentionally to understand what one sees. Daniel "saw the feet and toes" of the statue in a dream and observed the details to interpret what it meant (Daniel 2:41).
3. Contemplate a vision or a dream: to see in a dream or vision, a supernatural experience where God reveals something to a person who is asleep. Daniel "was looking" during his night vision when he saw the four beasts coming up from the sea (Daniel 7:2).
4. Attend, be a witness to: to be present and witness something happening. The king's advisors claim that it does not "seem fitting" for them to "see" (that is, to attend to) the king's contempt (Ezra 4:14).
5. Appear, seem: in certain passive contexts, the word takes on a nuance of appearance or suitability, like what "seems" good or fitting in someone's eyes.
H2370.origine: The Aramaic verb חֲזָה (ḥazâ) comes from a root that expresses the action of directing the gaze toward something. It is common in biblical Aramaic, particularly in the Aramaic sections of Daniel and the book of Ezra. The same root exists in Hebrew in a similar form (חָזָה, ḥazah), and it is also associated with the word "vision" (חָזוֹן, ḥazon): to see is the foundational act of prophetic vision. The family of the word emphasizes the importance of sight, whether ordinary or spiritual.
H2370.emploi: The verb "see" (חֲזָה) appears 29 times in the Aramaic Old Testament, almost exclusively in Daniel and Ezra. It is used in two main ways: on one hand, it describes ordinary perceptions (seeing something that exists before oneself), and on the other hand, and especially, it reports Daniel's night visions and prophetic dreams. In these visions, Daniel "sees" mysterious symbols — the statue with feet of iron and clay, the four beasts of the sea, the throne of the Ancient of Days — and these "visions" reveal both the hidden meaning of King Nebuchadnezzar's dreams and God's future judgments on the kingdoms. The context of prophetic visions largely dominates: looking is never passive; it is always the moment when God makes known His will and secrets.
H2370.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that "seeing" in the Bible is not just the physical act of perceiving. When God gives a vision or a dream, it is an act of revelation: He shows His servants what is to come. Daniel's dreams and visions teach us that God is in control of history and the kingdoms of this world. This word invites the believer to keep their eyes open to God's will, whether it manifests in ordinary circumstances or in moments when He speaks to us prophetically or personally.

sens: King of Syria at the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel and Judah
Man sent by his master Ben-Hadad to consult the prophet Elisha
Murderer who seized the throne of Syria by killing his king
Oppressor of Israel and Judah for several decades
H2371.detail:
1. Hazael is a king of Syria who first appears in history in 1 Kings 19:15, where God commands the prophet Elijah to anoint him to reign over Syria. His name means "the one who sees God."

2. At the beginning of his story, Hazael was sent by his master Ben-Hadad, the reigning king of Syria, to consult the prophet Elisha about an illness (2 Kings 8:9). He presented himself to Elisha as an obedient servant, bringing a rich gift.

3. But Elisha saw in Hazael a future king and oppressor. The next day, Hazael killed Ben-Hadad by suffocating him with a wet blanket, and then reigned in his place (2 Kings 8:15). This was the fulfillment of Elijah's prophecy.

4. As king of Syria, Hazael became a terrible oppressor of Israel and Judah. He fought at Ramoth-Gilead against Israel (2 Kings 9:14-15), conquered the city of Gath, and threatened Jerusalem (2 Kings 12:17). He oppressed Israel throughout the life of King Joash (2 Kings 13:22).
H2371.origine: The name Hazael literally means "the one who sees God" (from the Hebrew "hazah" = see, and "El" = God). It is a theophoric name, common in ancient Syria, that expressed piety toward the deity. Ironically, this pious name designates a man who became a murderer and tyrant.
H2371.emploi: Hazael appears in 21 biblical passages, mostly in 2 Kings (12 times) and also in 2 Chronicles and Amos. His story spans several decades of the reigns of the northern and southern kings. Initially presented as a respectful servant of Ben-Hadad (2 Kings 8:9), he is revealed by Elisha as a murderer who will overthrow and kill his master (2 Kings 8:12-15). Once king, the texts systematically describe him as an oppressor: he fights against Israel, conquers cities, oppresses the people, and makes neighboring kingdoms tremble. His domination is first exercised over Israel under Joash (2 Kings 13:22), then gradually weakens (2 Kings 13:24-25). Amos mentions him among God's enemies (Amos 1:4).
H2371.portee: The story of Hazael shows that God uses even evil instruments to accomplish His purposes. His prophecy through Elijah reveals divine knowledge of the future. The oppression he exerts on Israel and Judah reminds us that the sin of peoples distant from God exposes them to divine judgment through formidable enemies. However, his domination does not last forever: God preserves a remnant and allows Israel to gradually recover, demonstrating His faithfulness despite the chastisements.

sens: to perceive by the eyes, to look at
to know by experience or understanding
to notice, to observe
to receive a prophetic vision
to contemplate with attention or reverence
to choose, to discern
H2372.detail: 1. To perceive by the eyes is the simple act of looking at something or someone. Thus in Exodus 24:11, the leaders of Israel "saw God" in the sense that they had a direct and conscious experience in His presence. 2. To know by experience or understanding: to see also means to understand, to grasp by reason. In Job 19:27, "I shall see Him" expresses the expectation of encountering God in person and being aware of it. 3. To notice means to observe something that presents itself to us. Isaiah 26:11 states that the enemies do not "see" the mighty hand of God, meaning they do not discern it or refuse to acknowledge it. 4. To receive a prophetic vision is the meaning of the word when it designates the mystical experience of seers. Prophets like Isaiah (Isaiah 1:1) receive their messages in the form of visions: they "see" what God reveals to them. 5. To contemplate with attention or reverence: this is to see while focusing on what one is looking at, often with admiration or respect. Psalms 63:3 expresses the desire to behold God in the sanctuary, to fix one's eyes on Him with all one's heart. 6. To choose, to discern: to see can also mean to evaluate and select. In Exodus 18:21, Moses must "choose" capable men from among the people, in the sense that he recognizes and judges their competence.
H2372.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that primarily denotes the physical act of perceiving by sight. In Hebrew, as in other Semitic languages, "to see" naturally extends to the meaning of "to understand" or "to know." The word also applies, from the Old Testament onward, to the mystical experience of prophets who "see" divine revelations in states of trance or ecstasy — as clearly shown by the usages in the titles of prophetic books (Isaiah, Amos, Micah, Habakkuk), all introduced by "vision of" (literally "what he has seen").
H2372.emploi: This verb appears 51 times in the retained Hebrew text. It is especially prevalent in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and among the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Micah, Habakkuk). In the Psalms, "to see" expresses the desire to meet God face to face or to witness His action (Psalms 11:7, 63:3). Among the prophets, the word takes on its technical meaning of "to receive a vision" (Isaiah 1:1, Amos 1:1). In Exodus 18:21, it takes the rare meaning of "to choose" or "to discern." In Job, "to see" oscillates between physical experience and certainty of faith: Job hopes to "see" God and be justified (Job 19:27). Ezekiel criticizes false prophets who claim to "see" visions but lie (Ezekiel 13:6-9).
H2372.portee: This word invites the reader not to dissociate the physical "seeing" from the spiritual "seeing." For faith, to see God — not with natural eyes, but by faith, experience, and knowledge — is the pinnacle of communion with Him. The prophets who "see" visions receive a terrible and demanding gift: that of discerning God's will and speaking about it even when it costs. The text also teaches us that there is a deceptive seeing (the false prophets of Lamentations 2:14 and Ezekiel 13): having a vision does not automatically mean having the truth.

sens: Front part of an animal's body, between the neck and the belly
Part of the victim offered in sacrifice, waved before God
Portion reserved for the priests in the sacrifices
H2373.detail:
1. The chest refers to the front part of the animal's body, the area that extends between the neck and the belly. It is a well-defined region of the body, visible and easy to separate from the sacrificed beast.

2. In Israelite worship, the chest of certain victims (particularly the ram or the animal offered in a thank offering) becomes an element of the ritual: the priest takes it and waves it "back and forth before the Lord" (Exodus 29:26, Leviticus 7:30). This act of waving (called "the wave offering") symbolically consecrates the offering to God before it is distributed.

3. The chest forms a privileged part reserved for the priesthood: it belongs to the priest as his right in the thank offerings, just like the shoulder (Leviticus 7:34, Leviticus 10:14). This is why it is often called "the chest that is waved back and forth" — this phrase summarizes both the ritual gesture and the priest's food right.
H2373.origine: The Hebrew word חָזֶה (cha.zeh) is derived from a root that evokes the chest as what is visible or apparent on the front of the body. The related Aramaic word חֲדִי (cha.di) carries the same meaning. This term specifically designates this region of the body in a concrete and sacrificial context, without figurative connotation.
H2373.emploi: The word appears about twelve times in the Torah, exclusively in the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, all concentrated in the chapters of cultic law. It always refers to the chest of an animal offered in sacrifice: that of the ram of Aaron's consecration (Exodus 29:26-27), that of the thank offerings (Leviticus 7:30-34), that of the Nazarite (Numbers 6:20). In each case, the chest is mentioned alongside the shoulder, together forming the portion designated for the priests. The act of "waving" or "presenting" the chest is the heart of the rite: before the meat is eaten, it is offered to God through this solemn ritual gesture.
H2373.portee: For the biblical reader, this sacrificed chest reminds us that Israel's worship was never an abstraction: it involved the entire body of the victim, shared between God (the fat burned), the priest (the chest and shoulder), and the people (the rest of the flesh eaten in communion). This ritual sharing taught that serving God involved the whole body, all that we are.

sens: One who sees visions or receives revelations from God
Inspired prophet who communicates the word of the Lord
Man endowed with spiritual authority before the king
H2374.detail:
1. The seer is literally one who sees — not with the eyes of the body, but by receiving visions and direct revelations from God. It is an inner, spiritual vision: thus Isaiah describes the seers as men whose "eyes the Lord has covered" (Isaiah 29:10), unable to see what God reveals.
2. The seer is a prophet, a messenger of the Lord tasked with conveying His word to the people and to kings. Gad, the seer of David (2 Samuel 24:11), brings to David the words of the Lord. Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer are mentioned together as having received the commands of the Lord conveyed by the prophets (2 Chronicles 29:25).
3. The seer holds an important place at the royal court: as the king's spiritual advisor, he enjoys recognized authority. David surrounds himself with seers; kings consult them about God's plans. But false seers, deceivers, seek to mislead the people by hiding the truth from them (Isaiah 30:10; Micah 3:7).
H2374.origine: The Hebrew word חֹזֶה (chozeh) comes from the root חָזָה (chazah), which means "to see," "to behold." Thus, it refers to a seer, one who sees. In biblical Hebrew, this root evokes an inner, spiritual vision, not a mere physical sight. The word designates one who has access to the invisible world of God through revelation, unlike the ordinary people who can only hear it reported.
H2374.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the historical books (Samuel, Chronicles) and the prophets (Isaiah, Amos, Micah). It designates major figures: Samuel, Nathan, Gad with David, Jehu, Hanani, Iddo with other kings. These seers are trustworthy men whom kings rely on. But the word is also used to denounce false seers, charlatans who mislead the people with lies (Isaiah 28:15; Amos 7:12; Micah 3:7). The authentic seer sees what God reveals; the false seer fabricates illusions.
H2374.portee: For the Christian reader, the seer reminds us that true prophecy comes from God alone. It is not human divination or fantasy, but a vision granted by the Lord to the one He chooses. Recognizing the true seer from the false requires discernment: the word of the authentic seer always aligns with God's will and produces good, while the false seer deceives for his own profit or that of opposing powers. It is a lesson in humility regarding revelations: only the word that God Himself transmits matters.

sens: Son of Nahor and Milcah
Grandson of Abraham
H2375.detail: Hazo is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:22. He is the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He has brothers Uz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel, and shares with some of them the same father but a different mother. His name means "vision" in Hebrew, a poetic image that perhaps evokes a quality noted at his birth.
H2375.origine: The name Hazo means "vision" in Hebrew. It comes from a root expressing the action of seeing, having a prophetic or spiritual vision. It is a typical theophoric name from the patriarchal era, where names often carried a spiritual dimension. Hazo belongs to the family of Nahor, whose genealogy is preserved to show the connections between Abraham and the peoples of Aram-Naharaim.
H2375.emploi: Hazo appears only once in the entire Bible, in Genesis 22:22, where the apostle lists the children of Nahor, Abraham's brother. This genealogy appears immediately after the account of Isaac's sacrifice, in a passage that establishes the familial ties between Abraham and neighboring peoples. His mention shows that God was interested not only in Abraham's line but also in his extended kin. Hazo remains a very minor figure in the Bible, known only through this genealogical listing.

sens: Supernatural spectacle, image or scene that God shows to someone while asleep or awake
Divine message communicated through images
Divine manifestation in impressive images
H2376.detail:
1. A vision is primarily an image or scene that someone sees — but not with ordinary eyes. It is something that appears to the mind, usually when one is asleep or in a particular state. Daniel receives such night visions where he sees bizarre and terrifying creatures: "I looked in my night visions, and behold, there was a fourth beast, dreadful" (Daniel 7:7). The image remains etched in memory and deeply disturbs the one who sees it.

2. This vision is always a message from God: it is not a mere confused dream, but a divine communication through images. When "the secret was revealed to Daniel in a vision during the night," it means that God showed him something important that he could not discover otherwise (Daniel 2:19). The images are like a divine language: they tell something, they signify.

3. These visions are often impressive and even terrifying because they reveal the reality of the spiritual world and God's plans. Daniel reports that "the visions of my head troubled me" (Daniel 7:15), so powerful was the supernatural spectacle. It is an appearance — a veil that lifts on the invisible world.
H2376.origine: The Hebrew word חֱזוּ (chazou) comes from a root meaning "to see" or "to look." It is a name formed from the verb that expresses the action of seeing, but here it specifically designates what one sees in a divine revelation, not a mere ordinary vision. This word appears mainly in the book of Daniel, where visions are central: God shows Daniel what will happen, from successive kingdoms to the end of time.
H2376.emploi: This word appears 12 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the book of Daniel (about 11 occurrences), and once in Isaiah. It always designates a divine revelation through images. Daniel receives several: a night vision about the king's secret (Daniel 2:19), visions while he sleeps that fill him with fear (Daniel 4:5), night visions showing the four beasts of the apocalypse (Daniel 7:1-7). The word can refer either to the act of seeing the vision ("during my night visions"), or the content of what is seen ("the visions of my head"). In all cases, it is God who communicates through this means.
H2376.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God does not leave us orphans: He can speak to us and show us invisible things. Biblical visions are not hallucinations or fantasies, but real messages coming from the spiritual world. They require humility to receive and wisdom to interpret, but they are proof that God is at work in history and that He guides us.

sens: Supernatural appearance in a state of ecstasy or sleep, where God communicates with the prophet
Message or revelation received through this mysterious appearance
Prophetic word or divine oracle conveyed to the people
Title given to the books of the Lord's prophecies
H2377.detail: 1. A vision is a supernatural appearance where the prophet sees and hears in an extraordinary way, either during sleep or in a state of ecstasy where he is caught up out of himself. When Samuel was young, "the word of the Lord was rare in those days; visions were not widespread" (1 Samuel 3:1): this indicates that a vision is a rare and solemn event where God manifests directly. 2. The vision is the content of what the prophet receives: the message, the revelation that God communicates to him in this supernatural experience. When Daniel "had this vision and I sought to understand it" (Daniel 8:15), he tries to grasp the meaning of the message that was shown to him. 3. This word also designates the prophetic word, the oracle that the prophet proclaims to the people in the name of the Lord. Ezekiel reports that "They seek visions from the prophets" (Ezekiel 7:26): the people hope to receive prophetic words that guide them. 4. Vision is also the title given to collections of prophecies: the book of Isaiah begins with "The vision of Isaiah" (Isaiah 1:1), which means that the entirety of the prophet's oracles is presented as a coherent whole received in these divine experiences.
H2377.origine: The Hebrew word חָזוֹן (vision) comes from the root חזה (to see, to behold), which expresses the act of seeing with intensity or particular attention. The verb designates a mental or spiritual vision, not just a physical one. In Hebrew thought, "seeing" a divine revelation means receiving and understanding it. The word thus carries the idea of a supernatural and personal perception, quite different from merely hearing words.
H2377.emploi: The word vision appears 34 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the prophetic books: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel are its major users. It first designates the mysterious experience of the prophet (1 Samuel 3:1; Daniel 8:15), then the prophetic message itself (Ezekiel 7:26; Ezekiel 13:16). The context sometimes shows concern: the people "seek visions" when they are rare (Ezekiel 7:26), or false prophets claim to have "visions of peace" that are lies (Ezekiel 13:16). Proverbs 29:18 states a principle: "Where there is no vision, the people perish." Daniel receives several successive visions, which he must interpret the hidden meaning of (Daniel 8:1 to 8:26). The vision is always presented as a direct and authentic means of communication between God and His prophet.
H2377.portee: For the biblical reader, the vision means that God has never been satisfied with abstract words: He speaks to His servants through striking, often enigmatic images that require meditation and interpretation. It reminds us that encountering God engages the whole person, including imagination and spiritual senses. The rarity of visions at certain times (1 Samuel 3:1) invites recognition of the precious and serious nature of these divine calls.

sens: Supernatural communication through which God manifests Himself or communicates His will
Set of truths or facts that God has communicated to the prophets
H2378.detail:
1. A revelation is a message or manifestation that God directly addresses to His prophets to make known His will or His purposes. It is a supernatural act by which God unveils Himself and speaks. In 2 Chronicles 9:29, "the revelations of Jeedo the prophet" are mentioned as a source of information about Solomon's actions and reign.

2. The word also designates the entirety of the prophetic messages recorded in writing, that is, the words that God has made known through the prophets and which are preserved in books or accounts. These revelations form part of the prophetic corpus that a king can consult to understand God's will or the history of his people.
H2378.origine: The Hebrew word חָזוֹת (hazot) comes from the root חזה (hazah) which means "to see." It first refers to a visual experience or a supernatural perception: the prophet "sees" what God shows him. A revelation is therefore literally what has been "seen" or contemplated in a vision. This word belongs to the vocabulary of distinct prophetic experiences, where the seer (חוֹזֶה, hoze) receives directly from God what he must know or announce.
H2378.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 9:29, where it designates the written or reported revelations of the prophet Jeedo concerning Jeroboam. The context shows that the "revelations" of the prophets form historical and religious sources: they record important facts of a king's reign and reflect God's will regarding him. The singular use of the word suggests that it is a technical term for the prophetic messages preserved in writing.
H2378.portee: The word reminds us that God does not leave His people without guidance: He speaks through the prophets and reveals His purposes to them. These revelations are not human speculations, but authentic communications from God. They form the foundation upon which God's people must rely to know and obey His will.

sens: What is visible, what can be seen
Visual range, extent of what is perceptible to sight
H2379.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what is visible, what presents itself to the eyes. In the dream that Nebuchadnezzar recounts to Daniel, a gigantic tree "became great and strong, its top reached to the heavens, and it was visible from the ends of the whole earth" (Daniel 4:11) — the underlying Hebrew verb means that the tree was visible, that it could be seen from very far away, so impressive was it.
2. By extension, the word also expresses the idea of visual range, the distance or extent from which something can be perceived. When the text repeats, "The tree that you saw, which became great and strong, whose top reached to the heavens, and that was seen from all the points of the earth" (Daniel 4:20), it emphasizes that the visibility of this tree was universal, that it was visible everywhere, illustrating its extraordinary power.
H2379.origine: The word is Aramaic חֲזוֹת (ḥăzôt), which corresponds to the Hebrew חָזוֹן (ḥāzôn, "vision" H2377). These two words share the same root, related to the verb "to see" or "to look." Biblical vision is not just a mental act: it is primarily what is seen, what is visible, what presents itself to the gaze. In the context of prophetic dreams, like that of Nebuchadnezzar, seeing refers to the ability to perceive and understand a hidden or symbolic reality.
H2379.emploi: The word appears twice in the Aramaic New Testament, both in the book of Daniel, in chapter 4, where King Nebuchadnezzar reports his dream. The tree he saw symbolizes the kingdom or royal power, and the fact that it "was visible from all points of the earth" expresses the scope and universal domination of this power. It is a descriptive use, painting the image of a tree so large that no geographical limit can stop it — hence the repetition of the expression in verses 11 and 20 to reinforce the impression of incomparable splendor and boundless reach.
H2379.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, spiritual vision begins by seeing concretely, by perceiving the signs that God places before our eyes. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream, what the king "sees" speaks to him of the divine judgment that awaits him: God makes visible so that man may understand. For the believer, this invites us to pay attention to what God shows us, to cultivate discernment in the face of the signs He places on our path.

sens: Supernatural appearance or divine message received by a prophet
Agreement, pact, or covenant
Prominent aspect, what is seen first
H2380.detail:
1. A vision is a supernatural manifestation through which God reveals Himself to a prophet, often in the form of images or symbols. Isaiah says that a "terrible vision" was revealed to him (Isaiah 21:2), and the prophet Daniel reports his visions of beasts with impressive horns (Daniel 8:5). It is the oracle of the prophet, what he sees and what he receives from God to convey.

2. The word also refers to a visible or tangible agreement or covenant. In Isaiah 28:18, the "covenant with death" and the "pact with the realm of the dead" will be "destroyed" — the word here refers to the contract itself, the visible and tangible commitment.

3. It is also what is noticeable at first glance, the aspect that catches the eye: the "goat" has a "great" horn between its eyes (Daniel 8:5), and this "great" horn also appears in Daniel 8:8. It is the prominent feature, what stands out.
H2380.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to see, to look." The vision is what is offered to the sight, to the view. Prophets see what other men do not see: supernatural realities or symbolic divine messages. That is why the same word can also refer to an agreement or a pact — something concrete, visible, that can be "seen" with one's eyes.
H2380.emploi: The word appears 5 times, mainly in the writings of the prophets Isaiah and Daniel. In Isaiah 21:2, it refers to a terrible prophetic revelation. In Isaiah 29:11, the "revelation" is compared to a sealed book — it is the divine message, incomprehensible to the one who receives it. In Isaiah 28:18 and Daniel 8:5-8, the word takes on the meaning of what catches the eye: the visible covenant, the impressive horn of the goat. Each time, there is the idea of something prominent, that cannot be ignored: either a supernatural message that imposes itself, or an object that stands out.
H2380.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God communicates with His prophets through visions — a form of direct and supernatural revelation. It invites us to consider the prophetic vision as reliable and important, as it comes from God. It is also a call to vigilance: the agreements or pacts we make are visible, concrete, and God takes them into account.

sens: Levite from the time of David or Solomon, son of Shimei
Son of Shimei, brother of Shelomith and Haran
H2381.detail:
1. Haziel is a Levite who lived during the time of David or Solomon, from the family of Shimei belonging to the Gershonites (1 Chronicles 23:9). He is one of the three sons mentioned and represents an important line in the organization of Levitical worship.
2. He is the brother of Shelomith and Haran, all three forming a family unit within the tribe of Levi. These three brothers are presented as heads of paternal houses of the family of Laadan.
H2381.origine: His name means "vision of God," composed of two Hebrew elements: "vision" and "God." This name reflects a piety characteristic of Levitical names from this period, expressing a direct spiritual relationship with the Lord.
H2381.emploi: Haziel appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 23:9. He is mentioned in the context of David's census of the Levites and the organization of their families for the service of the Temple. His inclusion in this genealogy indicates his importance in the administrative and religious structure of the time, although few details are given about his personal life or specific functions.

sens: Man of Judah who returned from exile to Jerusalem
H2382.detail: Hazaja is a descendant of Shelah (a branch of the tribe of Judah) who returned to Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon, during the time of Nehemiah. He appears in the genealogy of Maaseiah, one of the inhabitants who resettled in the restored capital (Nehemiah 11:5).
H2382.origine: The name means "God has seen." It is composed of the divine Hebrew name (Yah) and a verb meaning "to see," expressing the belief that God has observed and cared for the one who bears this name.
H2382.emploi: Hazaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:5. He is listed in the register of families that returned from the Babylonian exile to rebuild Jerusalem. His name appears in a long genealogy, situating his importance as an ancestor of a house established in the restored holy city.

sens: King of Syria during the Divided Monarchy
H2383.detail: 1. Hezjon is a king of Syria who reigned in Damascus, before the time of King Asa of Judah. He is the father of Tabrimmon and the grandfather of Ben-Hadad, king of Syria mentioned in 1 Kings 15:18 as the recipient of the gifts that Asa sent to gain his support against the king of Israel.
H2383.origine: The name Hezjon means "vision" in Hebrew, formed from the word חֶזְיוֹן (vision). It designates a Syrian ruler from the Levant kingdoms in the 10th century BCE. Some historians believe he may be identical to Rezon, a contemporary of Solomon, although this is not definitively established.
H2383.emploi: Hezjon appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 15:18. He is presented there as the father of Tabrimmon and the grandfather of Ben-Hadad, king of Syria. The context shows that his descendants inherited the throne of Damascus and maintained diplomatic relations with the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

sens: Supernatural manifestation in which God reveals Himself to a person
State of ecstasy or sleep where a divine revelation appears
Message or prophetic word received from God
Spectacle or representation that disappears like a dream
H2384.detail:
1. The vision is a supernatural manifestation where God shows Himself to someone to communicate His will or plans. It can be very vivid and precise: when Nathan reports to David "all this vision" (2 Samuel 7:17), it is a divine word received and transmitted, carrying an important promise.
2. Often, the vision occurs at night, in that particular state between wakefulness and sleep where the mind is receptive. Job describes it well: "At the moment when the visions of the night stir the thought, when men are delivered to a deep sleep" (Job 4:13). It is in this state of vulnerability and openness that God speaks.
3. The vision is a means of prophetic communication. It carries a word or message from God, not just an image. Unlike simple human dreams, the vision has divine authority.
4. Like a dream that fades upon waking, the vision appears and then disappears: "It will fly away like a dream, and it will not be found; it will vanish like a night vision" (Job 20:8). It is a fleeting but striking reality.
H2384.origine: The Hebrew word חִזָּיוֹן comes from a root meaning "to see," particularly the prophetic vision or appearance. It is related to the verb חָזָה (to see, to contemplate, to be visionary). This word describes less the act of ordinary seeing than the supernatural perception, the appearance of a divine or hidden reality.
H2384.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books. In the books of Job, it refers to the troubling night visions that disturb sleep (Job 4:13; 7:14; 20:8; 33:15). In 2 Samuel 7:17, it refers to the prophetic vision given to Nathan regarding David's descendants. In Isaiah 22:1, the poetic expression "valley of visions" may refer to Jerusalem itself, presented as the place where God reveals Himself. Joel 2:28 asserts that in the last days, visions will be given to young men. Zechariah 13:4 mentions the garments of the visionaries. The word covers both the immediate experience (the vision received) and its content (the communicated message).
H2384.portee: The vision reminds the believer that God does not remain silent: He speaks, He reveals Himself, He communicates His plans. It is a comfort for those seeking divine guidance. But the biblical vision is not an escape from reality — it often comes at night, in the humility of sleep, and it disappears like a dream, leaving the visionary responsible for understanding and obeying it. It teaches me that listening to God requires both receptivity and discernment.

sens: A luminous phenomenon that accompanies a storm
A manifestation of divine power in nature
A sign of God's intervention for salvation
H2385.detail:
1. Lightning is the bright streak that shines in the sky during a storm. It is a meteorological phenomenon that God governs: in Job 28:26 and 38:25, God is the one who "traced the path of lightning," which means He completely masters these impressive natural forces.
2. Lightning becomes an image of a power that fills with fear and wonder. When God "produces lightning" (Zechariah 10:1), it shows His dominion over natural phenomena; it is a visible sign of His majesty and action.
3. In the context of Zechariah 10:1, lightning comes as a response to the requests made to the Lord and accompanies the beneficial rain. Lightning then becomes a sign of divine favor, of God's saving intervention that provides for the needs of His people.
H2385.origine: The Hebrew word חֲזִיז comes from a root that evokes something bright, shining. It is related to the idea of something that shines suddenly and intensely. The word belongs to the vocabulary of nature as God manifests it: like other meteorological phenomena in the biblical text, lightning is always linked to divine action, never to impersonal natural causes.
H2385.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, only in poetic or prophetic passages. In Job 28:26 and 38:25, in God's speeches to Job, lightning is among the natural phenomena that the Lord governs with wisdom and power — a response to Job who seeks to understand the mysteries of God. In Zechariah 10:1, the prophet invites the people to ask God for rain and lightning, promising a generous divine response. Lightning is always linked to rain, a symbol of blessing and life. The word is never used for destructive lightning: it designates rather the luminous phenomenon as a manifestation of God's creative power.
H2385.portee: This word teaches that the natural powers that terrified the ancients — the storm, lightning — are not in the realm of chance or rival gods, but in the exclusive domain of the God of Israel. For the believer, lightning becomes a visible reminder that God governs everything, including what exceeds our understanding, and a sign that asking the Lord is opening oneself to His blessing. This encourages trust in the One who masters phenomena that surpass humans.

sens: A domesticated animal with a stocky body and split hooves that does not chew the cud
Wild boar from the forests
An unclean animal according to the Law of Moses, forbidden for consumption
H2386.detail: 1. The pig is a domesticated animal raised for its meat, recognizable by its massive body and divided hooves; although it has split hooves, it does not chew the cud, which makes it unclean according to biblical criteria (Leviticus 11:7). 2. The wild boar is the wild form of the pig, which lives in forests and ravages fields and vineyards, as mentioned in Psalm 80:14 where it "devours" the vine. 3. For an Israelite, the pig is absolutely forbidden: one cannot eat its flesh or even touch its carcass (Deuteronomy 14:8). This impurity is so profound that eating pork symbolizes a total rejection of the covenant with God and a turning towards pagan practices (Isaiah 65:4, 66:3).
H2386.origine: The Hebrew word חֲזִיר (cha.zir) designates both the pig and the wild boar. Its exact etymology is debated, but it refers to this well-known animal of the ancient Levant. The distinction between the domesticated pig and the wild boar appears clearly in biblical usages: the word applies to both.
H2386.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the Law texts (Leviticus and Deuteronomy) that list unclean animals. The pig carries a strong theological charge: eating its flesh is not only forbidden by the Law, but it is a sign of rupture with God and the covenant. Isaiah denounces the Israelites who eat pork as those who indulge in abomination and idolatry (Isaiah 65:4, 66:3). The wild boar also appears as an image of devastation and destruction (Psalm 80:14). Proverbs uses the image of the pig symbolically: a gold ring in the snout of a pig is a beautiful adornment on a vile animal, an image of a beautiful woman without discernment (Proverbs 11:22).
H2386.portee: For the Christian reader, the pig reminds us that the Old Testament distinguished the clean from the unclean, the holy from the profane. This distinction was pedagogical: it taught Israel the separation from pagan nations. In the New Testament, this prohibition is abrogated (Mark 7:19), which shows that holiness comes not from what one eats, but from the heart. However, the image of the pig remains powerful in the Bible: it symbolizes baseness, moral impurity, and rejection of God.

sens: Priest during the time of King David
Chief of a monthly course of temple service
H2387G.detail:
1. Hezir was a priest who lived during the time of King David. He is mentioned in the register of priestly divisions established by David to organize the temple service. In 1 Chronicles 24:15, he appears in the list of heads of priestly families, assigned to the seventeenth monthly course.
2. Each course was to ensure the temple service for one month of the year. Hezir led his group of priests during his month of service, as clearly indicated by his appearance in this enumeration of the leaders of the eighteen divisions: he was the chief responsible for the seventeenth rotation.
H2387G.origine: The Hebrew name חֵזִיר (che-zir) literally means "wild boar" or "pig." Although the precise etymology is debated, this name was borne by this important priestly family. It was a common practice in Israel to give animal names to people, not out of disdain but sometimes to express strength or particularity.
H2387G.emploi: Hezir is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:15. This mention occurs in the context where King David, in preparation for the construction of the temple, organized the priests into twenty-four rotating divisions to ensure daily and regular worship. Each division, led by a head of a priestly house, served in turn for one month each year. Hezir was the chief of the seventeenth division, indicating a position of responsibility within the Davidic cultic system.

sens: Leader of the people during the time of Nehemiah
Priest during the time of King David
H2387H.detail: Hezir is the name of a person mentioned in the Bible. He is a leader of the people who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah upon the return from exile (Nehemiah 10:20). The name "Hezir" literally means "pig" or "wild boar" in Hebrew, but it is simply a personal name unrelated to the animal. Ancient sources also mention a priest of the same name during the time of King David, who led the priestly course of the 17th month, but only Hezir, the leader of the people during Nehemiah's time, is attested in the biblical text we know.
H2387H.origine: The name Hezir comes from a Hebrew root meaning "pig" or "wild boar." Although it is an uncommon name, it was borne by important figures in Israel's history, including priests and leaders. The animal associated with the name has no connection to the character of the person who bears it: it was simply a name given at birth.
H2387H.emploi: Hezir appears only once in the Bible: in Nehemiah 10:20. He is among the leaders of the people who affixed their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah's leadership during the return from exile to Jerusalem. This event, which occurred after the Babylonian captivity, testifies to the willingness of God's people to renew their commitment to the divine covenant and the Law of Moses.

sens: Become strong, grow in strength or vigor
Make strong, give strength or courage to someone
Become hard, rigid, or insensitive (especially the heart)
Persist, assert oneself or intensify (for a situation or feeling)
Repair or restore
Hold firmly, grasp, retain
H2388G.detail:
1. Become strong: this primarily refers to physical strength that increases and solidifies. Joseph notes that the famine "was increasing" in Egypt (Genesis 41:56) — the word describes how a situation worsens, becoming more severe and powerful.
2. Make strong: to give courage and energy. The Lord commands Joshua: "Be strong and courageous" (Joshua 1:9), it is a call to draw inner strength to move forward despite fear.
3. Become hard: Pharaoh's heart hardened with each plague (Exodus 7:13, 9:35) — it is the image of a will that hardens, refusing to bend, becoming insensitive.
4. Intensify: a reality that grows, asserts itself. The kingdom of Joram asserts itself when he "was strengthened" (2 Chronicles 21:4).
5. Repair: to restore, to fix. The priests "were repairing" what was damaged in the house of God (2 Kings 12:6).
6. Hold firmly: to maintain grip, to keep. It is the strength of the hand that grips, retaining what it has seized.
H2388G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of firmness, solidity. The word is used for anything that becomes robust, that holds firm. In the Hebrew Bible, it appears in three main forms: simple (to be strong), intensive (to make strong, to fortify), and causative (to cause to become strong, to support). The richness of the word shows that strength in Hebrew is not just a matter of muscle: it is also the will that asserts itself, the heart that perseveres, the structures that are consolidated.
H2388G.emploi: This verb appears about 179 times in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the historical and prophetic books. It is very frequent in the Pentateuch, especially in the passages about the hardening of Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 7-14). It is also often found in exhortations: leaders encourage the people to be strong before battle (Joshua 1, 1 Chronicles 28). The word also designates concrete repairs — the work on the Temple during the time of Joash (2 Kings 12) — or the strengthening of royal power. Depending on the context, it can express a positive reinforcement (courage, consolidation) or negative (hardening of refusal, intensification of oppression).
H2388G.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer: it reminds us that true strength does not come primarily from the body or numbers, but from courage and trust in God. When Joshua feels weak in the face of conquest, God invites him to be strong — which means turning to Him. At the same time, the word warns: a heart can also harden, refuse God, and this hardening is serious. For the Christian, the challenge is to ask God to strengthen his heart in faith, rather than allowing it to harden in indifference.

sens: Take someone or something with force or authority
Hold firmly someone or something in one's hand or under control
Attach oneself to something, seize it tenaciously
Show strength, vigor, capable of resisting
Affirm, reinforce, give strength to someone
H2388H.detail:
1. Seize someone by the hand or arm, take them to lead them somewhere or stop them: the men "seized" Lot by the hand to save him from Sodom (Genesis 19:16). It is a physical, concrete gesture that involves a quick and firm grip.

2. Seize something vigorously, master it: Samson "seized" the two pillars of the temple to bring it down (Judges 16:26). The verb implies a takeover, often energetic.

3. Attach oneself to someone or something with constancy and refusal to let go: the Israelites "clung" to other gods (1 Kings 9:9), meaning they held on to them, remaining faithful by a strong bond.

4. Be or become strong, vigorous, capable of holding firm: "Hold on to" instruction, do not let it go, for it is your life (Proverbs 4:13) — here the verb means both "hold firmly" and "persevere without weakness."

5. Strengthen someone, give them courage and strength: the Lord "takes" the righteous by the hand (Isaiah 42:6), supports them, strengthens them in their mission.
H2388H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of physical strength and firmness. It opposes weakness, cowardice, and slackness. The same verb can describe the action of seizing (active sense), but also the state of becoming strong or stiffening (passive sense). The root can also evoke the idea of hardening, making rigid, like a substance that solidifies.
H2388H.emploi: This verb is one of the most common in the Old Testament: it appears about 70 times. It primarily describes concrete actions — taking someone by the hand (Genesis 19:16), seizing an object (Exodus 4:4, Judges 16:26) — but also moral or spiritual attitudes: clinging to someone or something (1 Kings 9:9), holding firm in faith (Proverbs 4:13), remaining steadfast in obedience (Isaiah 56:2). The warrior context also shows it to describe strength and courage in battle (Jeremiah 6:23). In the Psalms and Isaiah, it often expresses the protective or supporting hand of the Lord toward His people.
H2388H.portee: This word speaks to every believer of two great realities: on one hand, the courage and perseverance that the life of faith requires — "holding firm," "not letting go" in the face of temptations or trials; on the other hand, the support of God who "takes" His child by the hand and "strengthens" him in his weakness. It also invites us to examine what we truly "cling to" — other gods, our own strengths, or the living God.

sens: Become strong, robust, or vigorous
Hold firmly, not let go
Support, encourage someone
Make stable, firmly establish
Press, insist forcefully
Become serious or severe
H2388I.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of physical strength increasing: to become strong, robust, capable of resisting. It is the image of a person or thing growing in power. In 2 Kings 15:19, King Menahem seeks to "strengthen the kingship in his hands," meaning to make it unshakeable and enduring.

2. To hold something firmly, not to let it go, to retain it with strength. It conveys the idea of a solid grip, a hold that does not yield.

3. To give moral strength to someone, to encourage, to support them in difficulty. Someone who "presses" or "troubles" acts with insistence, as in 2 Kings 4:8 where the woman of Shunem "pressed" Elisha to eat at her home, showing affectionate and caring insistence.

4. To make something stable, solid, durable. It is to establish firmly, without allowing for wavering or change.

5. The idea of urgency, of pressure: to press someone, to trouble them, to insist with them.

6. To become serious, severe, difficult to bear: the word that "presses" can be one that threatens or weighs heavily.
H2388I.origine: The Hebrew root חזק (ḥazaq) fundamentally expresses the idea of solidity and firmness. It appears in everyday life: a solid grip, a firm embrace, a word that imposes itself. The family of the word includes חֹזֶק (ḥozèq, "strength"), חֶזְקוּת (ḥezqout, "power"), and the adjective חָזָק (ḥazaq, "strong"). It is an ancient and widely used word in biblical Hebrew to express solidity and power in all its forms.
H2388I.emploi: This verb often appears in the Hebrew Bible with nuances depending on the context. The three provided usages show this variety: in Deuteronomy 12:23, the command "take care" means "abstain firmly" or "be careful not to"; in 2 Kings 4:8, the woman "presses" Elisha with caring insistence; in 2 Kings 15:19, the king "strengthens" his throne, meaning he makes it stable and secure. The verb can thus mean "to hold firmly," "to insist," or "to establish solidly" depending on whether it involves a moral restriction, an interpersonal action, or a political matter. In all cases, the idea of strength, firmness, or solidity remains central.
H2388I.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that faith requires moral firmness: to firmly guard against certain things, to stand strong in the face of temptations, to establish one's life on a solid foundation. It also evokes mutual encouragement—how we can support and strengthen one another. And it speaks of stability: not in self-isolation, but in an assurance rooted in God, capable of standing firm in trials.

sens: Be strong, become strong
Overcome, prevail over someone
Hold firm, persist, be obstinate
Seize, take possession
Make strong, give strength or courage
H2388J.detail:
1. Be strong, become strong: the word describes a physical or moral strength that develops. The idea is one of growth in power, of someone or something becoming solid. David was "stronger" than Goliath (1 Samuel 17:50): the young shepherd, armed only with a sling, overcame the giant.

2. Overcome, prevail over someone: this is the consequence of that strength—one prevails against an opponent. Those who followed Omri "prevailed" over those who followed Tibni (1 Kings 16:22): Omri's group became more powerful and won the succession struggle.

3. Hold firm, persist, be obstinate: strength becomes a will that does not bend. King David "persisted" in his order for a census (2 Samuel 24:4), despite reluctance: he stood firm in his decision.

4. Seize, take possession: strength allows one to grasp and dominate. Solomon "seized" Hamath toward Zobah (2 Chronicles 8:3): he conquered and occupied those cities.

5. Make strong, give strength or courage: this is the action of one person on another to support and strengthen them in their resolve or state.
H2388J.origine: The word חָזַק comes from a root that evokes hardness, solidity, and rigor. It is related to the idea of something hardening, becoming firm, and stable—like a hand that grips, a resolution that will not bend. The word appears in several forms: the simple form ("to be strong"), the causative form ("to make strong"), and the reflexive form ("to strengthen oneself"). It is a fundamental word in biblical Hebrew to express strength in all its forms.
H2388J.emploi: The verb חָזַק appears 12 times in the provided usages, especially in the historical accounts of the Kings and Chronicles. It describes both physical or military strength (David against Goliath, Solomon's conquests) and strength of character—the king's determination to persist in his orders despite opposition. The word can also express military success: to "prevail" is the result of being stronger. Often, it involves a comparison or a victory: who is stronger? who wins? The royal context shows that this strength is primarily of interest in political and military power.
H2388J.portee: Understanding this word helps to see how the Bible speaks of strength—not as arrogance, but as the ability to hold firm, to prevail, and to seize what is promised. For the Christian, the verb to strengthen reminds us that true strength comes from God, who supports those who trust Him; it is always put to the service of a purpose (conquest, kingdom, will).

sens: Become strong, gain strength
Make something solid, stable, resistant
Give courage, determination to someone
Stand firm, hold fast in the face of adversity
Support, maintain, uphold
H2388K.detail:
1. Become strong, gain strength: this conveys the idea of a strength that grows and asserts itself. In 2 Chronicles 32:5, Hezekiah "took courage" — literally he became strong internally — in the face of the Assyrian threat; this courage enabled him to act.
2. Make something solid, stable, resistant: one fortifies a wall, a structure, a covenant by making it unshakeable. The same verse shows Hezekiah who "fortified" the walls of Jerusalem, reinforcing them against the enemy.
3. Give courage, determination to someone: this means to encourage someone morally, making them capable of persevering. In Daniel 11:32, those who know God act with "firmness" — they remain unshakeable in their faith despite temptations.
4. Stand firm, hold fast in the face of adversity: to strengthen oneself, refuse to yield, maintain one's integrity. This is the moral strength that refuses to bend.
5. Support, maintain, uphold: a wall is repaired by being "supported" solidly; a person supports themselves by standing firm. In Nehemiah 5:16, they work on the "repair" — the restoration and support — of the wall.
H2388K.origine: The Hebrew verb חָזַק (ḥazaq) expresses the idea of strength and solidity. It comes from a very ancient root that paints the image of something hardening, becoming tight, compact — like a rope that is pulled or a muscle that contracts. The Hebrew word לֵב (lev, heart) — the center of will — often appears with this verb: "to harden the heart" means to become obstinate. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the idea of inner, moral, and physical strength.
H2388K.emploi: The verb חָזַק appears more than 240 times in the Old Testament, in all literary genres and historical contexts. It primarily denotes physical strength: to fortify a wall, a rampart. But its richest usage is moral and spiritual: to take courage in the face of danger (Hezekiah confronting Assyria), to act with firmness in faith (those who know God in Daniel), to persevere in obedience. The verb can also express the hardening of the heart — when Pharaoh "hardened" — showing that strength can become pride and rebellion. The nuance depends on the context: with an external object (wall, army), it is materially reinforcing; with a person or the heart, it is morally strengthening.
H2388K.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith is not a fragile emotion, but a strength that solidifies and cultivates. Knowing God is not enough: one must "act with firmness," that is, live their faith with determination, without wavering under pressure. The verb also invites seeking from God the spiritual strength to persevere, especially in times of trial — the same strength that supported the walls of Jerusalem can support the believer in their faith struggle.

sens: Having great physical or moral strength
Violent, intense, vigorous
Difficult to defeat, to surpass
Having authority, influence
Firm, unshakeable
Severe, rigorous
H2389.detail:
1. Strong primarily means one who possesses great power or remarkable physical strength. It is the strength of a man capable of great exploits or a numerous armed people. Jeremiah 31:11 speaks of a "stronger than he" to designate one who could dominate.
2. The word also describes the intensity of an action or phenomenon: a strong hand acting with power, a violent wind, a resounding noise. Exodus 10:19 mentions "a strong west wind" that carries away the locusts.
3. Strong characterizes what resists, what does not yield easily: a solid object like a cast-iron mirror (Job 37:18), or a people difficult to subjugate.
4. The word also designates one who exercises power or authority, one whose will must be respected, particularly the king of Egypt who refuses to let Israel go (Exodus 3:19).
5. Strong can mean firm, stable, unshakeable: that which is established solidly and does not waver.
6. Finally, the word applies to what is severe or rigorous: a strong judgment, a harsh or inflexible word, like the obstinate Israelites to whom God speaks in Ezekiel 3:7.
H2389.origine: The Hebrew word חָזָק comes from a root that evokes the idea of grasping, holding firmly, from which derives the meaning of strength and solidity. Words of the same family express strengthening, hardening, reinforcing. In Aramaic, a similar form also expresses strength. This root is very ancient in Semitic and paints the image of a solid grip, a hold that does not let go.
H2389.emploi: The word appears 54 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical books (Exodus, Deuteronomy, Samuel, Kings), prophetic (Jeremiah, Ezekiel), and wisdom literature (Job, Psalms). It primarily describes God's powerful acts: His strong hand delivers Israel from Egypt (Exodus 6:1, Deuteronomy 4:34), His arm rescues the people (Deuteronomy 5:15). It also qualifies enemies (Numbers 13:31: "this people is strong") or obstacles (Numbers 20:20: Edom presents itself armed). The word applies to physically solid people like Caleb, who remained vigorous until 85 years old (Joshua 14:11), or to intense physical phenomena like wind and drought. It can also describe moral or spiritual resistance: the Israelites are "a nation with a hard forehead and an obstinate heart" (Ezekiel 2:4).
H2389.portee: Understanding that God is strong — that His mighty hand acts on behalf of His faithful — strengthens the believer's trust in times of doubt. This word reminds us that true strength is neither in numbers nor in weapons, but in God who delivers and protects His people. It also challenges: the hardness of heart and obstinacy of men before God is a "strength" that breaks against divine power.

sens: Increasing in intensity, strength, power
Growing progressively
H2390.detail:
1. The word describes something that becomes more intense or more powerful. In Exodus 19:19, the sound of the trumpet "grew louder and louder": it is a noise that increases in volume and power as it continues. It is a progressive intensification.
2. It can also express growth or strengthening over time. In 2 Samuel 3:1, David "became stronger and stronger" during the civil war: his military and political power was steadily increasing, while that of Saul was diminishing. The word emphasizes movement, continuous change towards greater strength.
H2390.origine: The word comes from the root חזק (hazaq), which means "to be strong, to strengthen, to gain strength." This root evokes the idea of something hardening, becoming solid and resistant, like a fortress or a wall. The form here is a comparative: it is the "stronger" form that compares two states. The same root is found in other biblical words to describe physical, moral, or spiritual strength.
H2390.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible according to the provided usages. In the first case (Exodus 19:19), it describes a natural phenomenon: a sound amplification. The sound of the trumpet that resounds at Sinai becomes progressively more powerful, creating an impressive and solemn atmosphere for the theophany. In the second case (2 Samuel 3:1), it pertains to a political and military evolution: David grows in power during the war against the house of Saul. The context highlights an inexorable movement, a dynamic where one actor weakens while the other strengthens. Both usages share the idea of progression, of increasing intensification.
H2390.portee: This word reminds us that power increases gradually: it does not arise suddenly, but asserts itself step by step. For David, this regular growth foreshadows the establishment of the kingdom that God promised him. For the reader, it shows that God can strengthen His people slowly but surely, and that final victory is often a matter of perseverance and trust in His promise.

sens: Physical or moral power
Firmness, solidity
Support, assistance
H2391.detail:
1. Strength is the physical or moral power that enables one to act, resist, and persevere. In Psalm 18:2, the psalmist calls God "my strength": he expresses that God is his power, the one who supports him and enables him to face trials.
2. Strength can also refer to the firmness and solidity of something — that which does not yield or collapse. It is the image of an unshakeable structure.
3. Figuratively, strength becomes a support, a foundation on which one relies in times of need. God is this ultimate support for those who cry out to Him.
H2391.origine: This Hebrew word expresses the idea of strength, power, and solidity. Its root refers to what is firm, stable, and robust. In biblical Hebrew, strength can be physical (that of a fortress, that of a warrior) or spiritual (that of God, that of trust in Him). The word always evokes a tangible reality: one can lean on it.
H2391.emploi: The word appears once in the provided Segond translation, in Psalm 18:2. It is the cry of love from the psalmist who recognizes in God his personal strength, without which he would be powerless. This context of prayer and intimacy with God shows that the strength in question here is not a military or political strength, but a spiritual, moral, and intimate strength: the certainty that God is there, that one can count on Him.
H2391.portee: Calling God one's strength is to acknowledge that one can do nothing without Him, but also that with Him one can face anything. It is an act of faith that transforms weakness into trust. For today's believer, this word reminds us that our true power does not come from ourselves, but from the one who loves and supports us.

sens: Physical power or capacity to act
Vigor, energy to accomplish an action
Solidity, firmness of a structure or an army
Political or military power of a kingdom
H2392.detail: 1. Strength is the concrete power of the one who acts: it is that of the hand of God that brings Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 13:3 — "by His mighty hand"). 2. It also refers to the capacity to achieve something, the energy exerted: the Israelites attribute their own strength to the acquisition of power (Amos 6:13). 3. Strength can be that of an army, its solidity and military force: it is what God overthrows among the kingdoms of nations (Haggai 2:22 — "the strength of the kingdoms"). 4. Figuratively, it represents the power of a reign or political authority capable of conquering and dominating.
H2392.origine: The Hebrew word חֹזֶק (chozèq) comes from a root that means "to seize" or "to hold firmly." It carries the image of firmness and solidity: one who has strength "holds on," does not yield. The same root produces words in the family that express reinforcement, strengthening, or tenacity. In the Greek Septuagint, this word is often rendered by "ischys" (strength, power).
H2392.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, primarily concentrated in Exodus and the prophets. In Exodus 13:3, 13:14, and 13:16, it characterizes the mighty hand of the Lord that liberates Israel from slavery: it is God's sovereign strength in action. In Amos 6:13, the Israelites pride themselves on their own strength (military or economic), which provokes prophetic criticism. In Haggai 2:22, the strength of human kingdoms is what God overthrows at the end of times. The word is thus used for both God and the nations, but with a very different connotation: in God, it saves; in the nations, it can become pride.
H2392.portee: This word reveals that true strength belongs only to God: it is His power that liberates and overthrows. It invites the believer not to rely on human, military, or economic strength, but on that of the Lord. For the Christian, this resonates with the Gospel: true victory comes not from the power of the world, but from God who acts in ways often contrary to the logic of earthly power.

sens: Physical power, capacity to act with vigor
State of solidity or stability acquired
Domination or power over others
Divine grip, seizing
H2393.detail:
1. Strength is primarily physical power, the vigor that allows one to act effectively. It is what makes someone or something capable and robust. When Rehoboam "had acquired strength" (2 Chronicles 12:1), it was because he had consolidated his royal power and his ability to govern.
2. The word also denotes the state of stability or solidity: when a king "was powerful" (2 Chronicles 26:16), he had strengthened his throne and secured his authority. It is an acquired strength, which has crystallized.
3. Strength also becomes a domination exercised over others. Daniel 11:2 speaks of a king who will be "powerful by his riches": his wealth gives him political influence over other kingdoms.
4. In Isaiah 8:11, the hand of the Lord "seizes" the prophet: here, strength takes on the meaning of a divine grip, a possession that imposes itself on body and spirit.
H2393.origine: The Hebrew word חֶזְקָה comes from the root חזק (hazaq), which means "to strengthen," "to become strong," "to hold firmly." This root evokes the image of a hand that seizes, of a man who stands firmly on his legs. The same family is found in other forms in the Bible: חָזָק (strong), חוֹזֶק (strength), חִזִּק (to strengthen). The word always paints the idea of solidity, a firm grip, a hold that one exercises or undergoes.
H2393.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical and prophetic books. In 2 Chronicles 12:1 and 26:16, it describes the strength of a king who has consolidated his power: as soon as he feels capable, pride seizes him and he sins. In Isaiah 8:11, strength becomes that of God who "seizes" the prophet like a hand that grips him. In Daniel 11:2, the wealth of a Persian king becomes a source of political power. The word thus varies: political strength of a monarch, divine strength or grip, economic power. But the central idea remains that of an acquired solidity, a firm hold.
H2393.portee: This word teaches the believer that human strength, once attained, often becomes a temptation: Rehoboam and Uzziah, as soon as they feel powerful, abandon the law of God and rise up in pride. It is a warning: success and power are never an end in themselves, but a service that must be carried out under the gaze of God. Conversely, when strength is that of God who seizes the prophet, it becomes a grace: it dispossesses us of ourselves to place us in the hands of the Lord.

sens: Brute physical force, coercive power
Oppression exercised by force
Energetic intensity, strength of feeling or expression
H2394.detail: 1. Violence primarily refers to brute physical force, the power to constrain through might. In Judges 4:3, it is the strength of Jabin that "oppressed" Israel for twenty years — an overwhelming domination exercised by military and political power. 2. The word also describes oppression exercised with harshness and severity.
