In Ezekiel 34:4, the shepherds "ruled" the flock "with violence and with harshness" instead of caring for and feeding it — this is abusive and cruel authority. 3. It can finally express the strength, the intensity of an action or a feeling: in Jonah 3:8, the Ninevites cry out to God "with force" — a fervent, energetic prayer that springs from the heart. In 1 Samuel 2:16, "taking by force" means to seize by power, without permission.
H2394.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes strength, firmness, solidity. It is found in words denoting "strength," "power," or the action of "fortifying oneself." The basic image is that of raw energy, a power that acts without restraint — hence the meaning of domination, oppression, or more broadly, any force that is exerted strongly.
H2394.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. In Judges and Samuel, it describes military oppression or unjust appropriation by force. In Ezekiel, it characterizes the bad governance of shepherds who mistreat the people. In Jonah, the only context where the tone changes, "crying with force" expresses the intensity of a sincere supplication. The word thus oscillates between abuse of power and the simple intensity of effort.
H2394.portee: The violence that oppresses the weak is a sin against God's justice — this is what the prophets denounce. But the word also reminds us that there is a just and good force: that of crying out to God "with force," of pleading fervently. It invites us to denounce all abusive domination, and to use our own strength, our resources, and our authority, not to enslave, but to protect and serve.

sens: Benjamite during the divided monarchy
H2395.detail: Hizki is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Elpahal and brother to several other Benjamites: Eber, Mischam, Chemed, Berijah, Shema, Zebadiah, Meshullam, Heber, Ichmaraï, Izlia, and Jobab (1 Chronicles 8:17). His name means "strong" or "mighty" in Hebrew.
H2395.origine: The name Hizki comes from a Hebrew root that expresses strength and power. It belongs to a family of Hebrew names from that time that celebrate divine strength or human vigor. This name was borne by a descendant of Shaaraim, in the genealogical lineage of the Benjamites.
H2395.emploi: Hizki appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:17, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. He is part of a enumeration of the sons of Elpahal, with no other details about his life or actions. These genealogical lists reveal the importance given to family lineages and tribal identity in Israel at the time of the writing of Chronicles.

sens: The twelfth king of the kingdom of Judah
A king who eradicated idolatry and reformed the worship of the Lord
A king confronted with the Assyrian invasion and saved by divine intervention
A man who was healed of a deadly illness through prayer
A king known for his piety and wealth
H2396G.detail:
1. Hezekiah is the twelfth king of the kingdom of Judah, son of King Ahaz (2 Kings 16:20). He marks a turning point in the religious history of the country after the idolatrous reign of his father.

2. Unlike his father, Hezekiah destroys the idolatrous altars and restores the true worship of the Lord (2 Kings 21:3 shows that his son Manasseh will rebuild what Hezekiah had destroyed). He organizes religious festivals and reforms of worship documented in detail in 2 Chronicles 29-31.

3. His reign coincides with the formidable invasion of the Assyrian king Sennacherib (2 Kings 18-19). Faced with this peril, Hezekiah seeks the Lord's help through the prophet Isaiah, and Jerusalem is miraculously delivered.

4. Hezekiah falls gravely ill and receives the promise of healing from the Lord through Isaiah (2 Kings 20:1-11). His prayer and repentance save him from a foretold death.

5. The text emphasizes his wealth and glory: "Hezekiah had much wealth and glory. He made treasures of silver, gold, and precious stones" (2 Chronicles 32:27). He undertakes infrastructure projects, notably the Siloam aqueduct (2 Chronicles 32:30).
H2396G.origine: The name Hezekiah means "the Lord is my strength" or "the Lord has strengthened me": it expresses a trust in divine power and help. This meaning of the name illustrates the character of the king, a man of faith who relies on God in crises. In Hebrew, the name is written חִזְקִיָּהוּ (Chizqiyyahu), composed of חִזְקָה (chizqah), "strength," and יָהּ, the shortened divine name. Several members of his family bore names evoking the Lord, reflecting the piety of his lineage.
H2396G.emploi: Hezekiah appears more than a hundred times in the Bible, mainly in 2 Kings 18-20 and 2 Chronicles 29-32, as well as in the prophecies of Isaiah (Isaiah 1:1, 37:5). 2 Kings presents him mainly in his confrontations with Assyria and his illness, while 2 Chronicles details his religious reforms, including the purification of the temple and the organization of Passover. Proverbs 25:1 mentions his scribes who transcribed proverbs of Solomon. The prophet Isaiah accompanies him in his major spiritual crises (2 Kings 19:5, 20:11). Manasseh, his son, represents the antithesis of his piety: he will restore all that Hezekiah had abolished (2 Chronicles 33:3). Hezekiah thus embodies the faithful king of late Judah, contrasting with the unfaithful kings who preceded or followed him.
H2396G.portee: Hezekiah shows that a sincere return to God produces concrete fruits: moral reform, deliverance from enemies, and material blessing. His example teaches that confident prayer in trial attracts divine intervention. However, 2 Chronicles 32:24-26 also reveals his human fragility: after his healing, his heart became proud, and then he repented. His story reminds us that even the most pious king remains dependent on God's grace and must fight against pride.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah living during the divided monarchy
Son of Neariah and brother of Eljoenaï and Azrikam
Descendant of David
H2396H.detail: Hezekiah is a man from the tribe of Judah whose name is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 3:23, where he is presented as one of the three sons of Neariah. He appears in the genealogy of the royal house of David, indicating that he belongs to an important family in Judah during the divided monarchy. Although little information is given about his personal life, his inclusion in this genealogy suggests that he held a recognized place in the history of God's people.
H2396H.origine: The name Hezekiah comes from the Hebrew חִזְקִיָּהוּ (Hizkiyahou), which literally means "Jehovah is my strength" or "Jehovah is my fortress." It is composed of the divine name Yah (God) and the verb חזק (hazaq), which means "to be strong, to strengthen oneself." This type of theophoric name, where the divine name is linked to a divine quality, was common among the Hebrews and expressed the father's trust at the time of his child's birth in God's strength and protection.
H2396H.emploi: Hezekiah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:23. He is listed in the genealogy of the descendants of David, enumerated among the sons of Neariah with his brothers Eljoenaï and Azrikam. This unique mention, although brief, situates him in the historical context of the divided monarchy in Judah. He should not be confused with King Hezekiah (Hezekiah II), the twelfth king of Judah known for his religious reforms, who is a distinct and much more significant figure in biblical history.

sens: Head of a family among the exiles returned from Babylon
H2396I.detail: 1. Hezekiah is a man who lived at the time of the return from exile, after the Babylonian captivity. He is mentioned in Nehemiah 7:21 as the head of a family whose ninety-eight members returned to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple and the city.
H2396I.origine: The name means "The Lord is my strength" in Hebrew. It is the same name as that of the great king Hezekiah of Judah, but borne here by a much less famous man, a simple head of household among the repatriates. The form "Hezekiah" is that of the French translation; the Hebrew is chizqiyyahu.
H2396I.emploi: Hezekiah appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 7:21, in the list of those who returned from exile with Nehemiah. These genealogical lists in the book of Nehemiah record the names of the heads of families and the number of their descendants, which shows the importance of this return for the identity of the restored Jewish people. He is an ancestor of the Judeans who rebuilt the community after the Babylonian exile.
H2396I.portee: This passage reminds us that even the minor figures in biblical history are part of God's plan. The return from exile was an act of grace from the Lord towards His people, and each family that returned, led by a leader like Hezekiah, represented the hope of restoration. It is a lesson in faithfulness and continuity of God's people.

sens: Head of a family among the exiles returned to Jerusalem
H2396J.detail: 1. Hezekiah is a man who is among the heads of families who signed the solemn covenant with God upon the return from exile to Jerusalem, in the days of Nehemiah. His name appears in the list of signatories of this solemn document that commits the people to live according to the Law of Moses (Nehemiah 10:17).
H2396J.origine: The name Hezekiah means "Jehovah is my strength." In Hebrew, חִזְקִיָּהוּ (chizqiyyah) combines two elements: חוֹזֵק (chozek), strength or vigor, and יָהּ (yah), the abbreviated name of God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God and expresses trust in divine strength.
H2396J.emploi: Hezekiah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the book of Nehemiah, among the signatories of the covenant of the return from exile. He is not identified with the other Hezekiahs or Hizkiah of the Old Testament (notably the king of the same name from the 8th century B.C., who does not appear in this passage). This Hezekiah of Nehemiah 10:17 simply represents one of the many heads of families who, at the time of Nehemiah, solemnly committed to uphold the covenant with the Lord.

sens: Ancestor of Zephaniah the prophet
Father of Amariah
H2396K.detail:
1. Hezekiah is the great-great-grandfather of the prophet Zephaniah, whose genealogy traces back four generations to this Hezekiah (Zephaniah 1:1). This is a simple genealogical mention that situates the prophet within a respectable family lineage.
2. Hezekiah is the father of Amariah, whose name means "the Lord is my Lord," indicating a family devoted to the worship of the true God.
H2396K.origine: The name Hezekiah means "The Lord is my strength" or "Jehovah is my strength." It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name and expresses a confession of faith: the one who bears it acknowledges that God is his source of strength and power. This name was borne by several figures in Israel's history, the most famous being King Hezekiah of Judah in the 8th century B.C.
H2396K.emploi: This Hezekiah appears only once in the Bible, in Zephaniah 1:1, where he is named in the genealogy of the prophet Zephaniah. He was an ancestor of the prophet living during the time of the divided monarchy, according to the source definition. Unlike King Hezekiah of Judah, this figure is known only by his place in the genealogical lineage of the prophet, suggesting that he came from a family of faithful servants of the Lord.

sens: ring or hook used for ornament or fastening
ring passed through the nose of a captive or animal to dominate it
bracelet or jewelry worn on the wrist
H2397.detail:
1. A loop is a ring or a metal hook: it is an object that can be held in hand or threaded through. In Exodus 35:22, men and women bring loops of gold among the materials to construct the tabernacle, alongside rings and bracelets — these are pieces of jewelry.
2. The loop becomes an instrument of control when it is passed through the nose of a captive or animal. The Lord announces to the king of Assyria: "I will put my loop in your nostrils" (2 Kings 19:28, Isaiah 37:29), an image of total domination, like that of a shepherd holding his animal by a rope. Ezekiel uses the same image for a lion caught in a trap (19:4, 19:9) and for Pharaoh (29:4): the loop in the nose symbolizes humiliation and loss of freedom.
3. As a bracelet, the loop is an ornament of the wrist, part of the adornment of the offerers (Exodus 35:22).
H2397.origine: The Hebrew word חַח (chach) literally means "hook" or "ring." It evokes the action of hooking, seizing, or holding. The same root underlies several objects that hold or suspend: anything that catches. The word is used for all rings that serve to hold or adorn, from personal jewelry to the hook of domination by conquerors.
H2397.emploi: This word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophets. One occurrence concerns a gift of gold to the tabernacle (Exodus 35:22). The other six are metaphors of power and captivity: God threatens the king of Assyria with putting a loop in his nostrils and dragging him like an animal (2 Kings 19:28 and its parallel Isaiah 37:29). Ezekiel uses the image twice for a lion caught in a trap and taken into captivity (19:4 and 19:9), and then for Pharaoh of Egypt drawn from his rivers (29:4). Each time, the loop in the nose is the sign of complete defeat and the domination of the victor over the vanquished.
H2397.portee: This word sheds light on how the Bible speaks of God's judgment and victory. The loop in the nose transforms a powerful enemy into a humiliated captive, showing that the proudest of conquerors becomes docile in the hands of the Lord. For the believer, it is a reminder that true power is not in pride or rebellion, but in submission to God.

sens: Missing the target, failing to reach the intended goal
Transgressing God's law or will, doing evil
Incurring guilt and its consequences
Offering a sacrifice for sin, a purification offering
Causing or leading someone to sin
H2398.detail:
1. The Hebrew word first evokes the image of a warrior missing his shot: missing the target, failing to hit the goal. This is the basic image. In Judges 20:16, it speaks of slingers who "did not miss" the target — it is the same word applied to the bow and arrow.
2. But the meaning quickly expands into the moral and religious realm: to sin is to go astray, to transgress what God commands, to do evil intentionally or out of ignorance. In Genesis 20:6, God tells Abimelech that He prevented him from "sinning" against Him by taking Sarah. In 1 Samuel 2:25, to sin "against the Lord" is to violate His commandments.
3. Sin also has a judicial dimension: it is to "incur guilt," to become guilty, and thus to deserve punishment. In Exodus 32:33, God says: "Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book" — sin leads to condemnation.
4. In certain contexts (notably in Leviticus), the word designates the offering or purification sacrifice brought to atone for the wrong committed: "to make a sacrifice for sin." In Leviticus 4:3, it refers to the offering of the people who have committed a fault.
5. Finally, when the verb is in a causative form (to cause to do), it means to lead someone to sin, to push them toward evil. In 2 Kings 10:31, it is said that Jeroboam "had caused" Israel to sin — he had led them into it.
H2398.origine: The word comes from a root that literally means "to miss, to fail." This image of a missed shot then applies to anything that deviates from the straight path: morally, to sin is to deviate, to miss the right way. The family of the word includes the noun "sin" (חָטָא khata, the fault itself) and various verbal forms depending on the manner of acting (doing evil oneself, purifying, leading others to evil, etc.). It is a fundamental word in the Hebrew Bible, appearing more than 220 times.
H2398.emploi: The verb "to sin" is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible (220 occurrences). It can be found everywhere: in Genesis when Pharaoh acknowledges his wrongdoing (Exodus 9:27, 10:16), in the laws of Leviticus that enumerate sins and their purification sacrifices (Leviticus 4-5), in the history of kings who do evil (2 Kings 10:31), in prayers where the people confess their faults (Jeremiah 14:7, 1 Samuel 7:6). The meaning nuances according to the context: first transgressing (Genesis 20:6), then incurring guilt (Exodus 32:33), then bringing an offering (Leviticus 5), and even leading others to evil (2 Kings 10:31). In the accounts of confessions (Numbers 12:11, Judges 10:10), the people or individuals "confess" their sin. The word is central to the entire theology of the Covenant: to sin is to break the bond with God.
H2398.portee: This word reveals an essential biblical reality: sin is not primarily a vague fault or bad luck, but the act of missing the goal, deviating from the path that God proposes. The Bible does not hide the fact that humans regularly sin, and it organizes a whole system of offerings so that the sinner can be reconciled with his God. This shows both the holiness of God (He does not tolerate deviation) and His grace (He offers a way of repair). For the Christian, understanding that to sin is to "miss the target" helps to see that moral life is not a game of arbitrary prohibitions, but alignment with God's plan and love.

sens: Transgression of divine law, disobedience to God
Guilt and moral responsibility that ensues
Consequence and punishment of sin
Evil act or intention at its root
H2399.detail:
1. Sin is primarily the act of disobeying God, violating His commandments. It is missing the target that God proposes to us. Thus, Isaiah 1:18 speaks of sins that become white as snow: the Bible views sin as something real and serious that must be forgiven.
2. The word also designates moral guilt, the responsibility of the one who has sinned. When the chief cupbearer says in Genesis 41:9 that he wants to recall the "remembrance" of his fault, he acknowledges that he bears the guilt of his evil act.
3. Sin brings consequences: punishment or penalty. Numbers 9:13 states that a man "will bear the penalty of his sin" if he does not celebrate the Passover; Deuteronomy 24:15 warns that one will incur a sin if one refuses the wages of a poor worker.
4. Sin reaches the deep intention: Isaiah 31:7 speaks of "criminal hands," showing that sin originates from the heart of man before manifesting in his acts.
H2399.origine: The Hebrew word chet comes from a root that literally means "to miss the target." It appears in other forms of the verb meaning "to fail" or "to miss." This image of a missed shot well expresses the nature of sin: man aimed for good, justice, but he deviated from the path that God showed him. The Aramaic, a closely related language, has an equivalent form (chati) to express the same reality.
H2399.emploi: The word chet is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible (33 occurrences attested here). It is found everywhere: in the Law (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), in history (Kings, Chronicles), in prayers and meditation (Psalms), among the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Lamentations). Its main meaning is always "sin" or "transgression," but depending on the context, it emphasizes either the guilty act, the guilt of the one who committed it, or the punishment that results. Most of the time it describes the sin of man or the people before God; sometimes it also designates human crime (Deuteronomy 19:15 states that a crime is established only on the testimony of witnesses).
H2399.portee: The word chet confronts us with an undeniable truth: sin is real, it separates us from God, and it has consequences. But the Bible does not leave the reader alone in the face of this guilt. Isaiah 1:18 promises that red sins become white as snow through divine forgiveness. For the Christian, this word reveals the seriousness of evil, but also the need to turn to God for redemption and renewal.
